# MICHAEL ISINGRIN SENDS GREETINGS TO THE READER.
<note>The original Latin header "S D." abbreviates "Salutem Dicit," a formal greeting meaning "wishes health" or "sends greetings."</note>

Perhaps you wonder, fair reader, by what reasoning we have been led to present these small books to you, especially at this time, when both piety itself and—along with it—sound studies <note>A reference to "studia humanitatis" or the liberal arts</note> have scarcely been reborn before they have begun to fall into common contempt. You shall hear the reason. This age is, I confess, in a deplorable state; but for this very reason, we thought it our duty, as much as lies within us, to preserve for posterity—lest he perish entirely—an author from the deepest antiquity. This author, through so many centuries far more hostile than our own and through so many foreign languages, has finally been gifted to the Latin world. Having remained hidden meanwhile among the most learned and holiest of men, he has been delivered to us from Egypt, as if passed from hand to hand. 

The cause of this plan was not only a holy reverence for venerable antiquity, but also the persistent demands of certain people who wished to see this truly <term>Thrice-Greatest Hermes</term> <note>original: "ter maximum Hermetem," referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> published because of his rarity. He is one whom the Egyptians and "barbarians" <note>In this context, "barbarians" refers to non-Greek speakers, often implying the ancient Persians or Chaldeans</note> first, and soon even the early Christian theologians, admired with great astonishment because of his unique and theological teaching. Persuaded by these same reasons, we have added Iamblichus and Proclus, both commendable for their erudition and antiquity; they lean upon this man as if upon the very foundation of their assertions. 

Farewell, dearest reader, and embrace our zeal toward good literature.

<summary>The printer Michael Isingrin justifies publishing the works of Hermes Trismegistus, Iamblichus, and Proclus as an act of cultural preservation during a time of religious and intellectual decline. He emphasizes the ancient Egyptian origins of the text and its long history of being passed down through holy and learned men.</summary>

<keywords>Michael Isingrin, Hermes Trismegistus, Iamblichus, Proclus, Basel, Renaissance printing, Neoplatonism, Hermeticism, preservation of antiquity</keywords>

# THE PREFACE OF MARSILIO FICINO
# THE FLORENTINE, ON THE *PYMANDER*
# OF MERCURIUS TRISMEGISTUS, TO COSIMO DE' MEDICI,
# FATHER OF HIS COUNTRY.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring two figures, possibly cherubs or mythological beings, amidst foliage.</image-desc>At that time when Moses was born, Atlas the astrologer flourished—the brother of Prometheus the Natural Philosopher <note>original: "Physici," referring to a student of nature or physics</note> and the maternal grandfather of the elder Mercury, whose grandson was Mercurius Trismegistus. <margin>Jerome [says] that he was a contemporary of Moses, as some believe, vol. 1. <unclear>sec. v. fol. 213. tal. Tem pungina.</unclear></margin> Moreover, Augustine writes this about him; although Cicero and Lactantius maintain that there were five Mercuries in succession, and that the fifth was he who was called Theuth <note>A name for the Egyptian god Thoth</note> by the Egyptians, but Trismegistus by the Greeks. They claim that this man killed Argus, ruled over the Egyptians, and handed down laws and letters to them. Furthermore, he established the characters of their letters in the shapes of animals and trees. <note>A reference to Egyptian hieroglyphs, which Renaissance scholars believed were mystical symbols representing natural objects.</note> He was held in such great veneration by men that he was counted among the gods. Numerous temples were constructed to his divinity. Out of a certain reverence, it was not permitted for the common people to pronounce his proper name casually or rashly. The first month of the year among the Egyptians is named after him; a town was founded by him, which even now is called Hermopolis <note>original: "ἑρμόπολις," meaning "City of Hermes"</note>, that is, the City of Mercury. Indeed, they called him Trismegistus, which means "thrice-greatest," because [he was] both a philosopher

<summary>In this preface, Marsilio Ficino establishes the historical and divine lineage of Hermes Trismegistus, identifying him as a contemporary of Moses and the founder of Egyptian civilization, law, and writing.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Hermes Trismegistus, Cosimo de' Medici, Moses, Egyptian mythology, Hieroglyphs, Hermopolis, Thoth</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page continues the explanation of why Hermes was called "Trismegistus" (Thrice-Greatest). The previous page ended with "...because [he was] both [the greatest] philosopher..."</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

greatest, and the greatest priest, and the greatest king. For it was the custom among the Egyptians (as Plato writes) to choose priests from the rank of philosophers, and then to elect a king from the assembly of priests. This man, therefore, just as he had surpassed all other philosophers in sharp intelligence and learning, was subsequently appointed a priest, where he excelled all other priests in the holiness of his life and the worship of divine things. Finally, having attained royal dignity, he eclipsed the glory of all preceding kings through his administration of the laws and his great deeds; thus, he was deservedly called "thrice greatest." 

Among philosophers, he was the first to turn from the study of physics <note>original: *physicis*, referring here to natural philosophy or the study of the physical world</note> and mathematics to the contemplation of divine things. He was the first to discourse most wisely on the majesty of God, the order of demons <note>Ficino uses "demons" in the classical Neoplatonic sense: intermediary spirits between humans and gods, not necessarily evil beings</note>, and the transmutations of souls. Therefore, he was called the first author of theology. 

Orpheus followed him, holding the second place in this ancient theology. Aglaophemus was initiated into the sacred rites of Orpheus. Pythagoras succeeded Aglaophemus in theology, and he was followed by Philolaus, the teacher of our divine Plato. Thus, a single school of ancient theology <term>prisca theologia: the idea that a single, true theology exists which threads through history, revealed by God to the ancients</term>, consistent with itself in every part, was forged from these six theologians in a wonderful order, beginning with Mercury and being [completed] thoroughly by the divine Plato.

<summary>Ficino explains the title 'Trismegistus' as representing the three roles of philosopher, priest, and king, while establishing a 'genealogy of wisdom' (prisca theologia) that links Hermes Trismegistus to Plato.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Egypt, Plato, prisca theologia, Orpheus, Pythagoras, genealogy of wisdom, theology, Neoplatonism</keywords>

# PREFACE

->A 3<-

...thoroughly finished. Mercury wrote <term>very many: original *ꝙplurimos*, a common scribal abbreviation for *quamplurimos*</term> books pertaining to the knowledge of divine things, in which—oh immortal God!—how many secret mysteries, how many stupendous oracles are revealed. He speaks not only as a philosopher, but often as a prophet, and he sings of things to come. He foresaw the ruin of the ancient religion, the birth of the new faith, the coming of Christ, the future judgment, the resurrection of the age, the glory of the blessed, and the punishment of sinners. 

Because of this, it happened that Saint Augustine <note>Aurelius Augustinus (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian who discussed Hermes in his work *The City of God*</note> doubted whether he brought forth these many things through skill in the stars <note>astrology</note> or through the revelation of demons <note>Augustine was skeptical, suggesting Hermes might have gained his knowledge from spirits rather than direct divine inspiration</note>. Lactantius <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian advisor to Constantine who viewed Hermes as a pagan witness to Christian truth</note>, however, does not hesitate to count him among the Sibyls and prophets. 

Finally, out of the many books of Mercury, two are especially divine: one on the divine will, and the other on the power and wisdom of God. The former is titled **Asclepius**, the latter **Pymander**. Apuleius the Platonist <note>A 2nd-century Latin author best known for *The Golden Ass*, to whom a Latin translation of the *Asclepius* was traditionally attributed</note> turned the former into Latin; the other remained among the Greeks until these times. But recently, brought from Macedonia to Italy through the diligence of Leonardo of Pistoia <note>A monk and agent for the Medici family who recovered the Greek manuscript of the *Corpus Hermeticum* around 1460</note>, a learned and upright monk, it came to us. I, however, having been urged by your exhortations, decided to translate it from the Greek language into Latin: it seemed right... <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the final word "fo" is the beginning of "fore" (would be)</note>

<summary>Ficino describes Hermes Trismegistus as a prophetic figure who foresaw Christian truths and introduces the two primary Hermetic works, the Asclepius and the Pymander, noting the latter's recent arrival in Italy from Macedonia.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Pymander, Asclepius, Saint Augustine, Lactantius, Leonardo of Pistoia, ancient theology, translation history, prophecy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s dedication to Cosimo de' Medici, following the discussion of Hermes Trismegistus’s prophetic nature and the arrival of the Greek manuscript from Macedonia via Leonardo of Pistoia.</meta>

->### MARSILIO FICINO<-

...I thought it right, O fortunate Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), the statesman and patron who funded Ficino's work and the Platonic Academy in Florence</note>, to dedicate this little work to your name. For it is only fitting that I offer the first-fruits of my Greek studies to the very man by whose wealth I was aided and by whose books, supplied in abundance, I devoted myself to those studies. Nor was it right to dedicate the work of so wise a philosopher, so pious a priest, and so powerful a king <note>Ficino refers to the "Triple Great" (Trismegistus) nature of Hermes as philosopher, priest, and king</note> to anyone unless the recipient himself surpassed all others in piety, wisdom, power, and every other virtue. 

Now, to descend to the writings of Mercury <note>original: Mercurius; referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>, the title of this book is *Pimander* <note>Derived from the Greek "Poimandres," often translated as "Shepherd of Men" or "The Mind of Sovereignty"</note>; this is because, among the four persons who debate in this dialogue, the primary parts are attributed to Pimander. He indeed published the book in Egyptian letters; and likewise, being skilled in the Greek language, he communicated the mysteries of the Egyptians to the Greeks by translating them from that source. 

The purpose of this work is to discourse upon the power and wisdom of God. And since the operations of these are twofold—the first remaining within the very nature of God, the second extending to external things—the former indeed conceives the first and eternal world <note>The Intelligible world, or the divine blueprint in the mind of God</note>, while the latter gives birth to the second and temporal world <note>The physical, created universe</note>. He disputes most weightily concerning both operations and both worlds: what the power of God is, what His wisdom is, by what order they conceive inwardly, and by what progression they bring forth outwardly. Furthermore, how those things which have been produced...

<summary>Ficino formally dedicates his translation of the Pimander to his patron Cosimo de' Medici, justifying the choice by praising Cosimo's virtues and explaining the Hermetic theory of the dual "worlds" of God's creation.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Cosimo de' Medici, Hermes Trismegistus, Pimander, Hermeticism, Divine Wisdom, Intelligible World, Egyptian Mysteries</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s preface to his translation of the *Corpus Hermeticum*. # PREFACE.
A 4

...how they relate to one another, where they agree, or where they differ, and finally, in what manner they regard their author. The order of the volume is such that it is divided into fourteen little books; the first parts of the dialogue are given to Pymander <note>The "Divine Mind" or "Shepherd of Men" who acts as the primary teacher in the first book</note>, the second are held by Trismegistus, the third by Aesculapius, and the fourth place is occupied by Tatius <note>Tatius and Aesculapius are presented as disciples of Hermes Trismegistus</note>. 

Mercury <note>original: Mercurius; referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> therefore intends to instruct Aesculapius and Tatius in divine matters. He who has not learned cannot teach divine things. But by human wit we cannot discover those things which are above human nature. Therefore, there is need for a divine light, so that we may look upon the sun itself by the light of the sun. Indeed, the light of the divine mind is never poured into the soul unless the soul itself, like the moon toward the sun, is turned deeply toward the mind of God. 

The soul is not turned toward the mind unless it also becomes mind itself. But it does not become mind before it has cast aside the deceptions of the senses and the clouds of the imagination <term>original: phantasiae; the faculty that creates mental images from sensory input, which Ficino views here as a distraction from pure intellectual truth</term>. For this reason, our Mercury strips away the mists of the senses and imagination and withdraws himself into the sanctuary <term>original: adytum; the innermost, most sacred part of a temple, used here metaphorically for the deepest part of the intellect</term> of the mind. Soon Pymander—that is, the divine mind—flows into him. From there, he contemplates the order of all things, both those existing in God and those flowing out from God. Finally, he explains to other men those things which have been revealed to him by the divine power.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino outlines the structural division of the fourteen Hermetic books and explains the Neoplatonic process of spiritual purification required to receive divine wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Pymander, Aesculapius, Tatius, Divine Mind, soul, enlightenment, Neoplatonism, Mercury</keywords>

This, then, is the title of the book, its purpose, and its order. And you, <note>original: "Cosme felix"</note> blessed Cosimo, read happily, and live long, so that your fatherland may also live long.

### JACQUES LEFÈVRE D'ÉTAPLES TO THE READER.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut drop cap 'W' featuring a bird (possibly a swan or crane) amidst foliage.</image-desc>WE HAVE TAKEN CARE with as much diligence as we were able, to restore this work to a corrected state from a corrupted manuscript <note>Lefèvre is explaining that he edited the text to fix errors found in previous handwritten or printed copies</note>, moved both by love for <term>Marsilio Ficino<gloss>The original translator of these texts from Greek to Latin</gloss></term>, whom we venerate as a father, and by the greatness of <term>Mercury’s<gloss>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage</gloss></term> wisdom. Furthermore, for the sake of helping students, we have added a few things by way of <term>summaries<gloss>original: "argumentorum"; brief outlines or introductory notes for each section</gloss></term>; although we frankly admit that each one of these books requires a greater effort of explanation, and a genius far more excellent than our modest strength can provide. Farewell.

<meta>This page transitions from the editor's preface by Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples to a theological summary of the first dialogue of the "Pymander," the first book of the Hermetic corpus. Lefèvre d'Étaples uses this summary to harmonize the teachings of Hermes Trismegistus with the biblical account of creation in Genesis and Christian Trinitarian doctrine.</meta>

### SUMMARY OF THE FIRST DIALOGUE.
A 5

In the first Dialogue, <term>Mercury<gloss>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage</gloss></term> discusses the <term>Mosaic mysteries<gloss>Teachings traditionally attributed to Moses in the Book of Genesis regarding the creation of the world</gloss></term>. For Moses saw darkness over the face of the deep, and the spirit of the Lord moving over the waters; but here, Mercury sees a terrifying shadow transforming into a "watery nature," which this very watery nature the word of the Lord was nourishing. The former [Moses] announces all things created by the powerful word of the Lord; but the latter [Mercury] asserts that this shining word, which illuminates all things, is the "offspring of the mind" and the son of God. He claims that the Mind, as father, and the Word of the mind, as son, do not differ in nature: "It was <term>consubstantial<gloss>original: "Consubstantiale"; a term meaning "of the same substance," used in the Nicene Creed to describe the relationship between God the Father and God the Son</gloss></term>," he says. He saw also that there was a union of these. 

And if you desire a fuller explanation, and if it is permissible to attribute so much divine knowledge to men who lived before the "fleshly veil of the Word" <note>A reference to the Incarnation of Christ</note>, he saw the Son being born from the Father, and the Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son in a wondrous way, when he said: "Moreover, God, the Mind, most full of the fertility of both sexes, being life and light, brought forth with his Word another Mind, the <term>Maker<gloss>original: "opificem"; the creator or craftsman of the physical world</gloss></term>." 

He saw also the Mind, with its exuberant fertility, reaching out toward external things, forming the universe according to the pattern of its own divine word, and distributing to each thing in the air, in the water, and on the earth its own nature according to its kind. Soon, man was made in his own likeness and image, to whose use the Maker-Mind subjected all sensible things. This man soon fell from the <term>intelligible sphere<gloss>The realm of pure spirit and divine intellect</gloss></term> to the sphere of bodily and lustful things; from this source, he also contracted the origin of the "kindling of evils" <note>original: "fomitis malorum"; a theological term for the innate tendency toward sin</note>. And at last, by the will of God, the knot of all things was loosed, and man, along with the rest, was made subject to death. What else is this, [than that] God the Wor- <note>The text breaks off mid-word ("uerbum") at the end of the page.</note>

<summary>This page provides a summary of the first Hermetic dialogue, framing Hermes Trismegistus as a pagan parallel to Moses who anticipated Christian doctrines like the Trinity and the Fall of Man.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Moses, Genesis, Creation, Trinity, Word of God, Consubstantiality, Fall of Man, Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples</keywords>

# ARGUMENT

...through his holy word <note>original: *verbo sancto*</note> cried out: "Bud forth, grow, and propagate, all you seedlings and my works." How like that Mosaic command: "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth." <note>original: *Crescite & multiplicamini, & replete terram* from Genesis 1:28</note> Soon Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage-prophet of Egypt</note> instructs us on how the path to the Mind <term>Mind: translated from *Mens* (Greek: *Nous*), referring to the divine intellect or the part of the soul that can perceive God</term> lies open, and what evil error finally leads us away from it. He teaches those to whom the Mind is present as a generous giver of all good things, and those from whom it is likewise absent; and by what means, just as we slip down from our intellectual and immortal nature through certain steps and degenerate into perishable things, we are also restored to the former state of a purified mind through certain opposite steps. Moses, by divine appointment, became the leader of the Hebrew flock, as Mercury did for the Egyptian flock; and now, through holy instruction, he feeds his flock, living an active life; yet now, praising the Father of all things with hymns and thanksgivings, he rises into the life of contemplation and light. 

->This is the summary of the *Pymander*.<- <note>The *Pymander* (or *Poimandres*) is the first book of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, where Hermes receives a vision of creation from the "Shepherd of Men."</note>

<summary>This page concludes the introductory argument of the Pymander, drawing a direct comparison between the leadership and teachings of Moses for the Hebrews and Hermes (Mercury) for the Egyptians. It outlines the soul's journey of descent into the material world and its eventual ascent back to divine contemplation.</summary>

# THE PYMANDER OF HERMES
## TRISMEGISTUS, ON THE POWER AND WISDOM OF GOD.
### TRANSLATED BY MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or the narrator, in a contemplative or sleeping pose within a landscape or architectural setting.</image-desc>

When I was reflecting on the nature of things <note>original: *de rerum natura*</note>, and was raising the keen edge of my mind to higher things, the senses of my body being now stilled—just as usually happens to those who are heavy with sleep due to overeating or exhaustion—suddenly I seemed to see someone of immense bodily size, who, calling me by name, cried out in this way: "What is it, O Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes, the legendary Egyptian sage and prophet</note>, that you desire both to hear and to behold? What is it you wish to learn and understand?" Then I said: "Who are you?" He replied: "I am Pymander <note>Also known as *Poimandres*, likely meaning "Shepherd of Men" or "Knowledge of the Sun-God"</note>, the Mind <term>Mind: from the Latin *mens* (Greek *nous*), referring to the supreme divine intellect</term> of divine power; see what you desire, and I truly will be with you everywhere." I said: "I desire to learn the nature of things, and to know God." To this he replied: "Enfold me in your mind, and I will instruct you in all the things you have wished for."

<summary>This page marks the beginning of the Pymander, where the narrator (Hermes/Mercury) enters a meditative state and encounters a divine vision of Pymander, the Divine Mind. Pymander offers to reveal the secrets of nature and the knowledge of God to the seeking narrator.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Pymander, Divine Mind, Marsilio Ficino, vision, nature of things, knowledge of God, Renaissance Platonism</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page continues the visionary dialogue where the divine being Pymander begins to reveal the mysteries of creation to Hermes (Mercurius) Trismegistus.</meta>

# MERCURIUS TRISMEGISTUS

When he had said these things, he changed his form, and suddenly revealed all things. For I beheld a certain immense spectacle: everything was turned into light, exceedingly sweet and pleasant, which wonderfully delighted me as I gazed upon it. A little later, a certain dreadful shadow, sliding down in a twisting revolution <note>original: "obliqua reuolutione," suggesting a spiraling or coiled descent</note>, was transformed into a <term>moist nature</term> <note>Latin: "humidam naturam." In Hermetic philosophy, this represents the primordial, watery chaos from which the material world is formed.</note>, stirred by an unspeakable tumult. From there, a great smoke broke out into a sound; from the sound, a voice emerged, which I took to be the voice of light. From this voice of light, the <term>Word</term> <note>Latin: "verbum," translating the Greek "Logos," the creative principle of the universe.</note> came forth. This Word, standing near the moist nature, cherished it. 

Then, from the inner depths of that moist nature, a pure and light fire flew forth at once, seeking the heights. Light air, too, obeying the spirit, took its place in the middle region between the fire and the water. To the **second**, the plotting of evils and idle deception. 
To the **third**, the idle illusion of lust. 
To the **fourth**, domineering and insatiable ambition. 
To the **fifth**, profane arrogance and the rashness of audacity. 
To the **sixth**, evil and idle opportunities for wealth. 
To the **seventh zone**, inherent falsehood. 

Then indeed, the soul, stripped of the movement of the harmony, returns to its desired nature, possessing its own power, and together with those who are there, it praises the Father. <page-num>25</page-num>
# SUMMARY OF THE SECOND BOOK.
<sig>B 5</sig>

*The second book discusses how God is intelligible through a rational method <term>rationali modo: a systematic approach using human reason to understand divine truths</term> to man alone; and from the center, the pole, the location, and the forms of things, it hunts for God Himself—stable and unmoving—around whom, in whom, and by whom all things are moved. It argues that He remains always the same to Himself, and that nothing in the world can be empty; rather, those things which seem to be voids actually emulate the highest fullness with an even more fertile abundance. Next, Hermes suggests to Aesculapius <note>Aesculapius: in Hermetic writings, he is a disciple of Hermes Trismegistus, named after the Greek god of medicine</note> through his responses that it is easier to say what God is not than what He is. Nevertheless, he asserts that God is the absolute Good and the Father, whose duty is to beget all things. This refers to an internal generation which remains within the nature of God itself, bringing forth the piety of divine religion. His claim that the name "Good" belongs to God alone accords with this Gospel truth: "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone" <note>original: "Quid me uocas bonū? nemo bonus nisi solus deus." This is a direct quote from the words of Jesus in Mark 10:18 or Luke 18:19</note>. Furthermore, what he adds concerning the extreme calamity of those who die without children is a veiled discourse <note>original: "velatus sermo," meaning an allegory or metaphorical teaching</note>: for you should not conceive of this as a physical birth, but as a birth of the soul. You should consider the offspring and sons of the soul to be the birth of virtues, and a "masculine" wisdom used for contemplating God and His most divine powers. He hints at this openly when he says: "Finally, the punishment is such that a sterile soul <term>sterilitas animæ: the state of a soul that has not produced spiritual fruits or knowledge</term> is judged to migrate into a body that possesses neither the nature of a male nor a female," as if he were saying clearly: "Through which it may never perform good deeds, nor will it ever be capable of receiving anything of the good." You, therefore, must flee the sterility of the soul with all your might; instead, beget offspring that will one day make you blessed, and in this way (as much as you are able) imitate the fertility <term>fœcunditas: the creative, productive power of the mind</term> of the Father, who is always begetting, through the fertility of your own mind.*

<summary>This page summarizes the second book of the Pymander, focusing on the rational search for God, the rejection of the "void," and the allegorical necessity of the soul's fertility in producing virtues.</summary>
<keywords>Aesculapius, Gospel truth, sterility of the soul, divine fertility, masculine wisdom, nature of God, the Void</keywords>

## ASCLEPIUS. II

God and divinity itself: I speak now not of that which is created, but of that which is **uncreated** <note>original: "ingenitū", meaning something that was not born or produced by a cause, but exists eternally.</note>. If, therefore, it be divine, it is <term>essence</term> <note>original: "essentia", the fundamental being or "is-ness" of a thing.</note>. If it is God, He is even beyond essence. Moreover, He is <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "intelligibilis", meaning that which can be grasped by the mind or intellect rather than the physical senses.</note> in this manner: for the first God exists as intelligible not to Himself, but to us. For the intelligible occurs to the one who understands by means of the senses. 

Therefore, God is not at all intelligible to Himself; for He is not something existing as separate from that which He understands, but rather He understands from Himself. He is, however, something different from us, and for that reason He is understood by us. But if the <term>Word</term> <note>original: "logos", referring here to the divine reason or expression of God.</note> is intelligible, it is not God. If He is understood as God, He is certainly not understood as the Word, but rather as a distinguishing act. 

Moreover, everything that is moved is moved not in something moving, but in something **stable**. That which moves also remains still; for it is impossible for it to be agitated together with the thing it moves.

**ASCLEPIUS.** In what way then, Trismegistus, are the things within the world changed together with those things that are moved? For you were saying that the <term>wandering spheres</term> <note>original: "sphæras erraticas", the planets, which appear to "wander" across the sky compared to the stars.</note> are moved by the <term>fixed sphere</term> <note>original: "aplane sphæra", the outermost shell of the heavens containing the "fixed" stars.</note>.

**TRISMEGISTUS.** That is not motion, O Asclepius, but **resistance**: for they do not travel in the same direction, but in a contrary manner. This opposition, in truth, contains a stable reverberation of motion; for the repercussion of rest <meta>catchword: nis (completing 'stationis')</meta>

<summary>Hermes explains that God is uncreated and exists beyond "essence," being intelligible to humans only because He is distinct from them. The dialogue then shifts to cosmology, arguing that the movement of the planets is actually a form of resistance against the fixed stars, maintaining a type of stability.</summary>

<keywords>uncreated, essence, intelligible, logos, cosmic motion, wandering spheres, fixed sphere, stability, resistance, Asclepius, Trismegistus</keywords>

# P Y M A N D E R

Every movement is an agitation; therefore, the **wandering spheres** <note>original: "erraticę sphæræ", referring to the planets, which appear to move independently against the fixed background of stars.</note> move in an opposite direction and clearly in a subordinate way to each other. By meeting in this kind of opposition, they are agitated by that which stands firm. Indeed, it cannot be otherwise: for consider the **Bears** <note>original: "arctos", referring to the constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor.</note> themselves, which as you know never rise nor set but perpetually revolve around the same point—do you think they move, or rather that they stand still?

**ASCLEPIUS.** They move, O Trismegistus.

**TRISMEGISTUS.** By what kind of motion, Asclepius?

**ASCLEPIUS.** By a motion that runs forever around the same point.

**TRISMEGISTUS.** But indeed, that circulation is the same as a stationary state, for the motion around a center is contained by stability. For the center itself prevents that which is above it from wandering. That which is held back by the center presses around it, and so this contrary agitation remains firm, established perpetually by that very opposition. 

I will place an example before your eyes from the world of the living: just as when a person swims, while the water is flowing, the striking of the hands and feet together causes the person to stay still, so that they do not drift away with the current or be submerged by it.

**ASCLEPIUS.** You have brought forth a very clear example, O Trismegistus.

**TRISMEGISTUS.** Therefore, whatever is moved is moved within a stable state and is moved by something stable. Thus, the motion of a **living thing** <note>original: "animalis", referring here to the "anima" or soul that provides life and movement to a body.</note>...

<summary>Hermes explains how the celestial spheres and stars maintain their positions through a balance of contrary motion and a stable center, using the analogy of a swimmer staying in place against a current.</summary>

### OF MERCURY TRISMEGISTUS
<page-num>28</page-num>

...every motion <note>This sentence continues from the previous page's discussion on the mechanics of movement.</note> (of that which is composed of matter) is by no means produced by those things which are outside of the world; rather, it moves from the internal to the external—whether by the soul, or by the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritu*; here referring to the "pneuma," a vital breath or subtle substance that acts as a bridge between the divine soul and the heavy physical body</note>, or by some other incorporeal thing. For a body does not move a living body at all, nor indeed the whole body together, even if it should exist in an inanimate state.

**AESCULAPIUS.** By what reasoning do you assert this, O Trismegistus?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** Wood and stones and all other such things that possess a soul <note>original: *animam habent*; while wood and stones are usually considered inanimate, Hermetic philosophy often suggests a universal life-force or "world soul" permeates all matter</note> are not moved by bodies, O Aesculapius. For that which is within the body, moving the living thing itself, is certainly not the same body by which both are moved: namely, the body of that which carries and that which is carried. From this, it follows that even that which sleeps is alive, for the very reason that it moves <note>Hermes suggests that the internal movement of breath or dreams during sleep proves the soul is still active and moving the body from within</note>. Do you not then perceive that the soul is most heavily burdened when it supports two bodies alone? Furthermore, it is manifest that whatever is moved is moved within something else, and is moved by something that is stationary.

**AESCULAPIUS.** In that stationary thing, O Trismegistus, those things which are changed must surely be transformed.

**TRISMEGISTUS.** You speak rightly, Aesculapius; nothing in the order of things is a **void** <note>original: *uacuum*</note>. Only that which is not, and that which is deprived of existence, is to be called a void. For nothing can be found which, while it exists, is empty.

**AESCULAPIUS.** Are there not also found...

# PYMANDER

...there are also certain things that are empty, Trismegistus: such as an empty jar <note>original: *dolium*; a large earthenware vessel used for storing wine or grain</note>, an empty well, and many other such similar things.

**TRISMEGISTUS.** Alas, how far you wander from the truth, O Aesculapius! Those things which are vast and, above all others, the most full, you consider to be empty.

**AESCULAPIUS.** How can that be, O Trismegistus?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** Air is certainly a body <note>Trismegistus is arguing against the common perception that air is "nothingness." In Hermetic physics, air is a subtle material substance</note>; this body penetrates all other things and, flowing through them, fills everything. For a body of this kind is not composed of physical elements <note>original: *ex corporalibus non compositum*; meaning it is a subtle, non-composite substance unlike the heavy "compounds" of earth or water</note>. Whence it happens that whatever you call "empty" is actually full of air. Therefore, those things should be called hollow rather than empty; for they both exist as places, and they are full of air and <term>spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritus*; the vital breath or pneuma that gives life and connects the physical to the divine</note>.

**AESCULAPIUS.** This reasoning is invincible and beyond doubt, Trismegistus. Air is a body; that body permeates all other things and, flowing in, completes them all. But what shall we say of the "place" in which everything moves?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** It is <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: *incorporeum*; something that lacks a physical body or material weight</note>, O Aesculapius.

**AESCULAPIUS.** But what is the incorporeal?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** It is Mind and Reason <note>original: *Mens ac ratio*; representing the Greek *Nous* and *Logos*</note>, embracing itself, free from all bodily mass, alien to error, incapable of suffering, intangible, standing firm by itself, cleansing and preserving all things. Its rays are Goodness, Truth, the primary light, and the first form of souls.

**AESCULAPIUS.** Then what is God?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** He who is none of these things, yet the author of these...

# HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

...yet [He] is the cause of all things so that they may exist, being present indeed to all things, and present even to each individual thing; nor does He permit anything not to exist. All things are procreated from those things that already exist, for from nothing, nothing arises <note>original: "de nihilo autem nihil prouenit" — a fundamental principle of ancient philosophy (nothing comes from nothing).</note>. For those things that do not exist have no nature by which they are able to become, but rather a nature by which they are unable to exist. Conversely, those things that do exist do not have a nature through which they might at some point cease to exist.

**AESCULAPIUS.** What then do you say God is?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** God certainly is not Mind <term>Mind: the Latin *Mens* refers to the divine intellect or the source of all thought</term>, but He is indeed the cause that Mind exists; nor is He Spirit, but the cause by which Spirit exists; nor is He Light, but the cause by which Light exists. Therefore, it is necessary to worship God with these two names, which belong to Him alone, and which are completely unsuitable for any other. For among those who are called "gods" besides Him—whether they be spirits <note>original: "demones" — in this context, intermediary spirits rather than evil entities.</note> or men—none can be as good as the one God. For He is the Good itself, and nothing else besides the Good. All other things are separate from the very nature of the Good; indeed, both the body and the soul have no place in which they may contain the Good. For goodness is as vast as the existence of all things, both those that have bodies and those that are incorporeal <note>without physical bodies.</note>, those that are sensible <note>perceived by the senses.</note> and those that are intelligible <note>perceived only by the mind or intellect.</note>. That is the Good; that is [God...]

<summary>In this passage, Hermes Trismegistus explains that God is not the elements of existence (like mind, spirit, or light) but the foundational cause of them. He defines God's unique nature as "The Good," a quality so vast it cannot be contained by human bodies or souls.</summary>

# PYMANDER

...is God. Therefore, beware of ever calling anything else "good," for this would be a profane error. Nor should you say that God is anything other than the Good alone; for you would certainly fall into the same impiety. Therefore, though the word "good" is spoken by everyone, what it actually is is not understood by all. For this reason, God is not known by everyone; instead, due to ignorance, people call both certain other gods <note>In the Hermetic tradition, "gods" often refers to celestial bodies or administrative spirits, distinct from the Supreme Creator.</note> and even some men "good." Yet these can never be good, nor can they even become so. All the other immortal gods are honored with the title of "god," but God is the Good—not because of an honor bestowed upon Him, but by His very nature.

For the nature of God is one: namely, the Good itself. Both names <note>original: "in utrisque nominibus" — referring to the names "God" and "Good."</note> are truly one, and from them all kinds of things flow. For the Good bestows everything and receives nothing; God provides everything and desires nothing. Therefore, God is the Good, and the Good is God.

The other title for God is "Father," for the reason that He brings all things into being; for it is the duty of a father to generate. On this account, the procreation of children is considered the most excellent and pious <term>pious: acting in accordance with divine will or religious duty</term> pursuit in life among the wise. ### THE ARGUMENT OF THE THIRD BOOK.

*The third book recounts how, from the formless womb of matter—illuminated by forms like holy splendors—all things proceeded toward their birth in their proper order, and how the blessed minds of the heavens fulfill the work entrusted to them by the Supreme Father. It also explains that man was born for a dual duty: namely, for the contemplation of eternal things, and for the judgment of good and evil; and furthermore, for the management of human affairs through various inventions of the arts and through prudence. For this duty, the heavens, the earth, the herbs, the sprouts, the whole harmony of the world, and the most beautiful order of things provide him with abundant material for contemplation and for raising himself toward the divine. For nature is like a single book full of divinity, and a mirror of divine things.*

# PYMANDER.
## THE SACRED DISCOURSE. III
### C

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'G' featuring a figure, possibly a cherub or a classical figure, amidst foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

**G**lory of all is God, the divine, and divine nature. The principle of all things is God: mind, nature, matter, and wisdom for the manifestation of all. He is the principle, divinity, action, necessity, end, and renewal. For there was an infinite shadow in the abyss, and water besides; and a subtle, intellectual spirit existed within the <term>chaos<note>original: chaos. In Hermetic philosophy, this refers to the primordial, unformed state of the universe before the intervention of divine mind.</note></term> by divine power. Then a holy splendor broke forth, which brought out the <term>elements<note>original: elementa. The fundamental building blocks of the physical world—typically earth, air, fire, and water.</note></term> from the moist nature under the depths <note>original: sub arena. Literally "under the sand," likely referring to the heavy, material foundations of the world.</note>, and all the gods <note>In this context, the "gods" are the celestial governors or planetary powers through which the supreme God acts.</note> chose a generative nature <note>original: feminalem naturam. Literally "feminine nature," referring to the receptive, life-giving principle of the material world.</note>. And whereas all things had previously been indistinct and unformed, the light elements then flew up into the high region, while the heavy elements settled beneath the moist depths. For when all things had been distinguished and balanced, carried by the fiery spirit, the heaven shone forth in <term>seven circles<note>original: septem in circulos. These represent the seven planetary spheres (Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn) which ancients believed governed the cycles of time and fate.</note></term>. The gods were seen in the forms of the stars with their constellations. The stars were numbered according to the gods who inhabit them. The wider orbit, in its course, harmonized with the airy circle, carried by the divine spirit. Each of the gods, by their internal power, fulfilled the work assigned to them. Thus were born living creatures: four-footed beasts, reptiles, creatures of the water, and those that fly.

### THE WORKS OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

Likewise, every sowing that sprouts through seeds—the grass, the herbs, and the budding flowers—contained within them the seed of <term>regeneration</term> <note>original Latin: "regenerationis"; in this context, it refers to the cyclical rebirth of life through seeds</note>. The generations of humanity were created for the knowledge of divine works and to serve as a testimony to nature; they were made to rule over all things covered by the heavens, to discern what is good, to increase the human race, and to propagate their number. Every soul, though veiled by the shadow of the flesh, was made to look up at the wandering course of the celestial gods <note>The "gods" here refer to the stars and planets, which the Hermetic tradition viewed as divine agents</note>, to observe the works of God and the progressions of nature, to recognize the signs of good things, and to gain knowledge of divine power.

A certain portion [of wisdom] was granted to them for the judgment of good and evil, and for the discovery of various crafts and skillful works. Yet life begins to stir in them, and they obtain wisdom according to the portion or lot determined by the path of the circling gods. Furthermore, they are to be dissolved back into that state where great movements exist, along with the reminders of the crafts left upon the earth through the passing of time, and the decay and generation of living flesh. Even when the seeds of fruits and the works of nature and art have wasted away, old things shall eventually grow young again through the necessity and renewal of the gods, and by the rhythmic course of <term>numerical nature</term> <note>original: "numerosae naturae"; this refers to nature governed by mathematical cycles and harmonic proportions</note>. For the very <term>harmony of the world</term> <note>original: "conspiratio mundi"; literally a "breathing together," signifying the cosmic sympathy or interconnectedness of all things</note> is divine, as nature herself blossoms anew.

For indeed, nature also consists in divinity itself.

### ARGUMENT OF THE FOURTH BOOK

The fourth book urges us to lay hold of wisdom, which is an open mixing-bowl <note>original: "crater"; in antiquity, a large vessel used for mixing wine and water, here used as a metaphor for a vessel of divine influence</note> of the divine mind. Any soul that immerses itself into this vessel becomes a partaker of knowledge and gazes up at the Mind. But indeed, to lift itself toward that Mind, the soul must transcend the heavens themselves, surpass the circuit of the stars and their movements, and leave the choirs of the blessed far below. Then it stretches toward the one and only God—the insurmountable and infinite good without end. When the soul beholds this good, it looks down upon all physical bodies and considers the life we lead here to be misery, being intent only on the desire for the incorporeal <note>non-physical or spiritual</note> good. Yet no one is able to immerse themselves in this divine mixing-bowl who does not first hate their own body, and who has not loved God himself rather than themselves. Only the one who neglects mortal things and clings to divine things alone—being present to them, meditating on them, and burning with desire for them—can achieve this. Soon, through the analogy of unity and numbers, the text raises us to the contemplation of the true <term>Monad</term> <note>original Latin: "Monas"; the ultimate "One" or indivisible source of all things</note> and the true numbers of nature.

THE Creator <note>original: "opifex"; meaning a craftsman or artisan-creator</note> fashioned the entire universe with a word, not with hands. Think of Him indeed as always present, performing all things—the one God, establishing all things by His will. For that is His body: not tangible, not visible, not measured, not distant, nor like anything else. For it is neither fire, nor water, nor—

### ARGUMENT OF THE FIFTH BOOK.

*The fifth book teaches that God is hidden and yet simultaneously shines through every individual particle of the world. # THE ARGUMENT OF THE SIXTH TREATISE

The Sixth Treatise contends this: That the Good, and the nature of the Good (which is goodness itself), is found in God alone; and likewise the nature of the Beautiful, the Powerful, and the Wise. In the world, however, there is only the *name* of the Good. This text proves that men are blinded by errors, warns them to abhor vices, and teaches the path that leads us to Goodness itself and Beauty itself: namely, piety <term>pietas</term> <note>In this context, piety refers to a deep, active devotion to the divine</note> joined with knowledge <term>cognitio</term> <note>Specifically "Gnosis," or spiritual realization</note>. Ignorant mortals, wandering from the path of piety, can never reach this state.

---

->THE SIXTH BOOK<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial B featuring two figures, possibly cherubs or classical figures, amidst foliage.</image-desc>

O Aesculapius <note>Aesculapius, or Asclepius, is a frequent student figure in Hermetic dialogues, named after the Greek god of healing</note>, the Good is in no one at all except in the unique God; rather, God Himself is always the Good itself. Therefore, it is necessary that God be the essence of all motion and knowledge. Nothing is deprived of this essence; it possesses within itself a stable action, needing nothing, infinite, overflowing, and bestowing. This is the one principle of all things, providing good and pouring it forth. Whenever I name "the Good," understand that which is all good, and that which is good forever. This belongs to the unique God, for He is not in need of anything, such that He might become evil by desiring to obtain it; nor does the loss of anything ever fall upon Him, such that He would be affected by pain after a loss. For the greater part... <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

Therefore, since these things do not happen to Him, nothing remains of His nature except the Good itself. Just as none of those things which are evil are present in this essence, so also the Good is found in no other thing. For in individual things, other qualities are present—both in small things and in large ones, and even in those things which are unified—and also in that very Living Being <note>original: "animali"; referring to the "Cosmos" or the Universe itself as a living entity.</note>, the greatest and most powerful of all, which indeed fills created things with <term>passions<note>original: "passionibus"; in this philosophical context, "passions" refers to the state of being acted upon, changed, or affected by external forces, rather than just emotions.</note></term>. For <term>generation<note>original: "generatio"; the process of coming into existence, birth, or creation.</note></term> is a kind of passion. Where there is passion, however, there is in no way the Good; and where the Good is, there is no passion at all. Where there is day, there is in no way night; where there is night, there is no day. For this reason, the Good cannot exist in the process of generation; it remains, therefore, only in that which is <term>unbegotten<note>original: "ingenitum"; that which has no beginning and was not created, i.e., the Eternal.</note></term>. Just as matter is granted a participation in all things, so also the world is "good" through its participation in the Good. I say "good" insofar as it also produces all things; in that specific part, the world is good, but in all other respects it is not good. For it is subject to suffering and

### THE SEVENTH BOOK

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, amidst foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

Where are you rushing, drunken mortals, you who have swallowed down the unmixed wine of ignorance? Since you cannot bear it, vomit it up; live soberly, and look with the eyes of the mind. And if you cannot all do so, at least let those who are able do it. 

The plague of ignorance overturns the whole earth and corrupts the soul shut up in the bonds of the body, nor does it allow the soul to take up the path of salvation. Do not permit yourselves to be submerged in the lake of corruption and death: breathe now, come to your senses, run back to the fountain of life, and take hold of Him who will lead you into the <term>inner sanctum<note>original: "adytum", referring to the most private or sacred part of a temple</note></term> of truth.

There, no one raves with drunkenness, but all are sober and watchful, and with the eyes of the mind they gaze more keenly upon Him who wishes to be seen. He is neither perceived by ears, nor seen by eyes, nor expressed by speech. The mind alone beholds Him; the mind alone proclaims Him.

**TAT.** Does this living being not then perish?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** Speak better, speak better omens <note>original: 'melius melius ominare'—a warning against speaking of death or destruction in a way that is spiritually inaccurate or unlucky</note>, O son! Know therefore that the world is from God and at the same time in God; but man consists from the world and in the world. -># OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS<-

Yet both of these seem to return to a single point, nor can they be distinguished in humans by reason. In other living creatures, sense is united with nature, but in humans, it is joined with **intelligence**. Indeed, <term>understanding<note>original Latin: "intellectus"</note></term> differs from intelligence just as God differs from divinity. For divinity proceeds from God, but intelligence proceeds from man. This intelligence is the sister of <term>speech<note>original Latin: "sermo," often used to translate the Greek "Logos," meaning both the spoken word and the underlying reason or logic.</note></term>, or rather, both are instruments for one another. For speech is not uttered without understanding, nor does understanding come to light without speech. 

Therefore, sense and intelligence in man are, as it were, bound together and work in harmony with one another. For we are in no way able to understand without sense, nor to perceive without understanding. Nevertheless, it is possible to perceive understanding without sense, similar to those who see **phantasms** in their sleep. It seems to me that both operations are exercised in the visions of dreams, but that sense is awakened from sleep into wakefulness. 

Furthermore, man is divided into soul and body. Whenever both parts of sense agree with each other, then the understanding conceived in the mind is brought forth. The mind conceives all notions: good ones whenever the seed is infused by God, but the opposite kind when the seeds <insert>are cast</insert> <note>The Latin text here breaks at "sperma-" with the catchword "ta iaciuntur," indicating the full word is "spermata" (seeds) being "thrown" or "cast."</note> from certain demons...

For the revolution of the world, driving generations forward, produces certain qualities—staining some and defiling them with evil, and refining others and purifying them with good. The world, O Aesculapius, possesses sense and motion, not indeed similar to human sense and motion, but certainly more powerful and far simpler. For the sense and intelligence of the world is this one thing: namely, to make all things and to dissolve what has been made. It is an instrument of the divine will, constructed chiefly for this purpose: that, receiving seeds from God...

Bodies, indeed, consist of matter in its various forms: some of these are made of earth, some of water, others of air, and many also of fire. All are certainly composite, yet some are more densely packed, while others are simpler—some are heavy, and others are light. God, therefore, is the father of the cosmos (that is, the world); but the cosmos is the father of those things within the cosmos; and the cosmos is indeed the son of God. Those things which are in the cosmos remain under the dominion of the cosmos. # OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

...he is named by necessity and merit alike. The senses and understanding of all living creatures flow into them from the outermost regions, derived from that which contains all inspired things. The <term>Cosmos</term> <note>original: "Cosmus"; from the Greek *kosmos*, meaning both "the world" and "order/ornament"</note>, however, preserves forever whatever it received from God from its very origin. God is certainly not, as it seems to some, deprived of sense or mind. For those people, weighed down by their own misery, speak falsely against him.

Whatever things there are in God, O <term>Aesculapius</term> <note>The traditional student of Hermes in these dialogues, named after the Greek god of medicine</note>, they depend upon God; some act through the body, some move through the **essence of the soul**, others give life through the spirit, and others are merely the receptacles of the dead. It is more accurate to say that God does not "possess" such things, but rather, to express the clear truth, we must confess that **He is all things**. He does not receive these things from the outside, yet He extends Himself to the very limits of all things. This is the sense and understanding of God: to move all things eternally.

Therefore, there shall never be a time in which any existing thing shall vanish into nothingness. Whenever I speak of **existing things**, I am speaking of the **treasure of God**. For God himself embraces all existence; outside of Him there is nothing, and He Himself is not outside of nothingness. These things will seem true to you, O Aesculapius, if you understand them; but to the ignorant, they will seem beyond belief. For to understand is itself to believe; but to lack faith is, without doubt, to remain in ignorance. Indeed, my discourse reaches even to the truth...

### ARGUMENT OF THE TENTH BOOK

The tenth book constantly asserts that God is absolutely all things, which individual things contract through participation; yet God is Father and Good by the very fact that he is all things. Next, it discusses the soul’s rapture in silence, where things seen with the **eyes of the mind** are neither lawful to reveal, nor is the choice to reveal them granted. As for what is added regarding the transformation of animals, the following discourse of the same <term>Mercury</term> <note>The Latin name for Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom these texts are attributed</note> declares that one should follow not the literal fiction of the words, but the **allegory** of the fiction, when he says: *For no body other than a human one contains a human soul, nor is it lawful for a rational soul to collapse into the body of a creature lacking reason.* For **divine law** prohibits such a wicked generation. And a little later he adds: *Such is the fitting punishment of nature, not such as you, perhaps, my son, and some others might think—to whom it seems that our soul, after it has cast off its human form, [is cast] into degenerate bodies...*

**H**ESTERDAY'S discourse, O Aesculapius, I addressed to you; therefore, it is right to dedicate today's to Tatius <note>Hermes's son and disciple</note>, and all the more because the present discussion will be a certain summarized compendium <note>a concise summary</note> of all those things spoken by us before. God and the Father and the Good, O Tatius, have the same nature, or rather, the same activity <note>original: "actum," referring to actualized power or operation</note>. # PYMANDER.

...according to participation <note>original: "secundum participationem"</note> he is Father, yet not solely as the cause of life and goodness to living things. But if this is the case, he is apprehended and moved by the will of the Good, without which nothing can ever be nor become. The father is the cause of children, both of their procreation and their nourishment, undertaking this through the sole desire for the Good. For the Good itself is active <note>original: "activum," meaning it is the source of all action or energy</note>. This quality cannot belong to any other than him: because while he receives nothing, he wills all things to be. I do not say, O Tatius, that he *makes* all things; for the one who makes <note>the 'maker' or craftsman</note> is, over a long period of time, deficient and in need. Since sometimes he makes and sometimes he stops, he is lacking in both quantity and quality: sometimes arranging things of a certain sort and size, and at other times the opposite of these. But God is both Father and the Good, by the very fact that he is all things: such is he, then, to those who are able to perceive these things. For he wills to be this, and he is, and he is for himself—and most truly, he is the thing itself: for all other things exist because of him. Indeed, O Tatius, it is the property of the Good to make himself known: that is the Good, O Tatius.

The intelligible state also in this manner drives material motion: since the world is a sphere, that is, a head, nor is there anything material above the head, just as there is nothing intelligible under the feet. But all things are material, while the mind drives the head moved in a circle, that is, according to the motion of the nature of the head. Therefore, whatever things are contiguous to the membrane of that head, which is truly the soul, are born immortal, as if the body were established within the soul; and those things having a soul are full of body. But whatever is far from the membrane, in which are those things that participate more in soul, exists as body. But the whole is a living being. Thus the whole world is composed of a certain material and an intelligible part. The world is the first living being, man the second.

the second living being after the world, but the first of the remaining living beings. Indeed, whatever gift of the soul is granted to others, man also possesses. He is considered not only not good, but even evil, insofar as he is mortal. For the world is not "good" <note>In Hermetic philosophy, "Good" is an absolute attribute of the Divine; since the world is subject to change, it cannot be perfectly "Good."</note> because it is in motion; yet it is not evil, because it is immortal. Man, however, is judged to be evil both because he is in motion and because he is mortal.

The human soul is carried in this manner: <term>Mind</term> <note>original: *Mens*; the highest faculty of the human spirit</note> resides in reason, reason in the soul, the soul in the spirit, and the spirit in the body. The <term>spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritus*; refers to the "pneuma" or vital breath that connects the physical and spiritual</note>, diffused through the veins, arteries, and blood, moves the living being in every part, and sustains and carries the suspended mass of the body.

Because of this, some were deceived into thinking that the fluid of the blood was the soul. It clearly escaped their notice that first the spirit must flow toward the soul, then the blood must congeal and the veins and hollow arteries must expand, until finally the living being is dissolved; and this is the death of the body.

All things depend upon one single principle. This principle originates from the One and Only. And while the principle is moved so that it may once again exist as a principle, the "One" itself remains constant and does not depart from its unity. Therefore, these three exist: God the Father (who is the Good), the world, and man. **TRIS.** The <term>Mind (original: *mens*)</term> <note>In this context, "Mind" refers to the highest divine intellect or the "true self."</note> is separated from the soul, and the soul in turn is separated from the spirit. The soul is the clothing of the mind, and the spirit is the clothing of the soul. It is necessary, O son, for the listener to think along with the speaker and to be in harmony with him; the listener's hearing must even be sharper than the voice of the speaker. The weaving together of these "garments," O son, is completed within the earthly body. Indeed, it is completely impossible for the mind, naked in its own nature, to settle within an earthly mass. For the <note>original: *terrea fex*</note> lowly dregs of the earth are not able to receive a mind so divine, nor could such a great divinity endure being shaped into a body subject to suffering. Therefore, the mind took on the soul as if it were a cloak; furthermore, the soul, being divine, makes use of the spirit as its vehicle. The spirit runs through the entire living being. 

Thus, as soon as the mind is released from the earthly body, it immediately puts on its own proper cloak—namely, a body of fire. As long as it is wrapped in this fiery body, it cannot swell into <note>meaning: it cannot take on the density or weight of</note> an earthly body. For the earth cannot sustain fire; indeed, the whole earth would be consumed by even a tiny spark. For this reason, cold moisture was poured around the earthly mass, acting as a kind of obstacle against the burning of the fire. The mind, since it is the sharpest and swiftest of all divine concepts, encompasses the bodies of each of the elements.

# HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

...as impiety lacerates the soul: Do you not see by how many evils the impious soul is weighed down? Alas, thus, my son, the impious soul cries out: "I burn, I am consumed! I know not what to say or what to do; evils flowing together from every side devour wretched me; I see nothing, alas, wretched me, nor do I hear." Such are the voices of the afflicted soul; such is the punishment fitting its nature—not such as you perhaps, my son, and certain others think, to whom it seems that our soul, after it has cast off the human form, degenerates into the bodies of beasts. For this is an impious error <note>Hermes is refuting the common idea of transmigration—that humans could be reborn as animals—calling it a misunderstanding of spiritual law.</note>.

Truly, the mode of its chastisement is different. When the Mind <note>original: *Mens*; in Hermetic thought, the divine intellect or higher consciousness</note> becomes a divine spirit <note>original: *daemon*, here referring to a spiritual being or 'daimon' that serves as an agent of divine justice rather than a malevolent 'demon'</note>, it is commanded to take up a fiery body for the service of God; then, having entered into the wicked soul, it strikes it with the whips of its sins. The wicked soul, lashed by these, turns itself toward murders, insults, reproaches, and various robberies; it falls, finally, into all those things through which men commit crimes.

But when the Mind flows into a holy soul, it raises it to the light of wisdom. This soul afterwards never languishes in the torpor of sleep, but brings help to the human race equally in words and works, and assists in every way, always imitating its parent <note>Referring to God as the Father or Creator of all souls.</note>. Wherefore it is necessary, O son, that we, giving [thanks] to God...

<summary>Hermes explains that the true punishment of an impious soul is internal torment and lashings from a divine spirit, rather than reincarnation into animal form, while a holy soul is led toward wisdom and service to humanity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Hermes Trismegistus and his son Tat (Pymander, Libellus X), specifically discussing the soul's dependency on the divine Mind and the exalted status of human nature.</meta>

# OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

...to the lower regions. A soul <term>destitute</term> <note>meaning: deprived or lacking</note> of the presence of the Mind is able neither to act nor to speak at all. But often the Mind dwells outside the soul, during which time the soul neither hears nor sees, but is like a <term>brute animal</term> <note>Latin: "animali... ratione carenti", a living creature lacking reason</note>. So great is the power of the Mind which deserts a soul of this kind that is entangled in the body and dragged by it toward the lower depths. Such a soul, my son, possesses no Mind; therefore, it is not even lawful to call such a being a "man." For man is a **divine being**, and is not to be compared with the earthly brutes, but with the celestial gods. Indeed, if we must dare to speak the truth, the true man is either superior even to the heavenly inhabitants, or at least shares an equal lot with them. For whenever any of the heavenly beings descend to earth, they must leave the boundaries of heaven. Man, however, ascends into heaven and measures it; nothing that is lowest or highest escapes him, and he diligently investigates all other things. And what is even greater: without even leaving the earth, he is raised into heaven. So vast is the power of human nature. Therefore, we must dare to say that an earthly man is a **mortal god**, and a celestial god is an **immortal man**. Thus, by the power of these two—namely, man and the world—all individual things are governed, and ultimately all things are subject to the One.

<summary>This page defines the "true man" as a divine being whose Mind allows him to transcend his physical body, effectively making him a "mortal god" who governs the world alongside the celestial powers.</summary>

ARGUMENT OF THE ELEVENTH. 77

## ARGUMENT OF THE ELEVENTH.

The eleventh [treatise] concerning the mind, full of divine discourse, declares that eternity depends from God, the world from eternity, time from the world, change from time, and from change, both death and life. He most agreeably demonstrates, both by reasons and by analogies, that to the insuperable power of God no power is comparable—neither divine, nor human, nor of those above, nor of those below—and that He is the only one; who, since He cannot be idle, is always making all things. This you may rightly conceive as being said concerning the eternal generation of the Word: for he says that it was necessary for the divine work to be present, so that those things might exist which are made, which were being made, and which shall be made hereafter: that is life, that is the beautiful, that is the good, and that finally is God and the life of all things. But what is this, except what the trumpet of the Evangelist sounded more loftily, when he says: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was made nothing that was made. In him was life. Therefore, the life of all flows from God, and is itself God. From which it follows that true death, and that true destruction of things, is not what is commonly thought: but rather it is that by which the life of living things, withdrawing itself into the hidden, deserts things. Truly, he uses a wonderful proportion to comprehend Him who escapes all proportion, who, though grasped, remains incomprehensible, and who, unknown to all, presents himself as knowable in all things. You therefore, whoever are pious, be present now with your whole selves, and incline your mind to the discourses of the Mind, so that at last you may know Him, who for that reason fabricated all things, whom you might discern through each individual thing.

### ARGUMENT OF THE TWELFTH.

The twelfth [book], proceeding concerning the lower mind, which is the image or a certain vestige of the first mind, after a precise determination of the first mind, associates it with individual souls. But in irrational creatures mind is nature, while in men it is reason: of whose benefit whoever of men are deprived, they are snatched away by a certain burning impulse, after the manner of beasts, to the fulfillment of their desires. Nor do they set any end to their lust, nor do they find a limit to their evil passions; they who suffer by fate and divine decree, and finally pay the merited penalties of their ignorance. Good men, on the contrary, over whom the mind presides,

[This tabernacle,] my son, is established within the zodiacal circle, which consists of that number twelve; and those twelve numbers are one and all-formed according to the archetypes <note>Latin: *ideae* — the divine blueprints or "ideas" behind physical forms</note> of nature, guiding the wandering and circulation of man. Rightly, therefore, according to true reason, they create a separation only insofar as they are repulsed by the ten powers—that is, by the number ten <note>Latin: *denarius*</note>. For the number ten, my son, is the progenitor <note>Latin: *genitor*</note> of the soul. Indeed, where Life and Light are united—where they are the numbers of Unity itself—they are born of the spirit. Thus, according to reason, Unity encompasses the ten, and in turn, the ten encompasses Unity.

### ARGUMENT OF THE FOURTEENTH BOOK

*The fourteenth book asserts these things: That all things perceived by the senses have been made and are continually being made. For just as they flow from another, who, being almighty, rules over all things, so also he continually sustains them, lest by their own nature, being prone to falling, they collapse into nothingness. The knowledge of him alone makes one happy and blessed; he is God, the maker of all things, and the father, and he alone is the creator <note>original: "genitor"</note>, and all other things are the created <note>original: "genita"</note>. Between the creator and the created, no middle ground can be placed; and these two constitute the universe: for all things are these two, the creator and the created. Furthermore, he asserts this: that evil does not depend on God—just as rust does not originate from the blacksmith <note>A classic analogy suggesting that decay or "evil" is a byproduct of material existence rather than the intent of the creator.</note>, but follows the works created. And from human art, he lifts us up to conceive of divine art, showing that God himself brings immortality to heaven, change to the earth, and life and motion to the whole world.*

<summary>This page concludes a discussion on the secrecy of spiritual rebirth and introduces a new discourse on the inseparable relationship between God as the Creator and the material world as the created.</summary>

<header>THE FOURTEENTH.</header>

**S**INCE my son Tatius, in your absence, desired to learn the nature of all things, and indeed desired to inquire of me—as one who is younger and lately come to the knowledge of each matter—I was compelled to say many things, so that his understanding might be easy and ready: I have deemed it worthwhile that, choosing the more principal points from many, I should now repeat the preceding discourse to you in summary: for it is permitted to run through certain mysteries with you, as one expert in the nature of things. All things which are perceived by the sense have been made, and are made daily. Things begotten are not made by themselves, but by another. Many are the things begotten, each manifest to the sense, and differing, nor altogether similar. Whatever things are brought forth proceed from another. There is, therefore, some Maker of these, and he is unbegotten, so that he may be more ancient than the begotten: for we have said that begotten things flow from another. Now, nothing except the unbegotten can be more ancient than the begotten. The Maker is certainly more powerful, and unique, and alone truly wise in all things, since nothing at all precedes him. He also dominates over multitude, magnitude, the continuity of action, and the difference of all begotten things. Furthermore, begotten things are visible, but he is invisible: for this reason, indeed, he acts, so that he may become visible. He always, therefore, makes.

# OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

It is worthy for us to understand, to marvel through understanding, and in marvelling to call oneself blessed, recognizing our true father. For what is sweeter than a true father? Who is he, and how shall we find him? Is it fitting to attribute to him alone the name of "God," or "Maker," or "Father," or perhaps all three titles at once? Let him be named "God" because of his power, "Maker" because of his action, and finally "Father" because of his goodness. 

For his power is vastly different from those things that are begotten <note>original: *genitis*; things that are born, created, or brought into existence</note>, while his action is found in the production of all things. Therefore, setting aside the vanity and variety of long speeches, one must meditate primarily on these two: the Begetter and the Begotten <note>original: *genitorem* and *genitum*; in Hermetic philosophy, this represents the fundamental duality of the Creator and the Created</note>. 

Between these there is no middle ground, nor is there anything else besides them. When you wish to understand all things, remember these two, and remember that they comprise the universe; then nothing will be ambiguous to you—neither of things above nor things below, whether they be divine or changeable, manifest or those which lie hidden in darkness. For truly all things are these two: the Begetter and the Begotten, and one cannot be separated from the other. For it is not possible for a Maker to exist without a thing made <note>original: *facto*</note>. Both exist together as the same reality; thus, neither may be pulled apart from the other, just as neither [trum...] <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "trum" indicates the next page begins by completing the word *neutrum*, meaning "neither."</note>

<summary>Hermes explains that the Divine should be known as God, Maker, and Father, emphasizing a dualistic reality consisting only of the Begetter and the Begotten, which are inseparable.</summary>

[nei]ther can be divided from itself. For if the maker itself is nothing other than that which it makes—for it is simple—as it always is, so it is always acting, and the same to itself both in existing and in acting. Moreover, nothing that is begotten is begotten by itself: therefore, it is not made apart from the maker. He who withdraws one of these loses also the other, for the nature of the one always regards the proper nature of the other. If, therefore, two things are granted, the efficient and the made, they are indeed united to one another, yet in such a way that one precedes and the other follows: the preceding is surely God the efficient, while the following is that which is effected, whatever it may finally be. Nor let anyone distrust those things which we have said, being terrified by the variety of things, as if the construction of such diverse matters were either arduous or unworthy of the divine majesty. For the unique glory of God is the constitution of all things, and this making is, as it were, the body of God. From the maker himself, truly, nothing is evil, and nothing is base. Since these are indeed passions following upon created works, just as rust follows bronze, and filth follows living bodies. But neither did the blacksmith introduce the rust, nor did the begetter of the living body introduce the mud and filth. And in the same way, neither does God introduce evil. What is worse, he ascribes to Him the passions of mortals: envy, pride, ignorance, and weakness.
