He who is Good is neither prideful nor powerless; indeed, the Good itself is God. For the Good is the very power of accomplishing all things. Whatever is born <term>begotten (genitum): brought into being or created</term> is born of God—that is, from the Good and from Him who is all-powerful. # THE WRITINGS OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

...all things, even before he had created all things. Nor is he undeservedly called "the All," since all things are his members <note>The author uses the metaphor of "members" or "limbs" (original: *membra*) to describe how the physical universe is an extension of the Creator's own being.</note>. Therefore, throughout this entire discussion, take care to remember him who is the "One-All," or who is himself the creator of all. 

All things descend from heaven into the earth, into the water, and into the air. Only fire, because it is carried upwards, gives life; that which moves downwards is subservient to it. But indeed, whatever descends from on high is generative <note>original: *generans*; the active, fertilizing principle coming from the heavens</note>; that which emanates upwards is nourishing. The earth alone, standing firm in itself, is the receiver of all things, and it is the restorer of all the various kinds of things that it receives. 

This whole, therefore—as you recall—is either "of all things" or "all things." The soul and the world are held and moved by nature, and they are so varied by the multiform quality of all images <note>In this context, "images" refers to the diverse forms and species that populate the material world.</note> that infinite species of qualities are known to exist through their distinctness; yet they are joined together for this purpose: so that the whole might appear as one, and all things might be seen to come from the one. 

Therefore, the elements by which the whole world is formed are four: namely, fire, water, earth, and air. There is one world, one soul, and one God. 

Now, be fully present with me—I say, as much as your mind is capable and as much as you are skilled in discernment. For the divine logic <term>ratio: the underlying principle or "reason" that governs the universe</term> of divinity, which must be understood through the intense focus of the senses, is most like a torrential river plunging headlong from the heights...

# MERCURIUS TRISMEGISTUS

Man, observing all this, takes it as a task proper to his own diligence, so that just as both worlds <note>Meaning the spiritual/intellectual world and the physical world</note> are an ornament to one another, it is through this divine composition of man that the world is more rightly called <term>kosmos</term> <note>original: "κόσμος"; in Greek, this word carries the double meaning of "order" and "ornament" or "beauty."</note> in the Greek tongue. He knows himself and he knows the world, so that he may remember what is fitting for his own parts; he recognizes which things are for his use and which things he himself must serve. Offering the greatest praises and thanks to God, he venerates His image, being well aware that he is himself the second image of God—for God has two images: namely, the world and man. 

From this it follows that, because man is a single composite being, in that part which is divine—consisting of <term>soul, sense, spirit, and reason</term>—he seems able to ascend to heaven as if from the higher elements. However, in his worldly part—which consists of fire, water, and air—he remains mortal upon the earth, so that he does not leave the duties entrusted to his care abandoned and neglected. For in this way, humanity was made partly divine and partly mortal, existing within a body.

Now, the measure of this dual nature—that is, of man—is above all else religion, which is followed by goodness. This goodness is only seen to be perfect if it is fortified by virtue, holding in contempt the desire for all things that are foreign to it. For there are...

All things are alien to all parts of the divine kinship, whatever earthly things are possessed by bodily desire, which are deservedly called by the name of possessions, since they were not born with us, but began to be possessed by us only later. All such things, therefore, are alien to man, even the body, so that we may despise both those things which we desire, and that from which the vice of desire within us arises. For as the intention of reason leads my mind, man ought to have been constituted thus: that through the contemplation of divinity he might look down upon and despise that part which, joined there, is mortal, by the necessity of preserving the lower world. For so that man might be most complete in both parts, observe that he was formed with four elements of each part: with hands and feet, two of each, and with other members of the body, with which he may serve the lower, that is the earthly world; but in those other parts with the four: the senses of the mind, memory, and foresight, by whose reason he may know and look up to all divine things. Whence it comes about that man pursues the diversities, qualities, effects, and quantities of things with a searching investigation. Hindered, therefore, by the heavy and excessive vice of the body, he cannot discern these causes of the nature of things which are truly his own.

Because of this, any specific point or part of it located within a sphere is called *aeides* in Greek <note>original: "ἀειδής"; this Greek term literally means "unseen" or "formless," and was often used as an etymological root for Hades, the underworld</note>. # THE WORKS OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

For through the understanding of divine religion <note>original: "religionis diuine"; in Hermetic texts, "religion" refers to the philosophical and spiritual discipline of knowing the Creator</note>, by which all things were established, there is born a disdain for—and a remedy for—the flaws of the whole world. 
However, where inexperience and ignorance persist, all vices grow strong and wound the soul with incurable strikes; 
and once infected and corrupted by these same vices, the soul swells as if with poisons, unless for those whose souls find their supreme cure in discipline and intellect. 
If, therefore, this knowledge will benefit only a few, it is worthy to pursue and explain this treatise: 
namely, why the Divinity has deigned to impart His own intelligence and discipline to humans alone. 
Hear, then: God the father and lord, when He created humans after the gods <note>Hermeticism distinguishes between the "First God" (the Creator) and the "Second Gods" (the celestial bodies/stars)</note>, 
weighing them in an equal balance from the more corrupt part of the world and from the divine part, it happened that the flaws of the material world remained mixed within their bodies. 
And other flaws [arise] because of the food and sustenance which we necessarily have in common with all living creatures; from these things, it is inevitable that the desires of lusts and the remaining vices of the mind settle within human souls. 
But for the gods—since they were made from the purest part of nature and require no supports of reason or discipline—immortality and the vigor of a single, eternal age is itself their wisdom and knowledge, yet—

# MERCURY TRISMEGISTUS

In the very vitality of eternity the world <note>original: "mundus"; here meaning the entire cosmos.</note> is moved, and that same vital eternity is the place of the world; for this reason it shall never be corrupted, for the world is surrounded and, as it were, bound by the stable perpetuity of living. It is, therefore, the dispenser of life to all things that are within it, and it is the place of all things that are governed under the sun. The motion of this world consists of a twofold effect: for the world itself is quickened <note>or "given life"</note> from without by eternity, and it in turn quickens those things which are within it, differentiating all things by fixed and established numbers and times, through the effect of the Sun and the course of the stars. All things are temporal, prescribed by divine reason and law.

Earthly time, moreover, is distinguished by the quality of the air and the variety of heat and cold. But celestial time is marked by the return of the stars to the same places in their cyclic conversion. And the world is the receptacle of time, by whose course and motion it is nourished. Time, however, is maintained by order. Order and time bring about the renewal of all things that are in the world through alternation. Since all things are thus, nothing is stable, nothing is fixed, and nothing is immobile, whether among those things being born, those in the heavens, or those on the earth. For God alone—and deservedly alone—is entirely in Himself, and from Himself,

# THE WRITINGS OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

-> ### THE WORKS OF MERCURY TRISMEGISTUS <-

Even if it should happen that something seems to be void of these kinds of things—whether that which appears void be small or large—it nonetheless cannot be empty of spirit <note>The Latin 'spiritus' refers here to a vital, subtle breath or gas that the ancients believed permeated all space.</note> and air. Similarly, we must speak of "place," a word which by itself lacks any meaning. For what a "place" is only becomes apparent from the object that occupies it. Indeed, if the name of the primary object is removed, the meaning is changed; this is why we correctly say "a place for water," "a place for fire," or similar expressions.

For just as it is impossible for anything to be truly void, so also "place" by itself cannot be distinguished for what it is. For if you posit a place without that which belongs within it, the place will appear void—a condition which I do not believe exists in the world. But if the void is nothing, then what a "place" is does not appear by itself, unless you add to it lengths, breadths, or heights, just as you might mark the dimensions of human bodies.

Nothing corporeal can be mixed with his nature; that is, nothing that can be identified by quality, quantity, or numbers. For in Him, nothing of that sort exists. # MERCURY TRISMEGISTUS

the second effect is God, or the discipline of all celestial and earthly things established by divine laws. Therefore, this <term>heimarmene</term> <note>original Greek: εἱμαρμένη; refers to the fixed destiny or "allotted portion" of a person's life</note> and necessity are both joined to each other by an indivisible bond. Of these, the former, *heimarmene*, gives birth to the beginnings of all things, while necessity compels into actual effect those things which depend upon those beginnings. Following these is order—that is, the weaving together and the marking of time for the completion of all things. For nothing exists without the arrangement of order. In all these things, this world is made perfect; for the world itself is carried along by order, or rather, it consists entirely of order. 

These three, then—*heimarmene* (which is <term>fate</term>), necessity, and order—are brought about most especially by the will of God, who governs the world by His own law and by divine reason. From these three, therefore, every "willing" or "not willing" is entirely removed by divine decree. They are not moved by anger, nor are they swayed by favor, but instead they serve the necessity of eternal reason; and this eternity is irreversible, immovable, and indissoluble. 

First, therefore, is *heimarmene*, which receives the offspring of all future things as if a seed had been sown. Necessity follows, by which all things are driven toward their actual effect. Third is order, which preserves the texture <note>The Latin *textum* implies a woven fabric or structure of events</note> of those things which *heimarmene* and necessity have arranged. # TO THE MOST REVEREND FATHER IN CHRIST, LORD GIOVANNI DE’ MEDICI,
## Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church,
### *MARSILIO FICINO of Florence humbly commends himself.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting a landscape with a large bird (possibly an eagle or phoenix) perched upon a round pedestal or nest.</image-desc>

When I had decided to write a letter to you to congratulate you on the cardinal's dignity <note>original: "cardinea dignitate," referring to his recent appointment as a Cardinal at the remarkably young age of 13, though he did not take up the full role until age 16.</note> recently conferred upon you, and I was considering to whom especially I should give it to be delivered to you—someone who might make our congratulation much more pleasing—I suddenly betook myself to the Academy <note>The Platonic Academy in Florence, a circle of scholars led by Ficino under Medici patronage.</note>, hoping that in its inner sanctuaries at least, some greeter most acceptable to you would not be lacking. There, therefore, by a certain divine chance, I first encountered Iamblichus <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) whose work on theurgy and mysteries Ficino translated.</note>, known among the academics as "the Divine," and a great priest there. To him indeed I said, "Greetings, Iamblichus, great priest. At present (as you see), I am about to congratulate Giovanni de’ Medici, the new high priest of the Christian religion. I pray you, if I ask what is right, that you will make our otherwise meager congratulation fuller with your divine words and mysteries." He nodded to my prayers, and so, with this sentiment, Giovanni, great priest, that "Great Priest" <note>Referring to Iamblichus himself as a representative of ancient wisdom.</note> comes to you.

## ARGUMENT CONCERNING THE BOOK OF IAMBLICHUS.

Porphyry, who among the Platonists is called "the Philosopher" on account of his excellence, sent a long letter into Egypt to Anebo the priest, full of various and weighty questions pertaining to all parts of philosophy, especially to God and angels, demons and souls, to providence, fate, prophecies, magic, miracles, sacrifices, and vows. Iamblichus, his pupil, responded to Porphyry's questions. But he introduces Abammon, an Egyptian priest, as the one responding to Porphyry on behalf of his disciple Anebo, to whom Porphyry sent the letter. Of this whole inquiry, therefore, and of the truly divine response—being, as it were, excessively occupied with Plotinus—I have translated almost every single point not word-for-word, but by the sense, so that it ought not to be thought surprising if the discourse appears fragmented in places: especially among the very principles of the disputation, where the loss of words is slighter. Now henceforth, the context of the words also appears more continuous.

<meta>Continuity from page 173: The text continues from the catchword "appea." and completes the sentence as "apparebit" (will appear). Marsilio Ficino is explaining his translation method and his haste in publishing due to the encouragement of his friend Pierleoni.</meta>

...will appear. I have been forced, however, to interject at times some word of my own, either for the sake of continuity or for the sake of clarity <note>original: "intelligentiæ gratia"</note>. Furthermore, the reason for this speedier publication was Pierleoni <note>Pierleone Leoni of Spoleto (d. 1492), a famous physician and scholar who served Lorenzo de' Medici and was a close friend of the translator, Marsilio Ficino.</note>, a man most eager for all secret knowledge. But that which I wonder at most of all is that he always seems to strive for those things which he already possesses. For by a certain divine quality of his intellect, he grasps the secrets of the philosophers—both of the Greeks and the barbarians <note>In this context, "barbarians" refers to the "Ancient Theology" of non-Greek cultures, specifically the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Persians.</note>—even before he has read them.

### *Concerning the knowledge of divine matters.*

**T**HE Egyptian writers, thinking that all things had been discovered by Mercury, inscribed their books to Mercury. Mercury presides over wisdom and eloquence. Pythagoras, Plato, Democritus, Eudoxus, and many others, went to the Egyptian priests. The doctrines of this book are those of the Assyrians and of the Egyptians, and from the columns of Mercury. Pythagoras and Plato learned philosophy from the columns of Mercury in Egypt. The columns of Mercury are full of doctrines. Before any use of reason, there is naturally implanted a notion of the gods. Nay, rather, a certain touch of divinity is better than knowledge: from which is incited the natural appetite for the good, as well as reasoning and judgment. The essential knowledge of divine matters, which is perpetual to the soul, is not in truth this knowledge by which we enjoy God. For in knowledge there is otherness, but [in this] a certain essential and simple contact.

For indeed we cannot reach that very unity, unless by something most unified and by a unity of the mind, which stands above the unique nature <note>Latin: *proprietatem*, referring to the specific characteristics or essence.</note> of both the soul and the mind. The unity itself of the gods unites souls to itself from eternity through their own unities according to a proximity <note>Latin: *contiguitatem*</note> so personal and effective that it appears to be a continuity. The divine intellect gives being to the soul through its own essential understanding. Therefore, the being of the soul is a certain kind of understanding—namely, of God, upon whom it depends. Our very being is to know God: because the primary being of the soul is its intellect, in which being is the same thing as understanding divine matters in perpetual activity.

From that primary being, however, the discursive <note>Referring to "discursive reason," or logical thought that moves step-by-step, as opposed to direct, immediate intuition.</note> powers of the soul are derived. After the gods, we place demons, heroes, and pure souls; these three orders are the attendants <note>Latin: *pedisequi*, literally "foot-followers" or those who follow in the retinue of a superior.</note> of the gods. We cannot reach these attendants of the gods—demons, heroes, and pure souls—by the usual discursive paths of human reason. Instead, it is necessary to rise up to essential and eternal intelligence. Just as the gods are always reached by an innate notion <note>An inborn, intuitive awareness that exists prior to learned experience.</note>, so too these divine attendants are only reached when the soul has laid aside its shifting mode of cognition, which belongs to the rational power—a power which, through intellect and intelligence...

It is acquired, however, in the rational power by a certain zeal, and not so much by the duty of comparison and conjecture, as by the duty of separation and purification. Separable substances do not agree in a certain single genus in which they may be distinguished by differences, but are distinguished by themselves and by the order of their grades, insofar as they are related to the first through different grades of perfection. Essence is the property of all the gods. But the Good itself is above essence: and it is called the cause of good, namely the principle of essential good; accordingly, the grades of the gods are distinguished among themselves according to the grades of essence. In the lowest rational souls, essential good is not present as it is in the gods, but rather a participation in the good according to intellectual beauty. But this is present immovably.

# IAMBLICHUS
## On the order of superior beings.

Our souls are counted among the various classes of divine beings. Heroes are greater than humans, and therefore daemons <note>original: *dæmones*; in this Neoplatonic context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or "distributors" of divine will</note> are much loftier still. The first of the divine beings is the Good itself, followed by the gods; the last are the individual rational souls. Between these two are two intermediate classes: specifically, heroes, who are close to souls, and daemons, who are close to the gods—just as air and water exist as intermediates between the elements of fire and earth.

Although heroes surpass us in power, virtue, beauty, and greatness, they nevertheless share much in common with our soul and its way of life. Daemons are superior to heroes and serve as the ministers of the gods, acting like the skilled assistants of architects in the workmanship of the world. Those things that are unspeakable and hidden within the gods, the daemons express and make manifest. 

Daemons and heroes adapt the universal, simple, and unchanging gifts of the gods for the benefit of lower beings. They reconcile all things and are the authors of a "harmonic consensus" <note>a state of cosmic attunement or agreement</note> and a mutual sympathy <note>original: *compassio*; referring to a natural resonance where all parts of the universe "feel" or react together</note> between all parts of existence. They transmit divine things down to us, and in equal measure, they lead our own concerns back to the divine. Furthermore, they organize the various levels of gifts from the superior beings and ensure that those receiving them are properly prepared to receive them. These different kinds of divine beings differ from one another through a threefold manner of properties,

<meta>catchword: tatum (properties)</meta>

It describes these beings as cosmic coordinators who translate divine gifts into forms that humans can receive and ensure the harmony of the entire universe.</summary>

...ties, namely so far as it pertains to essences and powers and actions. The property of the gods is unity, immobile permanence in themselves, the causes of motions, eminent providence, and having nothing in common with those things for which they provide; and this property is preserved in them according to essence, and power, and action. The property of souls is an inclination toward multitude and motion, and conjunction with the gods, and toward receiving something from others, and filling those things with vital motion, and harmonizing everywhere with all things, partly with those that are abiding, but partly with those that are flowing; and toward tempering all things in themselves and through themselves. This property indeed is preserved in them according to essence, power, and action. The properties of demons are to contain within themselves the gifts of the gods, in a lower way indeed than the gods, but to contain under their idea and reason the conditions of inferior things; while indeed they are multiplied, they are so unitedly; they are also mixed, but unmixedly; finally, they are moved, but stably. Heroes, on the contrary, under the condition of multitude and motion and mixture, possess unity, identity, state, and excellence. Demons and heroes are closest to the extremes: the former indeed to the gods, the latter to souls.

I A M B L I C H U S

## The differences between demons and heroes particularly: 
### since heroes sometimes descend more toward specific and changeable things than demons.

Two mediating ranks, namely demons and heroes, are composed of the properties of the extremes—that is, the gods and the souls. However, in demons <term>daimones; in this context, these are not evil spirits but benevolent mediating spirits between the divine and the human</term>, there is more of the divine nature, while in heroes, there is more of the human nature.

->*How the actions of the superior beings are distinguished*<-
->*from one another.*<-

The gods hold the highest rank of all beings, while souls hold the lowest. The gods are capable of all things, being united in a single moment; souls, on the contrary, can neither do all things, nor act in a single moment, nor are they united. The gods produce and care for all things without being drawn down <note>original Latin: *inclinati*. This suggests the gods provide for the world without losing their station or becoming "tilted" toward the material</note>, whereas souls act with a certain inclination and a turning toward what they govern. The gods are the primary causes; souls perpetually depend upon the will of the gods. With the swiftest power, the gods grasp their ultimate ends together with their beginnings; souls move from one thing to another, proceeding from the imperfect toward the perfect. The gods cannot be contained by any measure or form; souls are held back and overcome by their own inclinations, habits, and impulses. Souls are affected by a desire for lesser things and by a familiarity with the material world, and from these they take on certain qualities.

<summary>This page distinguishes the hierarchy of beings, explaining that while demons and heroes bridge the gap between gods and souls, gods remain perfectly unified and causal while souls are characterized by change, effort, and material attachment.</summary>

### On the intellect & the soul.

**T**he Intellect, the maker of all things, is always present most fully to all the gods, through a single act remaining in itself. The soul is a participant in an intellect that is more divisible and multiform, adapted for governance, and it naturally provides for inanimate things, being affected at different times by different forms. Likewise, there is present to the gods an order from higher causes, and beauty itself, or the causes of both; to the soul, however, there is present order and intellectual beauty. Likewise, in the gods there is a measure powerful over all things; but for the soul, it determines that measure, and through it acts upon certain things. Daemons and heroes, as intermediaries between gods and souls, in a fitting proportion as pertains to the extremes and to themselves, are composed of the properties both of souls and of gods, which we have described in the preceding sections. Therefore, if you wish to apprehend the species of the gods, consider the properties of the lowest rational soul, and attribute the opposites in perfection to the gods. If it pleases you to compose the species of a daemon, compose it from both, attributing more of divinity in the meantime. If, finally, the species of a hero, truly from both, yet bringing in more of the conditions of the soul. He censures Porphyry for distinguishing separate things through their relations to bodies...

For they are not mere "habits" <note>original: "habitus"; here meaning a state or disposition of a physical thing</note> of bodies or material forms, but are self-subsisting and separable—or rather, they are already separate and live before the bodies exist. These separate and separable substances do not become what they are because they have chosen or been assigned a particular lot or province. On the contrary, whatever kind of life and form the soul has brought forth into act within itself before entering the body, it is allotted a corresponding organic body and a nature following from it, which is indeed subjected to the more perfect life of the soul itself.

### *Every divine and incorporeal thing is everywhere.*

Divinity is much more capable of this; far from being "nowhere," it is restrained by no limit. Likewise, the things that exist among us cannot be made or formed unless a certain single <term>demiurgic power</term> <note>The "opifex" or "crafting" power that shapes the material world</note> and a <term>participation in the forms</term> <note>The philosophical idea that physical objects "participate" in or mirror ideal, eternal patterns</note> is diffused through all things. Finally, unless divine things were everywhere, the power of sacrifice would be removed; for sacrifice consists in a certain communion of the gods with men. The gods contain all things primarily because they are contained nowhere. Since earthly things are created and exist by the gift of the gods, whenever they are rendered more ready for divine things, they suddenly obtain the gods <note>That is, they experience the divine presence</note>, who are present here even before the specific natures of earthly things exist. Furthermore, since in any god there is infinite power and an indivisible and incomprehensible nature, they rightly cannot be confined to certain specific places. Likewise, there would be no true union of universal <term>providence</term> <note>The divine care or guidance of the universe</note> among the gods unless all were equally present everywhere. It is also said that some gods are aerial, while others indeed are aquatic, not because they are only in those places, but because they rule there most especially. Priests used to call upon earthly and subterranean gods: they are certainly called such, not because they are only there,

### *On providence, and how the gods are everywhere.*

**W**hen the gods are said to have specifically obtained as their lot various parts of the world, cities, temples, and statues, understand that their essence and power, flourishing everywhere in itself, illustrates this or that most especially: and just as light, remaining in itself, illuminates diverse things everywhere without mixture and division of itself, so do the gods. Just as the light of the Sun is the same, whole, and continuous everywhere, and can neither be divided into parts, nor be shut up anywhere, nor be separated from its own source, nor is it mixed with the air, although it be present: indeed, since it leaves nothing of the light behind, though heat is left by that which heats: Thus the light of each god is present as a whole and indivisibly to the whole world: although it grants its power especially to a certain part that is most adapted to itself. Meanwhile, however, it fills all things in a certain way, on account of a perfect power and an altogether immense causal excellence, whence it perfects all things, and unites extremes with extremes, comprehending all things and itself in itself through the means, and thus reflecting them back to itself, altogether united to itself.

Indeed, the world also imitates this divine function by its circular motion and by a certain connection and reconciliation of its parts into one, transferring elements in turn into elements, and sending the power of the higher things to the lower. One who perceives this manifest statue of the gods <note>Iamblichus describes the entire physical universe as a "statue" or visible image of the invisible divine powers.</note> as being utterly united everywhere, must altogether fear to hold opinions foreign to the gods as the causes of the world—namely, that they are, so to speak, locally separated. 

For if there is no communion of the world with the divine powers <term>numina: the spiritual wills or presence of the gods</term> regarding essence, power, and action, and no mutual distribution or fellowship, then certainly there can be no coextension or mutual distribution according to place. Furthermore, in determining how far this pertains to them, mutual comprehension and mixture cannot be conceived in terms of species or genus. But things that differ entirely from one another in their whole being admit no mutual distribution, mixture, or comprehension at all. 

When the distribution of divine powers occurs throughout the various regions of the world, understand that different regions receive the gifts of the gods differently according to their own specific properties. Considering this, the art of sacred works <term>theurgy: "god-working," or the ritual practice of invoking divine presence through specific symbols and prayers</term> employs specific invocations that seem appropriate to such a distribution and to the property of the divine powers.

### *That every divine thing is alien to passions.*

**T**he divinities superior to us have nothing passible in themselves; and this (so to speak) impassibility they possess not by acquired virtue, but by nature. Nor even does the soul, which is the last of the divine beings, have anything passible: I mean the soul pure from bodies, which is not even touched by the disturbance of that pleasure which is a restoration to nature, since it is an unbegotten supernal life; nor by any dissolving pain, since it is outside every body and the nature divided around the body, and the harmony descending into the body from the principal harmony of the soul; nor does it even need passions preceding sense. For it is not contained by a body, nor is it compelled to perceive bodies through external instruments. ### *On the necessity and liberty of the gods.*

**I**t is necessary that the gods be as they are: not by a necessity brought in from without, but by one that is natural and best for them, and therefore most voluntary; so much so that they would never wish to be otherwise, were the option proposed. Porphyry and many philosophers say that the gods are indeed pure intellects, but that dæmons are certain animate intellects or participations of intellect. But Iamblichus objects that the property of dæmons is not thus rightly established. For souls are also animate intellects and certain participations of intellect itself. Nor, on the other hand, is the property of the gods rightly established, for the gods preside over pure intellects.

### *On the proximity of celestial bodies to incorporeal forms.*

The celestial gods, having their beginning in the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" (mundus intelligibilis) refers to the realm of pure Platonic Forms and Ideas that exist before the physical world.</note>, while they contemplate their own Ideas, move the heavens by this very act of intellect and will, which is most effective and perpetual. Therefore, they rule without effort, which is clearly evident from their always constant order. Thus, the gods affected in this way are joined to the "separate" divinities <note>i.e., the gods who exist purely as spirit/mind, detached from physical bodies.</note> rather than to the physical bodies of the planets. The governance of the heavens cannot distract the gods from their focus on pure intellect; for they rule more powerfully and easily the more attentively they speculate upon that higher realm. For the power of the latter proceeds from the former. The same would also happen to our own living creatures, if only they contemplated the cause from which they arise, which is the source of their power to grow and live.

The Divine Mind, through its Ideas, procreates the souls of the celestial gods, and through those souls, the celestial bodies; it keeps both perpetually joined to itself. By this unity, which is as if common to all, they are all one in a certain act, just as bodies are one among themselves through a certain material potentiality. The celestial gods are completely united to the invisible gods; partly because celestial souls exist outside of bodies, and partly because the higher gods—that is, the Ideas—possess an infinite unity, insofar as all are in any given one: through

For since all gods are defined by unity, one common unity is spread through all: through which they are one in the action of all, directed by one toward one single object, both beginning and end, all at the same point and moment.

### *Concerning providence, and concerning gods and demons.*

The providence of the gods is universal, whereas that of demons is particular. The first God <note>The 'One' or the supreme source of all existence.</note> gives all things to all; the subsequent gods grant some things to all; demons and souls grant things only to some, and only some specific things. There are invisible gods, and there are also visible gods in heaven; there are also demons. Indeed, the gods visible in heaven exist in that very union with the hidden gods; demons, however, are far distant from them, just as if the gods were pure contemplators while the demons themselves were more prone to being occupied in action: for this reason, they are also far distant from the visible gods. Likewise, the essence of both types of gods, as well as their power and providence, is universal, reaching through all things; the nature and providence of demons, however, is particular, concerned with certain things and provinces. Likewise, the gods so far transcend their own bodies, and their bodies are so obedient to them, that they are said to be separate from those bodies; demons, however, [are not].

### *How demons, heroes, and souls differ.*

There are in the gods generative and demiurgic <note>original: "opifices" — referring to the craftsmanship or building of the universe</note> powers, and there are also life-giving powers, which are contained more sublimely in the former. The first are more widely diffused than the second; the second are defined by the first. 

Demons <note>original: "daemones" — in this context, intermediary spirits that are neither inherently good nor evil, but fulfill specific cosmic functions</note> begin after a long progression of these powers, at the point where they are already diverted into a great deal of partition. 

Heroes <note>Semi-divine beings or elevated spirits that bridge the gap between humans and the divine</note> are defined by the second group of powers—that is, the life-giving ones—before they reach the final stage. For in the final stage of these powers, souls begin. 

Therefore, the duty of demons is the craftsmanship concerning worldly natures, to pierce through and perfect everything down to individual things, and to bind souls to bodies. But the duty of heroes is to give life, to reason, to guard souls, and to release them from bodies. The duty of demons is broader than that of heroes. The former work more concerning the universe as a whole, while the latter work rather concerning individual souls. We do not say that souls are created, but that they receive something from demons and heroes...

<meta>catchword: receive from demons</meta>

<summary>This page defines the hierarchical roles of gods as architects and demons as ministers, while refuting Porphyry's suggestion that gods are influenced by human emotions. It further distinguishes between demons, who govern material nature, and heroes, who oversee the life and liberation of individual souls.</summary>

...and [the soul] adds many things from itself besides, and begins its own duty near the boundary of divine things. This is not because divine things do not act further, but because souls are admitted at the furthest reaches of divine duties. Likewise, the soul can bring forth such various forms of living from itself that, according to their suitability, it may inhabit every region of the world. It can also commune with whomever it wishes, and return again into itself, and join itself both to the gods and to lower beings, insofar as it brings forth the principles of divine things like an inferior <note>The soul acts as a 'mirror' or 'echo' of the higher divine laws</note>: and even if it often joins with the gods through the mediation of demons and heroes, it can also join itself to the gods by its own specific middle nature, which differs from theirs. The soul sometimes reconciles itself to divine things through other harmonies of its essence and actions than those which demons use to join with the higher powers. Although the soul does not always maintain a consistent course of life, nevertheless, often illuminated by the benevolent will of the gods, it transcends the demons toward an **angelic life** rather than a merely **animal** one. Although the soul seems to exhibit all principles and whole <term>species|Forms or eternal patterns in the Platonic sense</term> within itself, it is nevertheless always determined according to some one thing—that is, a single form; and meanwhile, it coordinates itself with various others from preceding causes, moving itself by its own power.

*When different deities appear and act in different ways.*

All higher beings, when invoked, come into view: but some appear under different forms and powers than others. The souls of the stars also move the sight in certain new ways. The visions <note>original: "visa" — referring to theophanies or appearances during ritual</note> of the gods appear uniform and most simple; those of the archangels are somewhat less uniform or simple; those of the angels even less so; those of demons are varied; those of the **principalities** <note>original: "principatuum" — a specific rank in the celestial hierarchy responsible for governing large regions or nations</note> are even more varied, but with a wondrous order in their variety; those of heroes are almost similar to these; those of the **princes** <note>original: "principes" — likely referring to 'Archons' or worldly rulers of the sublunary realm, often depicted as more turbulent or difficult</note> are extremely varied and little ordered; and the visions of particular souls, naturally, are uniform. For since the higher beings are different in their natures and actions, and appear to each in their own way, they rightly appear in different ways to different people. The gods come into view as entirely health-giving <note>original: "salutares" — bringing safety, preservation, and spiritual health</note>; archangels are both terrifying and gentle at once; angels are milder; demons are to be feared; heroes are less awe-inspiring; principalities are astonishing; princes are harmful and hostile; and souls are similar to heroes, although inferior. The images of the gods appear completely immutable in their magnitude, form, shape, and action. Those of archangels and angels are gradually less immutable, yet they remain close to the gods. Those of demons are indeed mutable in magnitude and form, for to these...

Those of **Souls** are things that contribute to human life through a truly familiar encounter. **Porphyry** <note>A Phoenician philosopher and student of Plotinus who often questioned the mechanics of traditional religion.</note> recounted an opinion stating that it is common to gods, angels, demons, and finally all superior beings, that when they appear, they show themselves off and boast wonderfully, and produce an imaginary likeness of themselves. **Iamblichus** refutes both points. A god, an angel, and a good demon, when they appear, teach a person what their essence truly is and of what kind, speaking nothing beyond or short of the truth. For just as light naturally and constantly follows the Sun, so truth follows God and his attendants—especially since they are perfect and full, and neither need nor are able to claim for themselves more than what they are. the deifying and priestly faculty, they fail, then indeed it is not the good spirits that are desired that meet us, but worse and evil ones under the pretext of good ones. For evil spirits often transform themselves into the likeness of good ones, and they come boasting and claiming for themselves more than they are. Indeed, where a first falsified beginning arises, much falsehood proceeds from that perversity. Priests must examine the apparitions of spirits by the rule of the entire order, and remember that boasting arrogance is in no way characteristic of true and good spirits; they must take care that there is never a departure from the ritual of the sacred rites. And if, in an error of apparition, some spirits should suddenly arrive in an insolent manner, it is not right to judge the common and entire nature and condition of the divine beings based on their behavior. For those things which have been proven in sacred matters through many centuries and with painstaking labor must not be wickedly changed by judging rashly based on some things that happen suddenly. And even if false spirits lie, the good ones are truthful and legitimate regarding the fire. For in every genus, the primary things first begin from themselves and provide for themselves that which they exhibit to others: and this occurs in essence, life, and motion.

<meta>This page continues the refutation of the idea that divine beings present themselves through deceptive illusions. It builds on the previous argument that gods, angels, and good spirits are inherently truthful and show their true essence to the practitioner, rather than mere "phantasms."</meta>

-># IAMBLICHUS<-

<page-num>218</page-num>

Similarly, the higher beings, presenting truth to everyone, first speak true things about themselves, and they reveal their very essence especially to those who contemplate them. Therefore, they rightly show to the priests the fire to be beheld by itself and in its own form. For it is not the nature of heat to produce cold, nor of light to darken and hide, nor for anything that acts through its essence to ever do the opposite. A phantasm <note>original: *Phantasma*, meaning an illusory appearance or ghost-like image</note>, that is, a likeness sent by something without its actual nature, but only in the manner of a reflection in a mirror, vainly draws the soul of the one watching. It deceives while pretending to be something whose nature it does not possess. It is therefore a cause of falsehood, which in no way fits any true essence; therefore, it does not fit the gods. Rather, they and their followers reveal images of themselves that are not thin and empty, but natural and true—not (as I said) vain mirror-reflections. For why would they send such things? Not to demonstrate their essence and power, for those reflections are entirely lacking in those qualities compared to the divine nature. Nor for the benefit of those watching: for what benefit is there in a lie and simulated deception? Finally, they do not send them because it is their nature to cast out an image <note>original: *idolum*, here referring to a mental image or representation cast off from a thing</note> from themselves; for an essence is firm and remains within itself, and thus...

<meta>catchword: essence</meta>

---

<page-num>219</page-num>

-># ON THE MYSTERIES<-

...for the sake of essence and truth, it in no way sends into another any fallacious and deceptive imitation of itself that might pretend to be something whose nature it does not have. Therefore, neither the gods nor those who follow them transform their nature into any likenesses, nor do they produce these from themselves into something else; rather, they illuminate and demonstrate the true forms of themselves in the true dispositions <note>original: *moribus*, referring to the internal state or "character" of the soul</note> of the soul.

**Note:** Similar to this is the idea that the blessed mind in the heavenly homeland <note>original: *in patria*, a common theological term for heaven or the ultimate spiritual home of the soul</note> sees the divine essence, not through an image created by it which would be entirely deficient, but through that very essence itself: just as one who sees light through light and within light, and not like one who sees color through light or a body in a mirror. Separate substances <note>A philosophical term for immaterial beings like angels or gods who exist apart from physical matter.</note> do not have any genus in common with each other.

Likewise, gods, angels, and good demons do not appear in an illusory <note>original: *phantastico*</note> manner, but in a way that is entirely their own and true. However, evil spirits appear in an illusory and deceptive way. Nor is it right for us to judge, based on the condition in which these evil spirits appear, the manner in which the good ones shape the soul with their presence.

**Porphyry** says that knowledge of divine things is a sacred matter, while ignorance is profane. **Iamblichus** confirms these points: because since the gods act upon all beings through intelligence <note>original: *intelligentiam*</note>, we rightly [know them] through...

the understanding of beings pleases and is approved by the gods; but he <note>Iamblichus</note> places religious operation before intellect, as it alone is effective for acquiring the soul's deifying union with God. Such is the power of sacred rites performed correctly for God, that even if you are ignorant of them, yet observe them piously, they have no less efficacy. For it is not intellect that joins the sacrificers to God; otherwise, philosophers would achieve deifying union <note>original: *unionem deificam*, a central Neoplatonic goal of becoming one with the divine</note>.

-># On the power of the sacraments.<-

Proper observance of the divine precepts and works, which exceed all intellect, and the wondrous power of symbols and sacraments <note>original: *sacramentorum*, referring here to theurgic rites or sacred mysteries</note>, provides us with deifying union through prayers to the deities alone. When we perform sacred acts, we do not complete the sacraments through intellect, otherwise their action would be intellectual and would originate from us. On the contrary, even when we do not understand them, these rites perform their own work, and the power of the gods to which these refer recognizes its own ineffable images from itself, not excited by our intellects. For universal causes are not moved by particular effects, and therefore neither by our intellects 

<column-break/>

<page-num>221</page-num>
<header>ON THE MYSTERIES</header>

are divine things principally moved to act. However, it is necessary that intellect, an excellent disposition, and purity precede these acts as certain "co-causes." But those things which principally provoke the divine will are the divine sacraments themselves; and thus divine things are incited by themselves, and do not receive the beginning of their action from any subordinate source. Do not think, therefore, that the whole authority of effective reason in sacraments lies within us, nor that their true work is completed through the truth of our intellect, or that these rites "lie" because of our own deception. For even if we were to know the proper consequences of every kind of thing, we do not suddenly attain the truth of them in practice merely by knowing. Without knowledge, indeed, an effective unity with divine things never arrives, yet it is not entirely the same thing as knowledge. Therefore, divine purity is not achieved through right knowledge, just as bodily purity is not achieved merely through health; rather, it is united above knowledge—a "purified purity"—that is to say, through a power superior to knowledge. Therefore, nothing else human within us contributes anything to the final goal of divine actions. Conclude here the opinion of Iamblichus, the Egyptians, and the Assyrians. Just as in agriculture, medicine, or the art of image-making <note>The text cuts off here at *arte ima...*, likely referring to *arte imaginum* or theurgy as a craft</note>...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that spiritual union with the divine is achieved through the objective power of sacred rituals (theurgy) rather than through intellectual philosophy alone. He asserts that these rites function through divine power that recognizes its own symbols, independent of the practitioner's full understanding.</summary>

...origin, by human intercourse, man appropriately adapts the material, but the superior and universal cause applies the form. So it is in sacrifice: when symbols and <term>synthemata</term> <note>original: *synthemata*; these are sacred "tokens" or "signatures" believed to be placed in the natural world by the gods to allow for communication with the divine</note>—that is, signs and sacraments—are employed, the priest provides certain material elements according to the established order of beauty, but God impresses the effective power upon these sacraments.

->What prophecy is and whence it comes.<-

Prophecy <note>original: *Vaticinium*</note> itself is produced neither by art, nor by nature, nor by natural or animal reasons or movements. It does not come about in any [human] way; rather, it is surely eternal, sent down to us from the divine. All prophetic power is referred back to the gods, and all its authority resides in them and is handed down from them, being perfected by divine works or signs. It possesses divine spectacles and contemplations endowed with true knowledge. All other things are subjected as mere instruments to this gift of foretelling sent from the divine—whether they pertain to the soul or the body, or exist within the nature of the whole or within individual natures. Indeed, places and such things are required for prophecy only as the "matter" or setting. It is not fitting to derive prophecy without a cause—that is, from things that have no foreknowledge in themselves—but rather from the gods, who contain within themselves the boundaries of all knowledge

<meta>catchword: of things</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>223</page-num>
<header>ON THE MYSTERIES</header>

of things. It is fitting to contemplate prophecy as it is distributed throughout the whole world and throughout all the distinct natures within the world. Thus, the cause of prophecy is primary and most universal, possessing in itself whatever it provides to those who participate in it. It especially provides the truth which prophecy requires, and primarily holds within itself the essence and cause of all things that happen; from these, the perpetual sequence of foretelling necessarily proceeds. 

Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus and a critic of some theurgic practices, to whom Iamblichus is responding in this work</note> says: "When we sleep, we sometimes foresee the future without any awareness of our present state, even if we are not at all moved into a state of ecstasy." He means, I believe, that this happens not so much by an external influence flowing in from the divine at that moment, as from the very nature of the soul and the mind's own power to foretell. 

Iamblichus says: Dreams which arise from human causes—whether through our own nature, or through our emotions, thoughts, and actions—reach the truth only very rarely, far too obscurely, and more often than not by mere chance.

Furthermore, if through this universal form it is joined to the very minds of the gods, it will see those things that belong to the higher world as well as to this one. It does so according to the manner of divine providence. King Lysander had besieged the city of Aphytis, and in a dream he was commanded by Ammon <note>An Egyptian deity often identified with Zeus</note> to lift the siege. Many similar things happen daily that are beyond human speech and reason.

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s discussion on divine inspiration (enthusiasm) and how it differs from human states of waking and sleeping. # IAMBLICHUS

Those moved by divine power foretell the future, remaining so awake that they even use their senses, yet in the meantime, they are not in possession of human reason. Iamblichus says that souls which truly foretell and are inspired <note>original: "afflatosq;" from *afflatus*, literally a "breathing into" or divine breath</note>—even when they seem to sleep—do not sleep; and when they are awake, they are not properly awake, nor do they use their senses in the manner of humans. Souls that are divinely inspired and stirred have completely submitted their life to the god who breathes into them. Therefore, whether they submit themselves as a vehicle or as an instrument, they have set aside their former way of life and have either exchanged their own life for a divine one, or they lead their life entirely toward the god. Thus, they neither use their senses, nor are they awake in the way those with alert senses are, nor do they foretell or move by any human impulse or custom. They do not notice their own state, nor do they produce any knowledge or action of their own, but everything is conducted there under a divine form and action.

<margin>Many miracles are performed by the prophets.</margin>
That those divinely inspired do not live by their own animal life at that time is clear, because many of them are not burned when fire is brought near, since the god breathing within them evidently repels the fire. Or if they are burned, they do not feel it, nor do they perceive stings, or scrapings, or any torments. Likewise,

Through these things, it is clear that they do not live a human or animal life using senses and impulse, but a divine one, as if their soul were at rest <term>ocietur: from *otium*, meaning the soul is in a state of "holy leisure" or inactivity, stepping aside for the divine</term>, and the god is there in place of the soul, moving them as if he were a more excellent soul. There are various types of divinely inspired people, partly due to the variety of the gods (who inspire in different ways), and partly due to the difference in the modes of inspiration. These modes are as follows: either the god himself occupies us, or we devote ourselves to him and become entirely his, or we perform an action in common with the god. Likewise, we may come to possess the lowest divine powers, or the middle, or the supreme. Sometimes it is the bare presence of the god; sometimes, beyond presence, a communion occurs; and sometimes, beyond this, a union <term>unio: the highest state of Neoplatonic mystical experience where the soul and the One become one</term> is achieved. <meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s argument regarding the nature of divine inspiration. On the previous page, he began describing the physical signs of the spirit's presence. # IAMBLICHUS

...seized by divine fury, they prophesy truly. Later writers, however, by adding a ‘t’, gave it the name *mantia* <note>original: "mantiam." The author is likely referencing the Greek word for prophecy, *manteia*, and its linguistic connection to *mania*, or madness.</note>. Likewise, priests, sibyls, and prophets, as long as they remain in their right minds <note>original: "prudentes," meaning sane or rational</note>, foresee very little and only obscurely, or nothing at all; but when they are seized by a god, they prophesy truly. Hence, among many nations, they have foreseen dangers threatening by divine will, warned the people, and through sacrifices, they have appeased divine Nemesis <note>The goddess who distributed fortune and enacted retribution to maintain balance.</note>. He also says that a premonition made by human skill is called "conjectural opinion," and it is of no importance if compared to divine inspiration and prophecy. Iamblichus says that divine inspiration and prophecy are not in the mind or soul, either as a quality in a subject or as an action in an agent, but are entirely the act of God himself, depending simply upon God. I call it an "act" performed by God in the mind or soul simply, as if in instruments being free from all their own motion, and thus true premonitions are given. But if any motion from the body or soul, or any such quality, is introduced or precedes it in the meantime, the visions are confused; there will be neither true prophecies nor a legitimate divine inspiration where anything human is mixed in. There were generally three opinions concerning divine inspiration and prophecy. The first referred the cause 

<meta>catchword: eius (of it)</meta>

<column-break/>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

of it to the soul, the second to the body, and the third to the combination of both. The first places it in that state in which the soul is entirely reduced into the divine spirit, or into the mind, or when its action has become more vehement or more ample; or when thought has become sharp and most rapid in motion, or when the mind has grown heated. The second places its cause in the body, when it has a certain "complexion" <note>original: "complexionem," referring to the balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were thought to determine temperament.</note>, namely either melancholic <note>In ancient medicine, an excess of black bile was thought to cause both madness and profound insight.</note> or temperate, or a certain elemental quality, or moreover a special spirit. The third says its cause is a certain proportion by which the body and soul are joined together. Iamblichus says that inspiration is not the work of the soul, or the body, or the combination, nor does it have its cause in them. For that prophetic breath <note>original: "afflatus fatidicus"</note> acts both in foretelling and in accomplishing things beyond all the custom of human nature. However, a human being, or any part of a human being, cannot progress beyond its own limits to divine limits; nor can superior things be generated by inferior ones. Therefore, the cause of this is solely divinity itself, namely when lights descend from the gods into us, and spirits are delivered by them, and there is present with us the lordship and power from that place.

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s argument that divine inspiration is an act of God, not a product of human psychology. # IAMBLICHUS

...absolute, encompassing all things that are within us, and entirely banishing our own awareness and movement, bringing forth speech through the human being indeed, but not by the human’s own thought; rather, pronouncing these things through the mouth of one raving and placed outside of himself <note>The Latin "extra se positi" describes the state of ecstasy—literally "standing outside oneself"—where the person's own identity is suspended.</note>, while whatever is in us serves the deity entirely and yields to the sole governing divine action. Porphyry says <margin>☉</margin> that music brings passions into the soul, and likewise calms them, and that different sounds suit different souls and characters. Likewise, it changes the complexions and affections of the body, stirs up fury, and restrains fury. Iamblichus grants these points, but denies that these are the causes of divine inspiration <note>original: "afflatus diuini." Iamblichus distinguishes between the emotional effects of music and the actual presence of a god.</note>: since these things are human—partly natural, partly artificial—and have nothing divine within themselves. Porphyry seems to suspect this, saying that some are inspired when they hear flutes, or cymbals, or drums, and others when they hear other melodies. To the various orders of gods in the world, various species of motions correspond, specific ones to specific gods. From these, various melodies flow forth, which similarly agree through their own movements with the specific gods who are the principles of those motions. Since these gods are everywhere,

<column-break/>

## ON THE MYSTERIES

and impart their gifts especially to those who are their own, they are present primarily through melodies that are especially congruent with them; and creeping into our spirits <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to the *pneuma*, a subtle substance thought to connect the physical body to the immaterial soul.</note> affected by these melodies, they take possession of the human being, and soon fill them entirely with their own essence and power. The cause of this inspiration is not so much the passion of the human being excited by music, as it is the congruence of the music itself to the god, to which the god is naturally present. Things that come to sight are too imaginary and relate rather to intelligible things. Things that come to the senses below hearing are too material; things that come to hearing are "middle" things and suit the soul; and when they are introduced into the spirit with movement, emotion, and meaning, they affect it vehemently—the soul on one hand, and the body on the other. From this, the whole human being, according to the properties of the melodies, becomes a vessel <term>susceptaculum</term> <note>A technical term for a human "receptacle" capable of receiving and holding divine power.</note> of this deity or that one; and those who are inspired behave in various ways in movement and rest and other states, according to the diversity of the deities by whom they are principally inspired, rather than according to the difference in the music. For this affection of sound has already ceased when God acts. The soul in the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure forms and divine truths, existing above the physical world.</note> heard divine harmony, which it remembers here when it hears melodies containing a trace of the divine; and remembering it, it is vehemently affected by it, if it is from...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that music induces divine inspiration not through human emotion, but because certain melodies share a mathematical or "harmonic" resonance with specific gods. <meta>This page continues Iamblichus's rebuttal of Porphyry's naturalistic explanations for divine possession. Iamblichus argues that the effects of music and physical environments on the soul are merely preparations or reflections, not the cause of prophecy, which originates solely from the presence of the divine.</meta>

-># IAMBLICHVS<-

...the number of souls that especially contemplated the idea of harmony itself in their homeland <note>original: "in patria." In Neoplatonic thought, the "homeland" refers to the intelligible or divine realm from which the soul descends into the body.</note>. Indeed, having become familiar with God through an affection of this kind, the soul is now inspired by a certain unique presence of God, from which she performs wonders. Therefore, the cause of this inspiration and miracle is not a passion brought in by sounds, nor is it the nature of the soul being composed of harmony, but rather a likeness to God and the presence of God.

Much less should it be said that inspiration consists in this: that through music and the inspiration itself, certain superfluous things congealed in the soul and body are purged <note>Iamblichus is rejecting the Aristotelian idea of "catharsis" or medical purging as an explanation for the religious ecstasy of the mysteries.</note>. The power of prophecy is not derived from a certain physical constitution; for the gifts of the gods are not breathed in varying ways according to bodily variety. For the divine gift is <term>impassible</term> <note>original: "impatibile." This means the divine gift cannot be affected, changed, or harmed by external, material forces.</note>, and is given above the power of nature through the proper action of God.

Neither water, nor air, nor any other bodily thing provides prophecy; but rather the sacred rites performed around these things—or more truly, the purification of the mind along with the purification of the <term>vehicle</term> <note>original: "vehiculi." This refers to the "astral body" or "spirit-vehicle," a subtle substance that Neoplatonists believed connected the immaterial soul to the heavy physical body.</note>, and the fixed intention toward God—receives the divine power that is everywhere and always most ready. When the inspired mind both speaks and acts above and contrary to the habit of nature, the cause of such inspiration is not natural, whether from our body, the quality of a place, or the celestial disposition at the birth of the

<meta>continuity: mine,</meta>

->## ON THE MYSTERIES<-

man, or by his own action; but these things happen from the presence of God. Hence, the various types of inspired people do not follow the natural varieties within us, but rather the different species of both the inspiring deities and the modes by which we participate in the divine presence.

Therefore, as for why some divinely inspired men remain still, while others are agitated, some seek mountains and deserts, and others behave differently: this does not proceed from the differences of natural causes in us, or places, or the music they have recently heard or are hearing. Instead, it comes from the various properties of the gods by whom the inspired are governed, and from the various modes of inspiration.

Porphyry brings forward three oracles out of many: one at **Colophon**, where prophecy came from drinking water; another at **Delphi**, where the priestess would prophesy sitting at the mouth of a cave; and a third at **Branchidae**, where they prophesied by drawing vapor from the water <note>These were the three most prestigious oracular sites in the Greek world: the Oracle of Apollo at Colophon (Clarus), the Pythia at Delphi, and the Didymaean oracle at Branchidae near Miletus.</note>. Each of these acts and operates effects around itself according to the mode of its own nature; therefore, the spirits themselves which, hanging from the gods, arouse and excite men, exceed every natural and human movement in this very work. For just as when the Sun arrives, darkness cannot withstand its presence but suddenly flees away, in no way hindering the sun; so when the power of the gods shines forth from every side, filling all things with good, every disturbance that

is accustomed to happen because of evil spirits finds no place, but is suddenly dispersed. Magical images made of solid material preserve their power for a longer time. The gods give signs of the future in entrails and birds, and through new portents of the stars, from which human sagacity conjectures events by the proportion of the signs of their coming—for instance, from the fall of a bird, the fall of a man; from a defect of limbs in the entrails, a failure; or from a falling star, the downfall of leaders. [the gods] perform deeds and pre-signify events through new portents <note>original: "ostenta." These are marvelous or unnatural signs interpreted as divine omens.</note> and various signs; meanwhile, for the same cause and occasion, they sharpen our own natural sagacity. In these portents, the entrails of animals are transformed against their natural state by the animals' own souls, by the **daemon** <term>original: "daemone." In this context, a daemon is not an evil spirit but a mediating divinity or guardian spirit that bridges the gap between gods and the physical world.</term> presiding over them, and by the motion of the air and the heavens. This happens contrary to nature and according to the will of the gods to provide warnings to humanity. That this occurs by divine power is evident, because often certain principal organs necessary for life are not found in the animals, having been suddenly and miraculously removed, even though they must have been present shortly before.

In the taking of **auguries** <note>original: "auguriis." The ancient practice of divining the future or the will of the gods by observing the flight, songs, or behavior of birds.</note>, birds are moved miraculously by their own souls, by their presiding daemon, and by the motion of the air and the heavens. From the heavens, a power descends through the entire atmosphere, shaping and moving it according to the will of the gods to produce signs. I say this "will" is pre-signified and decreed from the beginning. Thus, birds often hurl themselves down, or strike against things, or otherwise kill themselves while contributing to a sign; they do this not of their own accord, but drawn by divine power. Certain flames resembling stars are also produced by divine power; these are easily formed in the air as signs of the future at the command of the celestial gods, when the

### ON THE MYSTERIES

highest air is ignited. This upper air is most easily shaped and directed into fire, especially by the gods. Occasionally, certain influences from the celestial bodies descend into this lower air, leading to the creation and movement of star-like phenomena similar to the heavenly bodies in their light, power, and motion. 

The **World-Animal** <term>original: "Mundanum animal." A central concept in Neoplatonism where the entire universe is viewed as a single, living, interconnected organism animated by a World Soul.</term> is so united with itself that its members suffer together <note>original: "compatiantur." This refers to 'cosmic sympathy,' the idea that all parts of the universe react to one another across great distances.</note> and are moved together, even those parts that seem remote from one another, as if they were close, like the limbs of a single animal. This union and "sympathy" allows the gods to exhibit signs to humans, first through the heavens and subsequently through the air. 

The gods do not act immediately, but through intermediate instruments—namely daemons, souls, natures, and all things dependent on these. They produce signs for humans by starting from a single principle and then diffusing a descending motion from themselves wherever they wish. Therefore, they govern these individual things without being bound or coordinated to the world of **generated things** <note>original: "generabilia." This refers to the physical world of birth, decay, and constant change, as opposed to the eternal realm of the gods.</note>. Just as in their creation and providence, their intellect is not diverted toward our affairs when exhibiting signs; rather, while the divine intellect remains within itself, it draws all signs and prophecy back toward itself, noticing that they proceed from its own being. All prophets confess that prophecy occurs through the gods or daemons.

Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234 – c. 305 AD) was a philosopher who wrote a critical letter to an Egyptian priest named Anebo, questioning the logic of religious rituals. This book is Iamblichus's detailed defense.</note> wonders why the gods would so subserviently serve humans that some prophets even practice **divination through flour** <term>original: "per farinam uaticinentur." This refers to aleuromancy, an ancient method of fortune-telling using flour or meal, which Porphyry considered beneath the dignity of the gods.</term>. Iamblichus responds that the gods do not do this out of a sense of service or obedience, but from an abundance of power and goodness. Because they contain the causes of all things within themselves, they remain within themselves without turning toward subordinate things, yet they bestow gifts and signs upon them according to their degree of preparation—just as the sun provides light to transparent objects and to the eyes. 

Because we see that humans care for things beneath them by turning toward their work, being distracted by various tasks, and laboring away from their own centers, we wrongly suspect the gods provide for the world in the same way. On the contrary, insofar as the gods are turned toward themselves and their own singular form (which is the ultimate cause of all inferior things), they act, move, and govern everything. They are not distracted by variety; instead, from a single principle and a simple command, they set all things in motion, which then depend on them in a specific order of succession. Nor do they bend themselves down toward lower things; rather, remaining in their own state and fullness, they bring all things into harmony with themselves. God supplies various modes of prophecy, not because he is himself distracted, but he suggests them all through an indivisible command and a simple form, and to different...

<meta>catchword: times</meta>

---

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...times he suggests different modes, without being varied by time himself. Instead, he inspires them all with the same eternal stroke of mind and will, even though these are unfolded at different times. Nor is he contained or distracted by portents <note>original: "ostentis." These are marvelous or unnatural signs interpreted as divine omens.</note>, but embracing all signs in his own singular form, he expresses them from that form while remaining within himself, handing everything down through a single act of will. 

Such is the exuberance of **providence** <term>original: "providentiae." In this philosophical context, providence is the divine care and orderly direction of the universe, ensuring that even small things reflect the higher truth.</term> in showing us signs, that it provides indications of the future even in pebbles, rods, wood, stones, grain, and flour. In these, it wonderfully seems to provide a soul to the inanimate, motion to the immobile, and a certain intelligence to those lacking reason, as if these objects actually know the future they are portending to us. 

And just as God often speaks wisdom through simple-minded men <note>original: "fatuos homines." Iamblichus refers to the idea that divine truth can manifest through those without formal education or "rational" status, proving the source is divine rather than human intellect.</note>, declaring that it is not the man speaking there but God, so through the lowliest things he portends the future. He stands far above these things, and through all of them, he instructs our intellect. Through the lowest things which lack knowledge, God reveals certain things superior in knowledge, whereby he testifies that he far transcends nature. While he offers various signs, he is not confined by them, nor distracted by them, but stands in his own singular and indivisible form...
