->*No work of any efficacy occurs in sacred rites except through the power, and indeed the presence, of some divine being.*<-

IN religion, no work of any miraculous efficacy can be performed unless one of the higher beings is present, as a witness and a fulfiller of the work. Indeed, the gods lead the perfected works, the angels <term>original: "angeli." In Neoplatonism, angels are messengers or intermediaries between gods and humans, not necessarily the winged figures of later tradition.</term> lead the intermediate ones, and the demons <term>original: "dæmones." These are "daimons," or spirit-beings that bridge the gap between the divine and the physical world; they are not inherently "evil" in this context.</term> lead the third. Human nature can neither undertake reasoning nor speech concerning the gods without the gods themselves, much less is it able to perform divine works without them. For human nature is so weak and dull that it has no remedy for its own nothingness, unless a certain portion of divine light descends from above—without which, nothing we do is divine. Just as those are mistaken who trust they can create a soul from inanimate things or a mind from the mindless, so too are they mistaken who believe they can create divine things from non-divine things, or perform the specific works of the gods without the gods. Such works include prophecies, miracles, and similar phenomena like apparitions and purifications <term>original: "expiationes." These were rituals meant to cleanse a person or place of spiritual pollution.</term>.

<meta>catchword: Divine beings</meta>

<column-break/>

ON THE MYSTERIES. 251 <page-num>251</page-num>

<warning>Faint ghosting/offset text at the top of page 251 repeats the section summary: "The divine beings invoked are present with us, not by compulsion, but of their own will."</warning>

->*The divine beings invoked are present with us, not by compulsion, but of their own will.*<-

IT is a settled matter that the effective works of religion are completed by the presence of gods, angels, and demons. Porphyry <note>Porphyry was Iamblichus's teacher and rival; he often questioned whether rituals were just psychological or if they truly commanded the gods.</note>, indeed, suspects that the divine beings are drawn to these rituals by some necessity of invocation <note>Porphyry worried that rituals implied humans were "ordering" the gods around.</note>. Iamblichus denies that necessity is imposed upon the divine beings either by man or by the world; since they are immaterial, they do not receive an order that comes from the outside. Likewise, invocation and sacred ritual bring the priests close to the divine beings through a kind of assimilation and familiarity—no violence is inflicted upon the priests, much less is it inflicted upon the divine beings. God, and the entire choir of divine beings joined to God, is above every necessity coming from the outside. Prophecy is fulfilled while the priest performs sacred rites; even then, no passive suffering <term>original: "passio." In ancient philosophy, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon by an external force, rather than being the source of action.</term> falls upon the priest or the diviner when they are divinely inspired; much less does it fall upon the divine beings, who do not descend into souls unless those souls are free from such passion. Nor should it be said that the prophetic soul is a mere middle instrument for the divine, nor that the priest who invokes is the efficient cause of divine works; rather, God is all, God can do all, and God fills all by himself—

<summary>This page argues that religious rituals only work because the gods choose to be present, and that humans lack the natural power to perform miracles or prophecy without divine light. Iamblichus corrects Porphyry by explaining that rituals do not "force" the gods to appear through magic, but rather prepare the human soul to be a fit vessel for their willing presence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s argument from the previous page, where he asserted that human nature is insufficient for divine works without higher intervention. Here, he specifically critiques the views of his predecessor and rival, Porphyry, regarding the origin of miracles and prophecy. The catchword "Opera" from page 252 correctly leads into the heading on page 253.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS ON THE MYSTERIES

itself. Indeed, human nature has no efficacy in these matters; for it is like a plaything <note>original: "ludus." This draws on the Platonic idea that human affairs are a kind of divine "play" or game compared to the serious reality of the gods.</note> compared to divinity. We mock those who say a god is present to certain people by a mere chance, or through the power of a celestial configuration <note>i.e., an astrological birth chart.</note> at the time of their birth. For it is not fitting for unbegotten and universal causes to be enslaved to anyone through the circumstances of birth, or its cycles, or through causes that are foreign to their nature. 

Certain people—because they did not want to burden God with cares, and because they could not imagine any mode of craftsmanship or providence other than the kind involving human anxiety—denied that the gods act and provide for us at all. Similarly, those who fail to see the excellent way in which the gods are present (without labor and without changing their own nature) would deny that the gods take part in prophecies and miracles. The manner in which all these things happen, however, is proper to the gods and known only to them. 

Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a philosopher who raised skeptical questions about the reality of religious rituals, suggesting they might just be psychological phenomena.</note> says that divine works, such as prophecies and miracles, are sometimes merely certain passions of the soul stirred up from small sparks, and that the soul by its own power can imagine, speak, and perform these things. Iamblichus, however, says that a divine work is neither done by chance (since it is ordered), nor by a human being (who is far inferior to the work): for it is necessary that a divine work be performed by divinity. Therefore, all works similar to divinity spring not from human nature, but from divine nature.

<column-break/>

->*The works of miracles and prophecy do not occur through*<-
->*any power of the stars, the body, or the soul, but by the*<-
->*pure and free power of God.*<-

The human soul is both limited to a single species and is too heavily overshadowed by the decaying body; therefore, it has no effective power for divine work. But if we ever seem to be able to do something of the sort in some way, we only do it by a divine illumination flowing from above, through which we seem to be a participant in divine action. 

If divine works were performed by the soul, then by the very nature and specific power of a soul—provided it possessed virtue and wisdom—either that soul, or indeed every soul, would perform such things. But as it is, not every soul does this; and even the soul that seems perfect in human terms is still imperfect compared to divine things. Therefore, it is not the soul, but divinity itself that is the cause of divine works. Otherwise, religion <note>original: "religio." In this context, it refers to the practice of sacred rites or "theurgy."</note> would not be necessary for us to achieve these things; instead, we would be capable of divine works without the worship of the gods if they were performed by the power of the soul itself. Finally, if the soul performed divine things by its own power, it would be done either by every soul or by those which possessed the specific perfection of the soul—namely, knowledge, art, wisdom, and the character acquired through wisdom. But now...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that miracles and prophecy are not products of the human soul or astrological luck, but are gifts of divine power. He refutes Porphyry’s suggestion that these phenomena might be psychological, insisting that religious ritual (theurgy) is essential because humans cannot reach the divine on their own.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosopher Iamblichus’s response to Porphyry’s "Letter to Anebo." Porphyry had questioned whether the soul itself is the source of divine inspiration or if it is merely a vessel. On the previous page, the text established that human nature is insufficient for divine works. Here, Iamblichus dissects Porphyry’s three theories regarding the soul’s causal role in theurgy and prophecy.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

It is not people in their normal state who perform these things, but rather those who are stirred up and drawn away <note>original: "abstracti." This refers to the state of "ecstasy," where the soul is literally "standing outside" its normal bodily consciousness.</note> from themselves. Porphyry had proposed three possibilities regarding divine works:

First, that for these works the soul acts as an **instrumental cause** <note>A "tool" used by a higher power, like a brush in the hand of a painter.</note>.

Second, that the soul is sometimes the **principal cause** <note>The primary actor or source of the power.</note>.

Third, that the soul can be an equal **co-cause**, in such a way that from the soul and the divine spirit, a certain third type of substance or existence is formed.

Iamblichus says that whenever a single new thing is made from several parts, those parts must be both related to one another and capable of changing from what they are into something else. This is how the four elements are mixed into a single fifth thing <note>The "quintessence" or a compound body.</note>, and how multiple souls are joined into one whole. For instance, the **vegetative**, **sensory**, and **motive** souls <note>These represent the hierarchy of life functions: growth, feeling, and movement.</note> within us may yield to the **intellectual soul** and be brought into its activity. Or perhaps a vital harmony results in the body from all of these together. Or perhaps souls in their "homeland" <note>The spiritual realm or "Patria" where souls originate.</note> unite into a single Idea of all souls.

Divinity, however, being exempt from all things, does not merge with the soul to form a "third thing," especially since the soul has already "fallen" from its higher state. Because divinity is vastly different, it does not enter into a mixture; and since it is immutable, it cannot be changed into something else that is common to both. Earlier, it had been said that from small sparks...

<meta>catchword: suscitar</meta>

---

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...divine forms <note>original: "species diuinas." In this Platonic context, "forms" refer to the spiritual realities or archetypes of the gods.</note> are stirred up in the soul. Let us grant that, but these would not be transferred to purely divine forms if they were merely bodily and natural in origin.

Now, finally, where it is suggested that the soul and divinity join together into a single third thing, the soul is being made equal to God. It would imply that God undergoes change and receives something from the soul, just as the soul is changed and receives something from God—which is absurd. This is especially true because it would mean the gods, much like physical elements, would merge in their effects into a single form that is created within time, even though they are eternal, and they would be contained within a temporary thing.

When it is said that from the soul and God, or from various gods together, a single temporal thing is created, we must ask whether a new result arises beyond the parts coming together. 

If no new thing results, then there is no true union and no true "one," just as there is no union in a piece of craftsmanship where the result depends on the art alone. 

If a new thing does result, then eternal things would have to "fall" from their steady state so that something temporal could be made; for unless the components change, a third result cannot emerge. 

Indeed, it is entirely absurd to claim that something produced by a temporal process of "becoming" is actually eternal. Yet, it is also not fitting to call it temporal, for eternal things should not be made to serve the temporal. Nor is it fitting to claim that this union can be dissolved on both sides...

<meta>catchword: utrinque</meta>

<summary>Iamblichus refutes the idea that divine power is a "mixture" of the human soul and the divine spirit, arguing that God is immutable and cannot be diminished or changed by joining with a temporal human soul.</summary>
<keywords>Neoplatonism, Iamblichus, Porphyry, soul, divinity, theurgy, causality, immutability, divine forms</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosopher Iamblichus’s refutation of Porphyry’s theories. Having previously discussed the soul as a potential cause of divine works, Iamblichus now addresses Porphyry's suggestion that human souls might actually "create" or "generate" spirits (daemons) through ritual or material means.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

...made from eternal things. And yet, through a new generation, it seems to be dissolvable. That opinion, therefore, is absurd. Porphyry says that the soul sometimes generates a daemonic <note>original: "dæmonicã." In this context, "daemons" are not evil spirits but intermediary beings between gods and humans.</note> power and essence, imagining future things through motions of this kind. It generates, I say, while it conducts into one certain materials having in themselves powers of this sort, especially materials taken from living beings. Iamblichus denies that daemons are generated and corrupted <note>original: "corrũpi," meaning to break down or cease to exist.</note>. For he denies that daemons, which are superior to bodies and the soul, can be generated by the soul from bodily powers. He also denies that the actions of a particular soul, enclosed in a body, can proceed into essences that exist in themselves outside the soul. He denies that the powers of bodies, which are entirely bound to matter, can be released from them to generate daemons. Furthermore, he asks what power it is that releases material forces from their matter, and in turn fuses them into one to generate a daemon; for it seems this power must itself be daemonic, and thus the daemon would exist even before it is generated. A soul, especially a prophetic <note>original: "fatidica," literally "fate-speaking."</note> one, cannot be generated from things lacking a soul and the power of prophecy. Something more excellent cannot be procreated from something inferior. No essence or substance can be established from the motions of the soul and the powers...

<meta>catchword: and the powers...</meta>

<column-break/>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...and the powers of the body, which are neither substances nor essences. Likewise, none of those things that are sown through generation possesses anything greater than what is handed down to it by its primary generating cause. Since, therefore, neither the body nor the soul possesses prophecy in itself, the soul cannot, from its own motions and from bodies, procreate a prophetic daemon. Perhaps someone will say that daemons are not generated by us, but that they preside over living things in an orderly way; and so, when materials from animals entrusted to this daemon are applied at the opportune time, this daemon is drawn here as if by "shared feeling" <note>original: "cõpatientem," referring to the concept of cosmic sympathy where parts of the universe affect one another.</note> toward such things. Iamblichus says that daemons who are subject to such feelings to that extent are unable to prophesy the truth. For true prophecy does not belong to a nature that is "passible" <note>original: "passibilis," meaning a nature that can be affected, changed, or moved by external emotions and physical conditions.</note> and enclosed by any body, place, or time, but is instead set free from all these things, so that it is able to look forward to things done in any place or time, equally and simply.

->*On divine and human dreams.*<-

Porphyry says that the foreknowledge <note>original: "præfagia," the ability to sense or know things before they happen.</note> of dreams is partly from ourselves and partly from an external source. Iamblichus says it comes only from the outside; because we often strive and do many things to hunt for this foreknowledge, and yet...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that human souls cannot create divine spirits (daemons) from material things, as the effect cannot be superior to its cause. He concludes that true prophecy must come from a source entirely independent of time, place, and human emotion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s point-by-point refutation of Porphyry’s materialistic or psychological explanations for divine phenomena. Having just argued that the soul cannot "generate" spirits, Iamblichus now focuses on why prophecy and divine dreams cannot be explained as mere "passions" or emotional states of the human mind.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

...it is given: and often it is given to those who do not seek it. For if a dream-like effect arose from our own nature and human choice, it would occur because of our own foresight. However, it is sent by the gods according to their own will—specifically when and how they wish—to demonstrate the future through a certain kindness. An Orphic hymn <note>The "Orphic hymns" were a set of late antique poems attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus, central to the mystery religions of the time.</note> declares the same thing. Porphyry says that the cause of prophecy <note>original: "uaticinij."</note> is a certain passion of the soul. Iamblichus denies this, saying that a passion <note>original: "passionem." In this philosophical context, a "passion" is not just an emotion but a state of being "acted upon" or "suffering" an external influence, as opposed to an active state of reason.</note> is by its very nature unstable, disordered, and disturbed; whereas prophecy must be entirely stable and ordered, and therefore it cannot reside in a passion.

Likewise, when the soul is prudent and constant, and acts according to its more excellent powers—namely the intellectual and rational ones—it does not foresee the future. How, then, will it attain these things when it suffers according to disordered and disturbed motions? Furthermore, passion has no inherent quality for the contemplation of beings and truth, but instead brings an impediment. Moreover, if the things in the world were themselves constituted by passions, then a passion might reach them through a certain similarity. But since they are constituted and governed by reasons and forms <note>original: "rationibus speciebusq;," referring to the formal, mathematical, or divine principles that Neoplatonists believed governed the universe.</note>, there is certainly some other kind of foreknowledge, alien to all passions.

->Again<-

<column-break/>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

Again, passion perceives only things that are present. Since prophecy also attains the future, it does not reside in a passion. Porphyry says that prophecy is a certain passion of the imagination <note>original: "phantasiæ."</note>, arising either from our own thoughts, or by the instinct of the bodily nature within us, or occurring in a similar way to how it happens that those in a frenzy <note>original: "phreneticis," referring to those in a state of delirium or mental disturbance.</note> prophesy. To support this, he offers signs: that in the state of prophecy, the imagination acts vehemently, while the senses are meanwhile occupied and restrained. Also, that fumigations <note>original: "suffumigationes," the ritual burning of incense or herbs to produce vapors.</note> are used by the one about to divine, clearly to affect the imagination. Also, that invocations are used to incite the same affection. Also, that not everyone is fit for this, but only simpler young people.

Iamblichus says that the occupation of the senses is a sign that no human phantom <note>original: "phantasma," here meaning a product of human imagination as opposed to a divine vision.</note> is then present. Vapors are used to produce a congruity <note>original: "congruitatem," a state of being "in tune" or "aligned" with a divine power.</note> with the god, not to affect the soul of the observer. Invocations do not excite either thoughts or bodily passions in us; for they are unknown to us, and known only to the god who is invoked. Only the simpler people are exposed to the divine spirit coming from the outside. As to what Porphyry says, that prophecy...

# IAMBLICHUS, ON THE MYSTERIES.

...that it is such a passion of the imagination <note>original: "passionem phantasiæ"</note>, as often happens to those who are melancholic <note>In ancient medicine, "melancholy" was thought to be caused by an excess of black bile, often resulting in erratic behavior or delusions.</note> or to those foolish people who frequently pretend to be prophets. He abuses the divine gift of prophecy when he compares the alienation <note>original: "alienationem." Here, it refers to a state of being "outside oneself" or in an ecstatic trance.</note> caused by the divinity for a higher purpose to the alienation arising from diseases, drunkenness, or madness, which happens for the worse. The alienation of the mind occurring from our own passions casts the mind down below the human state; but that which is performed by God lifts the human being above the human level and joins them to God. The former makes the mind unstable and immerses it entirely in matter; the latter makes it constant and possessed of order, and releases it from matter. In no way should it be said that divine inspiration <note>original: "afflationem diuinam," literally a "divine breathing-upon."</note> has anything in common with the alienation caused by the bodily humors, drunkenness, or madness. For these states are distant from God beyond what can even be imagined. Therefore, such insanity is as far removed from divine inspiration as possible: they have nothing similar or in common. Alienation caused by bodily factors is a depravity of the mind resulting from weakness; but that which is performed divinely is the salvation of the soul resulting from a fullness of power. In the former case, when the mind attempts its own operations, it produces them in a perverted and turbulent way; in the latter case, however, while the mind rests from its own life and intellect, it exposes itself to be used by a superior power. Finally,

<column-break/>

as much as divine things are distant from the lowest natural things, so much are their actions and effects distant from the effects of natural causes. Therefore, the alienation induced divinely has nothing in common with that which occurs through human means. When you contemplate the former, you must separate from it entirely all the defects and incidental qualities of the latter. Furthermore, when you meditate upon the sacred sobriety and vigilance received from God, do not compare it with the ordinary sobriety of men. In both cases, remove from the imaginations divinely granted to the mind whatever is in any way similar to those imaginations stirred up by the bodily humors <note>The "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were believed to dictate human health and temperament; an imbalance was thought to cause hallucinations.</note> and similar causes. Likewise, do not think that the ambiguous human state—the middle ground between a sober mind and an alienated one—is similar to the state of the sacred mind which gazes upon God with a single intuition. Nor should you believe that the most certain intuitions of divine things are similar to the imaginations raised by the art of sorcery <note>original: "arte uenefica," literally the art of poisoning or magic.</note>. For those things we imagine when bewitched have no truth of action or essence beyond mere figments <note>original: "imaginamenta."</note>. For the goal of such magic is not to actually do anything, but merely to extend appearances until they seem real. It is not to be thought that the divine prophet happens upon the truth by chance, as the insane are sometimes wont to do; nor even through some natural passion, such as...

Here, Iamblichus distinguishes between the natural instincts of animals or human "foreknowledge" and the perfect, unchanging nature of true divine prophecy.</meta>

262 I A M B L I C H V S
<meta>catchword: simul</meta>

Even animals are often affected by certain parts and forces of the world as they begin to bring about some future event, acting first in the air in some way before they manifest on the earth. And so, by being affected in this way, they sometimes sense upcoming earthquakes and storms—especially those animals that are either easily affected or possess sharp perception. For foreknowledge <note>original: "Prænotio." Iamblichus uses this term to describe a lower, natural form of sensing the future, as opposed to divine "Vaticinium."</note> arising either by chance or by such a feeling is rare, disordered, discontinuous, and entirely obscure. But divine prophecy <note>original: "Vaticinium uero diuinum."</note> beholds the order of the universe with a continuous, firm, and connected reason. If we happen to have some innate faculty for perceiving the future, it is not for that reason true prophecy; for this faculty is not always truthful, but only occasionally, and not in all people, but only in some. Truly divine prophecy, however, is truthful both always and in all things.

Likewise, foreknowledge produced by art <note>original: "arte facta," referring to technical methods like reading tea leaves, bird flight, or entrails—what we might call "divination" as a learned skill.</note> hunts for the future from signs that are not entirely reliable, because they do not always have the outcome joined to them; rather, it is accomplished by divine providence. It beholds effects from their causes with a firm, present, and entirely continuous gaze, connecting all things that are changeable and temporal and distant from one another, anticipating the future as if it were present. Someone might say that the future can be predicted from four gifts

Just as the image of the Good itself <note>A reference to the Platonic "Form of the Good," which Iamblichus views as the ultimate source of reality.</note> represents God in all things, so there is in all things some trace of prophecy. <meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s defense of divine theurgy against the critique of Porphyry. Having argued that true prophecy comes from a higher divine source rather than human instinct, Iamblichus now addresses the practice of making "animated" statues or idols (theurgy vs. "idol-making"). He distinguishes between the supreme creative power of the Demiurge (the Creator) and the lesser, mechanical arts that merely manipulate physical influences from the stars.</meta>

266 ->IAMBLICHVS<-

...he constructs all things through powers thus divided, but by means of intellects, wills, and immaterial forms, and through the eternal supermundane <note>Existing above or beyond the physical world.</note> and mundane soul, he brings worlds into being. To be sure, the maker of such idols <term>idoloficus: a craftsman or magician who attempts to create statues that possess life or divine power</term> is said to work through the stars; yet he does not work through the stars themselves in the way that it might perhaps seem. For while there are innumerable powers within the celestial gods, the lowest of all is their "natural" power. Within this natural power of the celestial gods are certain "reasons" <note>original: "rationes"; these are the rational blueprints or principles of the universe.</note>—some are "seminal" <note>original: "seminales"; the generative "seeds" of physical forms</note>, that is, the creators of forms, and others are immobile ones that precede the seminal reasons, which serve as the coordinators of forms. Therefore, the authority of both these types of reasons precedes the whole of creation. Below these are the qualities, forces, and movements in the celestial bodies, and from them come "effluxes" <note>original: "defluxus"; the streaming influences or "flow" from the stars that affect the earth</note> that dominate the entire arrangement of worldly things according to these higher reasons. Truly, the lowest power of the celestials—out of all those forces I mentioned—guides the generation of earthly things. Many arts, such as medicine, gymnastics, and agriculture—namely, whichever ones cooperate in their work with the workings of nature—use these qualities and forces transmitted to the lower realms through celestial effluxes. And yet...

<meta>catchword: idol-maker</meta>

<column-break/>

267 ->ON THE MYSTERIES.<-

...the idol-maker himself draws from these celestial effluxes some generative portion, however small and weak it may be. For he does not use the actual movements of the heavens, nor the forces inherent in them, nor the forces that are naturally established around those celestial movements; he cannot even reach them. Instead, he occupies himself with certain forces that have fallen away from their original nature to the very end, sinking to the lowest place in the world. He indeed uses a certain art, but it is not one that is pious or truly divine. These lowest celestial forces, conspiring together around some particular matter, are able to transmute, transfigure, and transform it, changing it from one state to another. Indeed, they even allow for a transposition from one thing to another by those powers that exist within specific materials. When someone constructs idols of this kind from many different materials and under specific celestial influences, then a variety—on one hand of celestial actions, and on the other of material powers gathered together—does indeed produce an effect; but this action degenerates far not only from divine workmanship <note>original: "opificio diuino"; the pure creative act of a god</note>, but even from natural production. For Nature performs its own work with one steady course and a simple action. Therefore, this making of idols is an artful mixing <note>original: "artificiosa commixtio"</note> concerning the ultimate "run-off" of celestial things, and concerning those...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that the creation of magical idols is a low-level art that only manipulates the weakest, furthest-removed influences (effluxes) of the stars, contrasting this with the pure, unified creative power of the gods and nature.</summary>

# I AMBLICHVS

Man cannot create the very forms of demons by his own devices; on the contrary, we ourselves are formed by demons according to the body. It should not be thought that from the coming together of elements there flows some multitude or composition possessing a power proper to demons. For the demon himself—simple, uniform, and consistent in his own nature—gathers diverse elements into one, generates compositions from them, and grants whatever perseverance <note>In this sense, the "stability" or "lasting quality" of a living form</note> is found within them. Nor is it fitting to call idols "demons," for the creator of idols is one thing, and the great leader of demons <note>The "great leader" refers to a high-ranking spiritual intelligence in the Neoplatonic hierarchy, far above man-made statues</note> is another. The very substance of demons is distinct from the phantoms of idols—idols which even you, Porphyry, admit can draw down neither a god nor any demon. Therefore, this manufacturing of idols, being devoid of both god and demon, provides neither prophecy nor any sacred work.

They emerge from there as the worst of men—profane, dissolute, and unjust—having a desire unlike that of the gods, and in all things most like the wicked demons with whom [they associate].

# IAMBLICHUS

...are constantly occupied. These people, therefore, being full of passions and wickedness, draw evil spirits to themselves through a natural affinity. Thus far the Chaldeans <note>Iamblichus is concluding a summary of the views held by the "Chaldeans," an ancient group of sages he considers authorities on divine matters</note>. 

When the profane handle sacred rites improperly, the outcome is frustrated; for instead of the gods, others are celebrated, and instead of good spirits, evil ones are introduced. Their errors should not be mentioned when we are discussing legitimate sacred rites, nor should what happens to those misguided people be taken as a rule for the divine law. Just as sacrilege is the opposite of divine worship, so too are those possessed by evil demons—the authors of excess and deceit—the opposite of legitimate priests. From these true priests, every wicked spirit, depravity, and passion is far removed. Instead, the presence of good divinities is near, and they are filled with truth from above by the divine fire. To such priests, evil spirits offer no hindrance to the blessings of the soul; no smoke of pride or soft flattery suggests itself to them, nor are they deceived by any incense-offering, nor disturbed by any force. On the contrary, all these evils, when the good...

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...presence of the divinity arrives, are immediately scattered and vanish as if struck by a lightning bolt. For such as these, a truthful prophecy results, with which nothing else can be compared. This must be studied rightly, with the holiness we have described. For by this method alone is unshakable truth acquired in prophesying, and absolute virtue in the soul. By these two means, the priest ascends to the intelligible fire <term>Intelligible fire: In Neoplatonic philosophy, this is the highest form of divine light or energy, accessible only to the mind or soul, representing the ultimate source of truth</term>, which ought to be the goal for every omen and sacrifice. 

Too rashly, O Porphyry, in discussing divine prophecy, did you think it necessary to mention the opinion of those who believe that every omen is granted by an evil demon. These people, having lived in darkness from the very beginning, can neither discern the true from the false, nor understand the principles from which these things arrive.

Often, they justly turn back the injuries that wicked men attempt to inflict upon others, so that those men suffer the very things they were striving to do. 

There is, again, another class of spirits surrounding us that is undiscriminating and unreasoning, which has been allotted a single power in its number, due to the very distribution of parts from the whole universe. For this reason, one spirit is devoted to only one task. For just as a sword only cuts and performs no other action, so it is with the spirits distributed throughout the world: because of the divisible necessity of their nature, this one only divides, while that one only collects the things that are being made and generated. Certain hidden spirits, therefore, having each been allotted a different power, perform only that single thing for which they were ordained. # IAMBLICHUS

<page-num>276</page-num>

...applying a divine form to the soul, clothed in which he is able—under the guise of a god and as if he were a superior—to command such spirits. But we solve the question more truly in this way: a certain communion of harmonious goodwill and an indissoluble embrace of unity contains the whole sacred operation <note>original: *expeditionem*; referring to theurgic or ritual acts</note>, so that this effect is divine and exceeds every limit of human activity. Therefore, we must remove all human qualities from this process. The priest does not summon the divinity as if it were absent, nor does he command a separate being to perform a task—as humans do among themselves. Rather, a single and identical action of the **divine fire** <term>divine fire: in Neoplatonism, the pure, active energy of the gods that purifies and elevates the soul</term>, ready of its own accord and present from within itself, shines forth. It acts in the same way through all things simultaneously: both through those that pass the power on to others and through those that are able to receive something from it. Therefore, the divine works fulfilled in sacred rites are not carried out through the opposition of one thing to another as in physical generation, nor through a distinction between the one who calls or moves and the one who is summoned or moved—as is common in human affairs—but the whole is completed through identity, union, and harmony; and with all dis-

<column-break/>

<sig>S 3</sig>

The gods do not look only at a single part of this life, but at the whole; nor at this life alone, but they behold the entire life of the soul from age to age. Thus, based on merits earned in a previous life, they often punish in a following one, whether they are asked to punish or not. Meanwhile, we—who see nothing beyond the present—imagine that adversities sometimes happen to us without merit. Yet we often suffer in this life what we have already inflicted on others in another, and what we do now, we shall one day suffer. Furthermore, many human sins are hidden from us but are not at all hidden from the gods. Likewise, we define justice as each person doing their own duty according to the current laws of the country. But the gods define justice much more broadly, looking toward the entire order of the universe and focusing especially on that principle by which the souls serve the gods’ judgment.

For if a communion of the same nature exists between souls living in bodies and those placed outside the body, it creates a certain identical and common connection for all toward the whole life of the world and the mundane order. It is therefore necessary to demand the execution <note>original: *expeditionem*; the carrying out or fulfillment of a sentence</note> of judgment from the whole—namely, from the universal order—and to require it from the relationship of souls among themselves, especially when the magnitude of crimes committed by one soul exceeds the punishment following from the sins [of a single lifetime]. <meta>This page continues the philosophical argument that the gods and the higher universal order are not the sources of evil. It explains how universal, divine "actions" (which are perfect and good at the level of the whole) can manifest as "passions" (sufferings or disturbances) when they reach the fragmented and weak level of individual material things.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

<page-num>280</page-num>
<header>IAMBLICHUS</header>

...it possesses their powers differing separately, and produces actions through different means. Likewise, by a certain mutual disposition, these parts can accomplish much more. Furthermore, a certain multiform action descends from the whole parts of the world into its particulars; it descends quite easily because of the similarity of powers, insofar as the powers that follow correspond step-by-step to those that precede them, especially where the receiver <note>original: *patiens*; the "patient" or object being acted upon</note> is moreover adapted to the actor <note>original: *agens*; the active force or "agent"</note>. Therefore, due to the necessities of the body, certain evils and destructive things happen to individual parts from the wholes—things which are indeed beneficial to the whole and in harmony with the music of the universe, although they are meanwhile harmful to the parts. This happens either because the parts cannot sustain the actions of the wholes, or because of the mixture occurring at the lower levels, or the natural weakness inherent in the lowest things, or because parts are not in proportion <note>original: *commensuratae*; measured to the same scale</note> with other parts. Furthermore, beyond the body of the world itself, the nature of the world can do many things. For it accomplishes much through both the concord of likes and the discord of unlikes; indeed, the coming together of many into the one living creature of the whole <note>The "World Soul" or "Cosmic Animal," a common Neoplatonic concept where the universe is viewed as a single, living organism.</note> and the powers flourishing in the world—whatever and of what kind they may be—act one way in the whole and another in the parts, because of the very weakness of the parts, which are distributed and divided to the furthest extent.

<meta>catchword: Friendship</meta>

<column-break/>

Friendship of the whole, and love, and strife, and similar things, are actions in the wholes themselves, but in the particles, they are passions <note>original: *passiones*; in this context, it means "receptions" or "undergoings"—the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note>. Likewise, those things which are forms <note>original: *species*; the ideal blueprints or Platonic forms</note> and pure reasons in the divine intellect, participate in a certain material deficiency within the nature of the universe; and finally, in individuals, they take on formlessness. What is united in the wholes is divided in the particulars. Moreover, certain particles are destroyed so that the wholes, established according to nature, may be preserved. Certain parts are also crushed and pressed, while the wholes arising from them remain free from such suffering. 

When some sorcerer <note>original: *veneficus*; a practitioner of "low" magic or poisoning, as opposed to the "high" theurgy Iamblichus defends.</note> by his imprecations draws down a calamity from above onto someone, namely by using certain natural and bodily powers for this purpose, the transmission of such an action from the universe comes from above without any choice or wickedness. Although the evildoer using this power meanwhile deflects the transmission toward entirely opposite and evil ends, the transmission and action itself descending from above is moved by a certain sympathy <note>original: *compassione*; here meaning "cosmic sympathy," the natural resonance between similar things in the universe.</note> because of the similarity under the "passions" of opposites. The evildoer, however, by his own choice, draws what has been transmitted beyond what is just; but the transmission itself, according to the one harmony of the world, leads toward wickedness...

# IAMBLICHUS

<page-num>282</page-num>

After this, you ask why the higher natures <note>original: *natura superi*; the gods or celestial beings</note> do not hear a petitioner unless he is chaste, while they themselves, when entreated, supposedly assist in illicit sexual unions and are not ashamed to incite their worshipers to shameful lusts. Now indeed, the instinct toward Venus <note>here referring to the cosmic principle of attraction and procreation</note> in the world tends toward friendship and harmony; but in the individual parts it becomes more violent, because these, due to their own physical constitution <note>original: *complexionem*</note>, are too easily and mu-

However, this kind of pull and desire can be increased beyond the proper order by a certain art <note>referring to the practice of magic or theurgy</note>. The unifying force itself infused in all things is good, and it is everywhere the cause of fulfillment, communion, harmony, mutual love, and worldly union; these exist and occur by the command of the one who contains them <note>the Demiurge or Creator</note>. But in the parts—because of their distance from each other and from the whole, and because of their weak and needy nature—it produces a mutual meeting through sympathy <note>original: *compassione*; here used in the technical sense of "cosmic sympathy" where things react to one another</note>. From this, a sharper desire is innate in most people.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the origins of human impulses. On the previous page, Iamblichus argued that while the cosmic order is perfect, individual human receipt of divine influences can be distorted. Here, he specifically addresses why "lower" or illicit sexual passions should not be blamed on the gods, but on lesser spirits, magic, or the corruption of human nature.</meta>

-># IAMBLICHUS. ON THE MYSTERIES.<-

...governs by its own judgment through mixture and brings about unions for procreation. Since there are powers in herbs and stones, both for dissolving and for congregating; and since these powers are much greater in larger things and natures, an impulse toward sexual intercourse can certainly be intensified by applying such things. Through these very things, without the work of artful magic, love can be kindled and attraction created. We have found that wicked demons <note>the term *daemones* here refers to spirits intermediate between gods and humans, which can be benevolent or malevolent</note> have the greatest power over procreation and earthly or human affairs. Therefore, it should not seem surprising that a passion for illicit intercourse is frequently kindled in us by them. Certain souls can also contribute their powers to the same end: both those living in this body and possessing a marvelous power of attraction, and also those who have been released from the body but are still wrapped in a turbid and moist spirit <note>original: *spiritu turbido humidoque*; in Neoplatonic thought, a "moist" spirit is one weighted down by material desires and passions</note> and are still wandering around places of procreation, thereby committing such acts. Therefore, let no one say that either the gods or the demons who follow them are the causes of unlawful love and intercourse; rather, it is either our own depraved natural instincts, or the art of sorcery <note>original: *ueneficam artem*</note>, or evil demons, or souls that are not yet pure.

### On sacrifices: from where they derive their power, and what they contribute.

It is asked by what reasoning sacrifices are appropriate for those 

<column-break/>

above, what they contribute to humans, and what they do in the world. Porphyry <note>a student of Plotinus and a critic/interlocutor of Iamblichus</note> says that not only prophets but also "hypophets" <note>term: *hypophetas* — translated in text as "all priests who hand down a prophecy received from others"</note> must abstain from animal meat, lest the gods be contaminated by the vapors exhaling from them. Contrary to this opinion is the common saying that the gods are greatly soothed by the smell of animals as if by bait, and are thereby captured. Iamblichus condemns both views: namely, that the gods are either infected or ensnared and lured by the smells of meat. The World Soul <note>term: *Anima mundi* — the spirit that animates the entire universe</note> and the celestial beings, by virtue of being present in their own bodies, neither suffer passions from them nor are they distracted from their intellects. Individual souls, however, suffer both. It would be a great error to attribute similar defects to the higher souls; for the condition of universal and particular beings, or of causes and effects, is not equal. Eating the bodies of things once joined to a soul undoubtedly brings a burden and defilement upon us and creates a downward tendency in the soul, through which it may dissolve into and succumb to pleasures, and it creates many other diseases in the soul. But the vapor exhaling from animals and the sacred smoke-offering <note>original: *suffumigatio*</note> performed according to rite, to the gods...

<summary>Iamblichus clarifies that illicit lust is caused by malevolent spirits or human corruption rather than the gods, and begins a critique of contemporary views on animal sacrifice, arguing that gods are neither contaminated nor enticed by the physical matter of offerings.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus's defense of the divine nature against the idea that the gods are influenced by base human passions or material filth. On the previous page, he argued that illicit desires stem from lower spirits or human corruption, not the gods. Here, he begins to discuss why material sacrifices and physical "vapors" do not defile the celestial realm.</meta>

-># IAMBLICHUS ON THE MYSTERIES.<-

...harms nothing among the worldly and universal causes. For the material world does not contain and order the higher beings <note>the gods and celestial spirits</note> toward itself, but rather it is contained by them, and is coordinated with the universe just as it is with the gods. Therefore, it can be harmoniously adapted to the higher beings through their command. The religious, therefore, abstain from animal flesh, yet not because the gods could be defiled by the vapors of animals; for the power of the gods, before any material thing can even touch it, scatters it without contact. Not only does this power destroy and erase these bodily things from its proximity before they can approach, but even the celestial bodies themselves <note>the stars and planets, which Neoplatonists viewed as divine, eternal bodies</note> do not receive any material element into themselves. Nor do they let in anything foreign, nor do they lose what is their own; indeed, the vapors of earthly things, having barely traveled five stadia <note>a *stadium* was an ancient unit of length; five stadia is approximately 3,000 feet or 0.5 miles</note>, flow back down. They do not infect or nourish the immaterial and revolving body <note>the heavens</note>, which has no capacity for change within itself, nor contains anything contrary to itself, nor is carried toward or away from the center, but must either remain at rest or revolve. Therefore, the bodies below the moon, since they are composed of conflicting powers and movements and are entirely subject to change—moving either up or down—have nothing in common with the heavens, neither in nature, nor in power,

<column-break/>

nor in action. Therefore, neither vapor nor anything else from them reaches the heavens, being entirely separate from them. It is right, then, that those things which are unborn <note>eternal or uncreated</note> receive no change from general things. Can the nature of the gods then be defiled by such vapors—vapors which the gods repel (so to speak) with a single blow? Such things are therefore not harmful to the higher beings, but to us. For these divisible and material things, which are akin to us, have something in common with similar things in their suffering or action; but against the celestial and divine things, which are placed in another class of essence and endowed with different natures and powers, and which entirely exceed us, they can neither act nor communicate anything.

## What is the reason for sacrifices, and what is their utility?

Porphyry <note>a student of Plotinus who often questioned the literal or "theurgic" efficacy of religious rituals</note> thinks that sacrifices are offered to the gods for this reason: that we may honor them with such gifts, as we are often accustomed to do for our elders, and also that we may return thanks for the good things received from the divine, rendering good things for good things. Iamblichus says that a reason of this kind is drawn from the common custom of humans toward other humans, and it does not suit the nature of the gods, which exceeds human customs beyond measure. Indeed, such explanations and declarations regarding sacrifices do not fully demonstrate the greatest efficacy <note>original: *efficaciā*; the actual power to effect change or connect with the divine</note> of sacrifices. Efficacy...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that the divine and celestial realms are entirely unaffected by material vapors or earthly corruption, explaining that religious abstinence and sacrifices are for human benefit rather than to satisfy or "feed" the gods.</summary>

Having established that the gods are not harmed or nourished by material offerings, Iamblichus now addresses why sacrifices are nonetheless effective and how they relate to the cosmic order and the liberation of the soul.</meta>

<page-num>288</page-num>
-># IAMBLICHUS<-

...I say, without which we are not delivered from plague, famine, and scarcity, nor do we obtain timely rains; indeed, it is also through this that we achieve the purification and perfection of our souls, and liberation from this province of generation <note>the material realm of birth, change, and decay</note>. Therefore, someone following your line of reasoning will not greatly approve of these methods, as if you had assigned a worthy cause for their effects. And if by chance he does approve, he will certainly accept them in a secondary place, as if they were following and adapted in a secondary manner to the first and most ancient causes of such works.

We desire, therefore, the reason why sacrifices have efficacy for accomplishing things, and from what source they are adapted to the principal gods, who are the causes and principles of those things which are done. Someone might say that because the world is one living being <note>the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, a central concept in Neoplatonism where the universe is viewed as a single, interconnected organism</note> and possesses one and the same life everywhere, it moves similar things through the communion of like powers, or even the distance of unlike ones, or certainly a certain fitness of the agent toward the patient <note>the 'patient' is the entity receiving the action</note>; this occurs while it runs according to a single compassion <note>original: "compassionem." In this context, it refers to *sympatheia*, the "sympathy" or resonance where one part of the universe affects another regardless of distance</note>, even from the most remote point to the most remote, as if these too were near. For even between these very things, the communion of life is an equal distribution of this kind. But...

<meta>catchword: indeed</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>289</page-num>
-># ON THE MYSTERIES<-

...indeed, he speaks of that which necessarily follows from sacrifices. However, the true mode of sacrifices is not demonstrated in this way. For the very essence of the gods is located neither in nature nor in natural necessities, by which obligation they might be stirred by natural passions, or moved by powers extended throughout all of nature. Instead, the divine essence is determined outside of these things according to itself, having nothing in common with them either in essence, power, or action—nor, likewise, in passion <note>here meaning "being acted upon" or "suffering change"</note>.

Some add to the previous explanation a certain "congruence" in lower things for the higher, which therefore contributes to the efficacy of sacrifices. For example: in the crocodile, the hexagonal number <note>the number six, which was considered "perfect" and associated with the Sun in Pythagorean numerology</note> corresponds with the Sun. In the dog and the dog-headed ape <note>original: "cynocephalo," referring to the baboon, which was sacred to Thoth/Hermes and associated with the moon in Egyptian tradition</note>, there are certain physical reasons and powers, common ratios that relate to the moon. Likewise in other things, there are certain material species, such as the colors, figures, and forms in sacred animals, which suit some of the higher beings; or some member of an animal, such as the heart of a rooster <note>often used in ancient divination and solar rituals</note>. These and other similar natural things employed in sacrifices are said to be the causes of wonderful works.

Yet, from the above assignment of causes, the divine cause—which is altogether supernatural—is not assigned, nor are the divine causes of natural prayers...

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s explanation of the mechanical and spiritual hierarchy of theurgy. He is currently refuting the idea that sacrifices are merely material interactions, arguing instead that they engage a chain of causes from the lowest natural forces up to the highest divine "craftsmen" of the universe.</meta>

<page-num>290</page-num>
-># IAMBLICHUS<-

...is moved by these things, but assigns a certain natural power contained in matter and bodies: and therefore it is excited along with bodily movements and material things, and is calmed again—naturally, I say—and likewise for those things which pertain to nature. If, indeed, any such thing follows upon the sacrifices, it certainly adapts itself to the preceding causes, as if it were a necessary co-cause <note>original: "concausa sine qua non" — an essential condition without which a result cannot occur</note> without which the work would not happen.

It is better, therefore, to say that the miraculous effects of sacrifices proceed from a cause through a certain friendship, adaptation, and a reconciling relationship that joins the craftsmen to their works <note>original: "opifices ad opificia" — referring to the Demiurgic or creative powers and their creations</note>, and parents to their offspring. Therefore, when—with this common principle leading and preceding us—we take some animal, or another living thing born of the earth, which sincerely and exactly preserves the will and purpose of its maker, we then properly move the creative cause presiding over this mixture through such a medium.

Since, indeed, there are many such causes—some presiding closely and familiarly, such as daemons <note>intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humanity</note>; while others are ordered superior to these, such as divine causes in their sequence; and one most ancient cause presides over all of these—certainly in a perfect sacrifice, all the causes are moved in their proper order. But according to the

<meta>catchword: order</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>291</page-num>
-># ON THE MYSTERIES<-

order which each has obtained, they are familiarly adapted to the sacrifice by a certain kindred condition, and (so to speak) appropriated. If, however, the sacrifice is imperfect, it ascends to a certain degree, but does not transcend further.

Hence, many people believe that sacrifices are made to good daemons; many also believe they are for the lowest powers of the gods; others believe they are for the worldly or earthly powers of daemons or gods. These people are indeed explaining a part of the sacrifices, yet they remain ignorant of their total power and of all the goods that extend themselves deeply to every divine thing.

We, however, admit all these perspectives and comprehend them all at once. Natural things indeed—and those which are moved together as if in one living being according to fitness or sympathy <note>original: "compassionem" — here meaning "sympatheia," the Stoic and Neoplatonic idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected and resonate with one another</note> or reaction—we accept as simply subject to, following, and serving the effective cause appearing in the sacrifices. We accept the daemons and the divine powers surrounding the earth and the world as those nearest to our own order and presiding over us. But we judge that the most powerful causes of effective sacrifices belong to the most perfect and creative powers <note>the Demiurgic powers that shape the cosmos</note>. Since, indeed, those highest creative powers embrace all the other causes in themselves according to their order...

<summary>Iamblichus explains that sacrifice is not a simple material transaction but a hierarchical process that engages different levels of reality—from natural sympathy to the highest creative gods—depending on the "perfection" of the rite.</summary>

Therefore, we believe that all efficient causes are moved together in a single stroke along with these things: because in a perfect sacrifice, the causes that follow in order are moved together with the highest causes and the craft-working causes <note>original: "opificijsq́ȝ" — referring to the Demiurgic or creative powers that "craft" the universe</note>. From all of these, then, a common benefit proceeds into the whole of generation <note>original: "generationem" — the realm of birth, change, and physical existence</note>: sometimes reaching through cities, peoples, and all kinds of nations, or through larger or smaller groupings than these; at other times, blessings reach individual households or each person, as the higher beings bestow them abundantly out of a beneficent will. They do not exhibit their distribution through any passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to emotional instability or being affected by external things</note>, but judge with an impassive mind that these things should be given according to what is appropriate, familiar, and kindred—all while a certain friendship, which contains all things, brings about this binding together through an ineffable communion.

These things are surely more true, and participate more in the essence and power of the gods, than what you suspect—namely, that the higher beings are primarily lured by the odors <note>original: "nidoribus" — the smell of burning fat or meat from a sacrifice</note> of animals in a sacrifice. For if the daemons <note>intermediary spirits between gods and humans</note> are wrapped in any body, which some believe is nourished by sacrifices, that body is certainly immutable, impassive, and luminous, and not unworthy; so much so that nothing flows out from it, and it becomes necessary for nothing

<column-break/>

-># ON THE MYSTERIES<-

to flow in. And yet, even if such a thing were perhaps necessary, why would it need to flow in through sacrifices, when the world and the air possess an unfailing exhalation from the earth, surrounding them on all sides? Indeed, if the bodies of daemons did suffer such an outflow, sacrifices would not restore them in an equal portion, nor would they preserve a balance between the natural excess and deficiency of daemons, nor a similar proportion. Finally, since the maker of the world <note>The Demiurge</note> provided abundant and ready nourishment for all earthly and marine animals, would he have left those beings superior to man destitute of nourishment? And when he established for other living things that their food be prepared copiously through their own daily labor, why did he wish for an "imported" nourishment to be provided by men for the daemons alone? Furthermore, if we should perhaps neglect such nourishment, the bodies of the higher beings would starve and perish. Consequently, if we nourished the daemons, we would also be their creators, and we would be superior to them. But the reality is quite the opposite: for they themselves nourish us, and higher things everywhere nourish the lower; thus, celestial things nourish terrestrial things. Indeed, the soul is perfected and nourished by the intellect <note>original: "intellectu" — the higher Mind or *Nous*</note>, and it in turn perfects nature. <meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s defense of theurgy—the ritual practice of connecting with the divine—against the skepticism of the philosopher Porphyry. Having argued that sacrificial fire purifies the worshiper, Iamblichus now begins to categorize different types of gods and the specific sacrifices appropriate to each, moving from the material to the immaterial.</meta>

### IAMBLICHUS

According to the priestly art <note>original: "sacerdotiam artem" — theurgy, or the ritual craft of contacting the gods</note>, it is proper to begin sacrifices with the material gods; for in no other way is the ascent to the immaterial gods opened. These gods, then, have a certain communion with matter, insofar as they preside over it and watch over it. They also rule over the things that happen within matter, such as division, impact, resistance, change, birth <note>original: "generationi" — the process of coming into physical existence</note>, decay, and all material bodies. Therefore, if anyone wishes to worship these gods rightly, they must surely offer worship according to the nature and sovereignty of those beings—that is, material worship for material beings. For in this way, we shall be led as whole beings into a proper familiarity with them through all their parts, and we shall offer a kinship in worship that is suitable to them.

Therefore, bodies deprived of life, the slaughter of animals, the destruction of bodies, and the multi-form change and corruption <note>original: "corruptio" — the natural process of physical breakdown</note>—and in general, the casting off of preceding matter—is appropriate for the material gods. This is not for their own sake, but for the sake of the matter over which they preside. For although they are most distant from matter, they are simultaneously present to it; and while they contain matter within an immaterial power, they nonetheless exist together with it. Indeed, the things governed are not alien to the governors, just as the things adorned are not alien to those who adorn them.

<meta>catchword: Indeed. Moreover</meta>

<column-break/>

### ON THE MYSTERIES.

Moreover, those things which serve the users, just like instruments, are easily fitted together by right proportions. Therefore, for the immaterial gods, it is alien to use matter in sacrifices; but for all the material gods, it is entirely appropriate.

It is worthwhile, moreover, to consider the dual condition of our life. Sometimes we become entirely soul, set outside the body and elevated in mind; then, together with all the immaterial gods, we are lifted up through the heights. At other times, however, we are bound to the earthly body and held by the vapors <note>original: "fimus" — likely meaning "fumus" (smoke/vapor) or "fimus" (muck/dregs), referring to the heavy, physical nature of the body</note> of matter. Similarly, there will be a double method of divine worship. One will be simple, incorporeal, and pure from all generation <note>the cycle of birth and death</note>, suitable for purified souls. The other, however, is full of bodies and entirely material action, fitting for souls that are not yet pure, nor yet purged of all generation. There are, therefore, two types of sacrifices: the most pure sacrifices belong to men who are supremely purified—which, as Heraclitus says, "happens rarely to one, or to very few." But material sacrifices, and those which involve change, are for souls still occupied by the body.

# IAMBLICHUS

...they seek. Therefore, for cities <note>or states/communities</note> not yet purified from their generative and bodily association <note>original: "genitali forte contubernioq; corporeo" — referring to the soul's entanglement with the process of physical birth and the material body</note>, unless you offer sacrifices of this kind, you will miss out on both immaterial and material goods alike. The former [the immaterial gods] cannot receive [the worshiper], while to the latter [the material gods], one does not offer what is appropriate and fitting. Added to this is the fact that everyone ought to care for their own essence according to what they *are*, not according to what they are *not*. It is not right, therefore, for a worshiper to violate their own proper measure and nature; I judge that the constitution <note>original: "complexionem" — the specific blend of soul and body in a human being</note> properly adjusted between the humans who perform the service and the powers being served will choose a mode of worship that is suitable for itself. 

For a constitution that is immaterially tempered in this way chooses an immaterial mode, insofar as it joins itself to purely incorporeal powers to reach things that are purely incorporeal. But a constitution that is bodily adapted to bodies chooses a similar worship for the essences presiding over bodies. Often, for the necessary use of the body, we make vows and perform rituals toward the gods who govern the body and toward good daemons <note>original: "dæmones" — intermediary spirits who act as messengers or guardians, distinct from the higher gods</note>, specifically when we strive to purge the body of certain old stains and filths, or to free it from diseases, and to provide health, or to remove heaviness 

<column-break/>

and sluggishness, and to provide lightness and efficacy, or to obtain some other good thing for the body. In such a case, we will not treat the body properly through some intellectual and incorporeal method. For the body is not born in such a way that it can be cured by these means; rather, when it obtains things akin to itself, then a body is cured and purified by bodies. 

Therefore, the rite of sacrifice for such a purpose will necessarily be bodily; thus, it will purge the superfluities of the body and supply what is lacking as needed, and it brings back to proportion and order whatever things have been distributed <note>or "disordered"</note>. We often sacrifice asking from the higher powers for things accommodated to human life—namely, those things necessary for food or pertaining to what we desire for the sake of the body. What then will come to us from the gods themselves, who are completely separated from all human generation <note>original: "generatione" — the realm of physical birth and change</note>, that might contribute to driving away poverty and sterility, or bringing us abundance, or leading to other necessities of life? Nothing, truly. For those who are detached from all things do not handle gifts of this kind. But if someone should say that those entirely immaterial gods comprehend the material gods within themselves, and embrace the gifts of these according to one primary cause...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that because humans possess a physical "constitution," they must use material sacrifices to communicate with the gods who govern the body. He asserts that while the highest gods are immaterial, ritual must match the nature of the practitioner and the specific needs (health, food, purity) being addressed.</summary>

# 500 IAMBLICHUS
## ON THE MYSTERIES 501

...one will surely speak of a certain abundance of the divine gift descending from there below. However, as for the fact that those who handle these rituals perform actions very close to human life and deeds, no one should be allowed to speak [ill of them]. For the administration of the things that exist here <note>the material world</note> is divided and specific, and is carried out with a certain turning toward these material things; it is not entirely separated from bodies, nor can it admit a purely unstained government or presidency. Therefore, the mode of sacrificing that is appropriate for such things is one that has commerce with bodies and the process of physical birth <note>original: "generatione" — the cycle of becoming and physical existence</note>, not one that is entirely separated from matter and the body. 

For he who is completely pure <note>referring to a highly advanced spiritual person or a higher being</note> transcends such things and has no proportional relationship to them. But he who makes use of bodies and their powers is most akin to all such things, being able to supply the prosperous things of life, turn away the adversities hanging over us, and provide a balanced temperament for the human race. The vast majority of people <note>original: "Plurima hominum turba" — literally, the "greatest crowd of men"</note> are subject to universal nature; they are governed by natural forces and incline downward toward the works of nature, fulfilling the distribution of fate <note>original: "fati" — the causal laws governing the physical world</note> and receiving the order of fatal works, exercising practical reason <note>term: "ratio practica" — the use of reason for navigating the physical world and moral actions, rather than for abstract contemplation</note> regarding only na-

<column-break/>

tural things. Very few, relying on the supernatural power of the mind, depart from nature and betake themselves to the separate and unmixed intellect <note>term: "intellectus" — in Neoplatonism, the higher mind that perceives truth directly and is superior to the reasoning soul</note>, whereby they become superior to natural forces. Yet some hold a middle ground between pure intellect and nature: some of these follow each in turn, others lead a life mixed from both, and others are freed from lower things and transfer themselves to the better. 

Those, therefore, who are governed by universal nature and live a life enslaved to their own nature—enjoying the powers of nature—will perform a worship appropriate to nature and suitable for bodies moved by nature. For this purpose, they choose specific locations, qualities, the substance of the air, the powers of matter, bodies, the qualities and conditions of bodies, appropriate movements, and the changes of those things involved in the cycle of birth, as well as similar things, both in the other parts of divine worship and in the ritual of sacrifice. But those who live by the mind <note>original: "mente" — the higher intellect</note> alone, freed from the bonds of nature, will meditate upon an intellectual and bodiless rule of worship in every part of their religion. Those who lead a middle life between the intellect and nature will also follow a middle path of religion,

<summary>Iamblichus explains that because humans vary in their spiritual advancement—from the "common crowd" tied to nature and fate to the "very few" who live by pure intellect—religious rituals must vary accordingly, using material or immaterial means as appropriate to the worshiper's state.</summary>

...and according to the differences of this "middle life," different people will pursue different modes of worship through these intermediate means. In the category of essential and divine powers, some indeed have the soul and nature <note>In Neoplatonism, "Nature" is the lowest level of the divine creative force, responsible for the physical world</note> subject to them, which serve their creative works as far as they themselves wish. Others, however, are entirely separated from soul and nature—I do not mean only from the mundane <note>original: "mundana" — relating to the physical cosmos</note> and generative soul, but even from the divine soul and its nature. 

Finally, others hold the middle position and reconcile the communion between these extremes, either according to a single indissoluble bond, or according to an overflowing tradition of the greater beings, or according to the unimpeded reception of the lesser beings, or according to a bound-together consensus of both. 

When we worship the gods who rule over soul and nature, it is not out of place to offer natural powers to them, and to consecrate to such gods the bodies which are governed by nature. For all the works of nature both obey them and contribute something to their administration. But—

—as for the gods who are far-withdrawn <note>original: "secretos" — set apart or transcendent</note> and gathered within their own unity, we desire to venerate them with honors that are entirely freed from matter. To the middle gods, however, who are the leaders of middle goods, intermediate things will be appropriate, just as we have said. Therefore, beginning from another principle—namely, from the world—we have easy access to the truth of sacrifices through the mundane gods, through the distribution of the four elements in the world, through the common allotment made according to the measures of the elements, and through the movement from the circumference toward the centers in a regular order. 

For if we exist within the world, and are contained in it as parts—firstly, being generated by it and perfected by its total powers, and being composed of its four elements, and having obtained and holding a certain portion of life and nature from it—we certainly must not overlook the world and the mundane orders in our divine worship. Let us suppose, therefore, that around every part of the world there is some body, just as we see, and that there are also incorporeal powers distributed in order within those bodies. But he who makes all the <term>numina</term> <note>original: "numina" — divine wills or powers</note> favorable to him, by offering each gifts and most similar—

If the entity invoked in the priesthood and moved toward us were something simple and of only one order, then a simple mode of sacrifice would indeed suffice. But in truth, no one knows what a great multitude of powers is stirred up when the gods descend and move, except for those priests who have already experienced it in the <term>sacred work</term> <note>original: "opere ipso" — refers to theurgy, the practical performance of ritual</note> itself. Only they, then, know what constitutes the most perfect fullness of worship, and how much the outcome fails us if even a few things are omitted. 

Just as in a musical harmony, if one string is broken, the whole suddenly sounds dissonant; so if one deity is overlooked without the proper rite, religion itself, held in common, does not reach its desired end, for while this one part is missing, the sacred work lacks its structure and integrity. When the divine powers are about to descend openly to our senses, we suffer a manifest loss if we neglect any of the higher beings...

The multitude of deities is like a certain cosmos, containing many ranks that all breathe together into one order. In the same way, sacrifices ought to maintain the order of the deities, likewise breathing together into a single arrangement, so that individual rites correspond correctly to individual deities.

For this reason, whatever part of matter is perfect, pure, and <term>god-like</term> <note>original: "deiforme"</note> is not unfit for the reception of the gods. Therefore, the wisdom of sacred matters, having contemplated this and diligently finding suitable <term>receptacles</term> <note>original: "susceptacula" — physical objects or bodies prepared to house a divine presence</note> for each of the gods according to their harmony, often combines stones, herbs, animals, incense, and other such things—sacred, perfect, and god-like—and from all these, it constructs a pure and complete receptacle.
