### *On the sacrifices of animals.*

Porphyry is in doubt as to why the law of sacred rites requires that he who is about to inspect divine matters should not touch a dead body at that time. Nevertheless, they frequently perform invocations and seek divine results through the bodies of dead animals. Iamblichus solves the problem in this way: The prophets command that a witness of divine things must not touch a perishable, lifeless body that has not been made sacred; however, they permit touching that which is consecrated. Furthermore, they forbid even looking at or touching human bodies from which the soul has already departed. For a certain trace, or image, or manifestation of the divine life is extinguished in the human body through death. But no religious law forbids touching the dead bodies of other animals, since they did not participate in a more divine life while living. Moreover, insofar as we rise toward the immaterial gods, it is expedient not to have touched such a body; but insofar as we strive to approach the material gods, it will frequently

<column-break/>

### PAGE 315

## ON THE MYSTERIES

be expedient to touch them. For through animals we are accustomed to advocate for gods of this kind—those who clearly preside over such animals, especially those who govern them closely and through a certain kindred condition. Likewise, for humans who are bound within matter, bodies deprived of life bring a certain stain—that is, the non-living to the living, the filthy to the pure, and the one in a state of privation to the one who possesses a habit of life, and the dead to the one who has the potential for dying—because of a certain common relationship between these states. But to a completely incorporeal and impassible demon <note>original: "dæmoní"—in this context, a "daimon" is a mediating spirit between gods and men, not an evil entity.</note>, such bodies are not a hindrance at all, for he greatly transcends all perishable things.

### *On divinations through animals.*

When divination <note>original: "uaticiníum"—the act of foretelling the future through signs.</note> is carried out through the bodies of sacred animals, such as birds, one must not think that the gods approach these things—that is, the universal providers attending to a divided, particular, material, and proportional care concerning individual animals. Rather, it is the demons—and these indeed are highly divided, distributed individually to each species of animal—who have been allotted the immediate care and oversight of animals. For these spirits have obtained a leadership that is not entirely sufficient on its own and is not free from matter; therefore, they are accustomed to appropriately touch instruments of this kind. To this end, therefore...

<summary>Iamblichus explains why ritual purity forbids touching human corpses but allows the use of sacrificed animals, arguing that different classes of spirits (gods vs. demons) interact with matter in different ways. He clarifies that divination through animals is governed by specific intermediary spirits rather than the high, universal gods.</summary>

In order that we may obtain prophecy of this kind from <term>daimons</term><note>original Latin: "dæmonibus." In this Neoplatonic context, a daimon is a mediating spirit, not necessarily an evil "demon."</note> through animals, it is necessary to prepare for them a seat of such a nature that they might move among men and interact with us. It is necessary that this seat be incorporeal, so that the incorporeal spirits may be present to us through it. This seat will therefore be the soul of such animals, now released from the body. Since the soul is itself, in a certain way, separated from the body, it accords with the spirits, and it also accords with us because of a certain kinship of life. Therefore, acting as a medium, it serves that presiding spirit by suggesting foreknowledge to the human, declaring the commands of the spirit, and reconciling us with that spirit. 

Indeed, a soul using these kinds of <term>vaticinations</term><note>original Latin: "uaticinijs," meaning prophecies or divinations.</note> not only hears or receives the prophecy, but also contributes not a little from its own nature toward its execution regarding the work at hand. For the soul is moved and cooperates, and simultaneously foresees through a certain necessity of "sympathy" <note>The concept of "cosmic sympathy" (sympatheia) suggests that all parts of the universe are interconnected and react to one another.</note>. But divination of this kind is very far removed from the true and divine; it is concerned with small and fleeting matters which are placed within the divided parts of nature, and which are carried along together with the process of generation, exhibiting their own motions to those capable of receiving them,

<meta>catchword: and passions-</meta>

---

<page-num>317</page-num>
<header>ON THE MYSTERIES</header>

and they bring about passions in many ways in those things that are naturally exposed to such sympathy. It is through this sympathy, therefore, that this kind of foretelling arises. However, a perfect foreknowledge cannot occur through passion. For that which is immutable and pure in the world is especially accustomed to grasp what is to come. But that which has commerce with the material, the passive, and the dark is overwhelmed by ignorance. Therefore, we do not consider this artificial machinery of foretelling worthy of the name of legitimate prophecy, nor should it be treated seriously, nor should the person using it be believed as if he were a teller of truth.

### How those who offer prayers used to threaten the spirits.

Porphyry <note>A Phoenician philosopher and student of Plotinus who wrote a "Letter to Anebo" questioning various Egyptian religious practices. This book is Iamblichus's systematic response to that letter.</note> relates that priests were accustomed to use certain violent threats against the higher beings: such as, "unless you do this," or conversely, "if you do something, I will shatter the heavens," or "I will reveal the hidden things of Isis," or "I will divulge the secret hidden in the abyss," or "I will stop the *baris*"—that is, a certain sacred ship among the Egyptians—"or I will scatter the limbs of Osiris to <term>Typhon</term>"<note>Typhon is the Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, the brother and murderer of Osiris.</note>, and other similar things. # IAMBLICHUS

There is a certain class of powers that is greatly divided, indistinct, and unreflective; it receives <term>reason</term><note>original Latin: "rationẽ siue sermonẽ," referring to the Greek "logos"—the rational principle or a formal command.</note> or speech from another and listens to it, but possesses no intelligence of its own. It distinguishes neither truth from falsehood, nor the possible from the impossible. Therefore, when this class of spirits is provoked by threats, it is immediately stirred up and stunned, seeing as it is naturally moved by vehement words. It leads and drags other things along with it through a certain dull and unstable imagination.

Furthermore, the priest often commands and threatens the worldly deities not through human virtue, but by the divine power of the ineffable <term>sacraments</term><note>original Latin: "sacramentorum." In this context, these are not Christian rites but "theurgic symbols" or "synthemata"—divine tokens believed to hold the power of the gods.</note>. At that moment, the priest is established within the order of the superior gods themselves. Therefore, he employs commands and threats that are greater than his own human nature. He does not do this as if he were actually going to carry out the things he asserts, but rather to declare how much power he has obtained through his union with the gods. This power is acquired from the knowledge and possession of those ineffable symbols or seals which we call sacraments.

Likewise, <term>daimons</term><note>original Latin: "dæmones." These are mediating spirits in the Neoplatonic hierarchy, responsible for maintaining the physical laws of the world.</note> are divided by provinces and regions, guarding specific parts of the world. Each of them has such great care for the parts committed to them that they cannot bear to hear even a single word

<column-break/>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

contrary to the order and dispensation of that place; they obstinately guard the perpetual and immutable perseverance of worldly things. Indeed, they have received their own immutable order because the order of the gods remains immobile within those same things. Therefore, regarding the very existence of these daimons—whether they are of the upper air or distributed around the earth—they cannot bear to hear that order attacked even by threats.

Accordingly, the daimons zealously attend to the guardianship of the ineffable and secret mysteries. They do so with such great observance because they understand that the order and distribution of the universe is chiefly contained within such mysteries. This is because the deities and the worldly orders are designated allegorically through these words. For this reason, the parts of the world remain in their proper order: because the beneficent power of **Osiris**<note>The Egyptian god Osiris is used here as a symbol for the pure, ordering principle of the universe.</note> remains pure and intact, and is not mixed with any contrary tumult or error.

Moreover, the life of all things remains always pure and uncorrupted because the life-giving and beautiful <term>principles</term><note>original Latin: "rationes," translating the Greek "logoi"—the underlying rational patterns of creation.</note> which are hidden within **Isis**<note>The goddess Isis represents the receptive, generative principle that holds the forms of life.</note> remain established there. While the world is driven from that source, those principles themselves do not descend into this physical body visible to the eyes. And yet, all things remain immobile and everlasting—namely, those of the realm of generation...

### On Divine Names

Porphyry asks why priests use certain names that signify nothing <note>Porphyry is questioning the use of "voces magicae"—strange, seemingly meaningless words often found in magical papyri and rituals.</note>. Iamblichus responds that all names of this sort signify something among the gods, although to us the meanings in some cases are unknown. Some, however, are known, the interpretation of which we have received from the divine, but generally the manner of signification within them is ineffable. It is not according to human imaginations, nor according to rational discourse, but according to the intellect <note>original: "intellectum," referring to the *Nous*, the highest part of the soul in Neoplatonic philosophy.</note> which is divine within us—or rather, in a simpler and more excellent way, according to the intellect united to the gods. 

Therefore, one must remove from divine names all human inventions, rational discourses, and natural comparisons of the voice itself that are tied to things found in nature. Just as a symbolic mark <note>original: "character symbolicus," likely referring to the *synthemata* or tokens used in theurgy.</note> of divine likeness is intellectual and divine in itself, so we ought to assume and accept this same quality in all these names. But because here to us it becomes...

<meta>catchword: becomes,</meta>

---

<page-num>345</page-num>
# ON THE MYSTERIES

...becomes unknown, this very fact is what is most to be revered in it: for it is more excellent than can be divided into our common knowledge. In those divine names where we have received their explanation from the divine, we possess the entire knowledge of the divine essence, power, and order comprehended within the name itself. Furthermore, we preserve in the soul the mystical, ineffable, and simultaneous whole image of the gods, and through these names we lift the soul toward the gods, and once elevated, we join it to them as far as our power allows. 

Furthermore, it is asked why we prefer foreign <note>original: "barbara," referring to languages other than Greek, specifically those of the "sacred nations."</note> names over others among the names of the gods. It is because the gods have approved the entire speech of sacred nations, such as the Egyptians and Assyrians, as being most suitable for sacred rites. For this reason, we judge that common expressions and modes of speaking should be applied to the speech and prayer related to the gods, especially because that mode of speaking was the most ancient and primary. Those who first received these names from the gods, while they mixed them with their own language, tempered them with a voice familiar and consistent to themselves, and thus handed them down to us to be preserved forever. Therefore, we ought to rightly preserve the rule of tradition...

<summary>This passage defends the use of "barbarous names" in ritual, arguing that although they may seem meaningless to human reason, they possess a divine, intellectual power that connects the soul directly to the gods. Iamblichus asserts that ancient languages like Egyptian and Assyrian are inherently more sacred and effective for prayer than Greek.</summary>

...we [can]. For if anything else is suitable to the gods, that which is eternal and immutable is most akin to the gods above all else. Among these points, Porphyry says that he who hears the sound of divine names looks to their meanings; therefore, he claims the concept itself—remaining the same everywhere—is sufficient, regardless of how it is spoken. 

Iamblichus responds in this manner: "However, it is not as you think. For if names were established by human agreement and convention, it would make no difference if some were substituted for others. But if they were adapted to the nature of things, those which most closely match this nature are also most dear to the gods. 

From this, it is clearly evident that the speech of sacred nations <note>Iamblichus specifically refers to the Egyptians and Assyrians/Chaldeans as "sacred nations" because he believed their languages were more primordial and closer to the gods.</note> is reasonably preferred over others. For names translated into another language do not preserve exactly the same meaning; rather, there are certain things unique to individual nations that cannot be expressed to other nations through speech. To this it is added that, even if we could translate the specific properties of the meanings through another language, they still do not preserve the same power once changed. 

Furthermore, foreign names <note>original: "nomina barbara." In the ancient world, "barbarous" simply meant non-Greek; here it refers to the sacred Egyptian or Chaldean words used in rituals.</note> possess great emphasis—that is, effectiveness in suggestion and demonstration—and they possess a concise brevity. Indeed, very little...

<column-break/>

of ambiguity, variety, and the multitude of words [is found in them], and for all these reasons they are most fitting for the higher beings. Therefore, set aside these suspicions that fall away from the truth—namely, those by which you suspect that the Egyptian language is only effective when the one invoking is Egyptian or uses the Egyptian language. 

Instead, consider that since the Egyptians were the first of all to be granted the presence and participation of the gods, the gods especially approve of the one who invokes them when they are called upon according to the Egyptian rite. Nor should it be said that these 'barbarous' and obscure divine names are merely the schemes of tricksters and sorcerers. For how can those things which are most closely joined to the gods, and join us to them, and possess power almost equal to the higher beings, be imaginary fictions—especially when no sacred work can be accomplished without them? 

Neither are such coverings and veils created by our passions <note>original: "passiones." In Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the irrational, emotional parts of the human soul that can distort one's perception of the divine.</note> through popular report and attributed to the divine. For we do not begin from those things that we ourselves experience; rather, starting from the properties of the gods themselves, we attribute to them expressions that are appropriate to them according to their nature. Nor do we form contrary notions of the divine—contrary, that is, to how it truly is—but rather just as its nature truly exists...

# IAMBLICHUS

Just as those who first achieved the truth about [the divine] and passed down the laws concerning religious sanctity to us, so we persevere in them. For if anything else in sacred laws and rituals pleases God, stability itself pleases him most and is especially fitting. Therefore, it is necessary to always preserve the ancient rites of adoration intact as sacred things, neither taking anything away nor adding anything from elsewhere. For this has recently been almost the cause of everything—both names and prayers—being weakened: because through that very transgression and the desire for innovation, they are always changed, and they do not stop being changed. 

For the Greeks are by nature eager for new things <note>Iamblichus, though writing in Greek, critiques Greek culture for its intellectual restlessness and lack of tradition compared to the East.</note>, and are carried headlong in every direction like a ship lacking ballast, having no stability, nor do they preserve what they have received from others. Instead, they quickly let go of this, and they are accustomed to transforming everything through the eloquence of new invention because of their instability. 

But the Barbarians <note>original: "Barbari." In the ancient world, "barbarous" simply meant non-Greek; here it refers specifically to the Egyptians and Assyrians whom Iamblichus considers more spiritually grounded.</note>, just as they are serious and firm in their customs, so they also persevere firmly in those same words; and indeed, because of this stability, they themselves are friends to the gods and offer prayers acceptable to them, which it is never lawful for anyone to change by any reasoning.

a certain defined limit by his command, and especially by the exalted unity which is the cause of all things. God produced **Matter** from "materiality" <note>original: "materialitate." In this philosophy, matter is not an accident but an emanation derived from the divine essence.</note>—that is, matter is derived from "essentiality"—which the Creator, taking up as something vital, used to fashion the simple and impassive spheres. He took the last part of this matter for the making of generated and corruptible bodies. Since these things are so distinguished, the doubts you say you have conceived regarding the Egyptian books you have read are easily resolved. For those works which are circulated under the title of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius," the Latin name for Hermes Trismegistus.</note> contain "Mercurial" opinions, even if they often speak in the style of Greek philosophers. For they were translated from the Egyptian language into Greek by men not unskilled in philosophy. I would wish, however, that whoever touches upon the primary causes of worldly things would also declare the ultimate principles. Likewise, I wish those who treat the planets, the zodiac, the **decans**, the **horoscopes**, and the powerful leading stars would hand down the particular distributions of the principles. Consequently, the doctrines found in the *Salmeschiniaka* <note>original: "salaminiacis," likely a corruption of "Salmeschiniaka," an ancient Egyptian astrological work.</note> contain only a very small part of the Mercurial arrangements. Likewise, those things treated concerning the appearances or occultations of the stars, or the waxing or waning of the moon, are assigned the lowest place in the Egyptian system.

<summary>This page outlines the Neoplatonic hierarchy of the gods (from the One to the Creator) and explains that matter is a divine emanation. Iamblichus also defends the authenticity of the Hermetic "Books of Mercury," explaining they were translated from Egyptian into the language of Greek philosophy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus's defense of Egyptian theology against the skepticism of Porphyry. Having established the hierarchy of divine beings, Iamblichus now moves to distinguish between the physical laws of nature and the higher intellectual life of the soul, drawing on the secret wisdom of Hermes Trismegistus to explain how humans can transcend the power of fate.</meta>

<page-num>354</page-num>
<header># IAMBLICHUS</header>

...they possess as causes. Indeed, the Egyptians do not believe that all things are natural, but they distinguish between life that is **intellectual** <note>original: "intellectualem"</note> and life that is **animate** <note>original: "animalē"; referring to the life of the soul/animal vitality</note> from nature itself: not only in the universe at large, but also within human beings. And since they have placed **intellect and reason** <note>original: "intellectū & rationem"</note> as existing independently at the head of all things, they believe that whatever is made is created in this way; they assert that the first and most excellent father of those things which exist in the process of **generation** <note>original: "generatione"; the world of physical birth and change</note> is the **Architect** <note>original: "opificē"; the Demiurge or Creator</note>. They also recognize a vital power, both that which is in the heavens and that which exists above the heavens. Likewise, they place a **pure intellect** above the world, and one indivisible intellect throughout the whole world, and another that is distributed through all the celestial circles. Now, they are not accustomed to contemplate these things with mere words and naked reason alone, but they further advise and teach that our nature can progress to the higher, more universal things that are superior to **fate** <note>original: "fato"</note>, toward God himself and the Architect of the world—provided that the soul carries no matter with it, nor anything else except the observance of the proper timing. They teach that we attain this through the performance of **sacred works** <note>original: "ſacrorū opera"; theurgy or religious rituals</note>, and through them we are simultaneously perfected. **Mercury** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage and purported author of the Hermetic texts</note> himself handed down this path to us; but the prophet **Bitis** <note>A legendary Egyptian figure mentioned in Hermetic literature</note> interpreted it for King **Ammon**, having found it in the inner sanctuaries of a temple in the Egyptian city of **Sais** <note>original: "Saym"; an ancient city in the Nile Delta</note>, engraved in sacred characters. He also provided

<column-break/>

<page-num>355</page-num>
<header>### ON THE MYSTERIES</header>

the name of God for us, which runs through the entire universe. There are many other ranks of being concerning these same matters. Therefore, you do not seem to me to be correct in reducing all Egyptian teachings to purely natural causes. For among them, there are many things belonging to many different **essences** <note>original: "eſſentijs"</note>; there are also super-mundane powers which they have worshipped with a particular religious sanctity.

->*On free will, and how we are freed from fate.*<-

After these things, **Porphyry** says: "Many of the Egyptians have also subjected our own **free will** <note>original: "arbitrium noſtrum"</note> to the motion of the stars." **Iamblichus** responds from the Hermetic <note>original: "mercurialibus"</note> teachings in this manner: Man has **two souls**, as the Hermetic writings teach. One is from the **First Intelligible** <note>original: "intelligibili primo"</note> and participates in the power of the Architect himself. The other, however, is instilled in us from the circuit of the heavenly bodies, into which the soul that contemplates divine things also creeps. Therefore, the soul that descends into us from the worlds <note>meaning the planetary spheres</note> follows the circuits of those worlds. But the soul that comes from the Intelligible, and is present in an intellectual way, stands above the circuit of **generation** <note>original: "geneſicū circuitū"</note>; and through it, we are both **freed from fate** and ascend to the intellectual gods, and we possess a religion that reaches toward eternal things. Therefore, one should not think—as you were doubting—that all things are bound by the indissoluble chains of **necessity**, which they call fate.

<summary>Iamblichus explains that Egyptian theology transcends mere nature and astrology, revealing that humans possess a dual soul: one part governed by the stars (fate), and a higher, intellectual part that can be liberated through sacred rites.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus's explanation of how the soul relates to fate and the divine hierarchy. He is addressing the concern of how a soul can be subject to the laws of the physical world (fate) while also possessing a spark of the divine that allows for liberation.</meta>

<page-num>356</page-num>
<header># IAMBLICHUS</header>

...to be bound. For the soul has a principle proper to itself, through which it may betake itself to the **intellectual** <note>original: "intelligibile"; referring to the realm of pure, divine thought</note> realm, and indeed depart from those things which are brought into being <note>original: "quæ gignūtur"; refers to the realm of physical birth and change</note>, and approach being itself and the divine. Nor, again, have we assigned **fate** <note>original: "fatum"</note> to the gods, whom we worship in temples, sacred places, and statues as those who release us from fate. Indeed, the gods themselves dissolve fate. However, the natures that descend last from them, and are already intertwined with **generation** <note>original: "generationi"; the cycle of physical birth, death, and decay</note> and the body of the world, carry out the work of fate.

Rightly, therefore, we offer every form of sanctity to the gods, so that they alone—dominating necessity through **intellectual persuasion** <note>original: "intellectualem persuasionem"</note>—may dissolve the evils threatening us from fate. For not everything is bound within the nature of fate; rather, there is another principle of the soul, superior both to nature and to generation, through which we can be joined to the gods, surpass the mundane order, and participate in the **eternal life** and the activity of the **super-celestial gods** <note>original: "supercœlestiumque deorum"; gods who exist above the physical heavens</note>. Therefore, through this principle, we can exempt ourselves from fate. For when the more excellent parts of those things within us are active, and the soul recalls itself to its own more excellent parts, then it is entirely separated from those things which bind it in generation, departs from the inferior things, and exchanges one life for another,

<column-break/>

<header># ON THE MYSTERIES. 357</header>

and inserts itself into another order, while entirely deserting the prior order. What then? Is it not possible to free oneself from fate through the **circulating gods** <note>original: "deos circumcurrentes"; the planetary or celestial gods who move through the sky</note>, and yet meanwhile consider them the leaders and authors of fates, who bind our lives thoroughly with indissoluble chains? Perhaps, in truth, nothing prevents this from being so. For since the gods embrace many essences and powers within themselves, what prevents there being other differences and contrarieties in them that are inestimable to us? Indeed, one might even say this: that in each of the visible gods, there are certain **intelligible principles of essence** <note>original: "intelligibilia quædam essentię principia"</note>, through which flight and freedom from the world's generation may happen for souls.

If, however, someone does not admit two orders of gods for the duty of liberation—namely, the **mundane** <note>original: "mundanos"; those within the physical world</note> as well as the **super-mundane** <note>original: "supermundanos"; those beyond the physical world</note>—at least through the super-mundane ones, a release will eventually occur. But these matters are declared more carefully in the treatise on the gods: which gods specifically are the **conductors to the heights** <note>original: "supera reductores"; those who lead the soul upward</note>, and how they recall us, by what powers, and by what reasoning they dissolve fate; and through which specific **returns** <note>original: "redditus"; likely referring to the ritual stages of the soul's journey back to the divine</note> performed by sacred operation; and what the order of the mundane nature is; and in what way the **perfected intellectual action** dominates this order.

<summary>Iamblichus explains that while the lower aspects of nature are bound by fate, the human soul possesses a higher principle that allows it to connect with the gods and achieve liberation. He suggests that certain gods act as "conductors" to lead the soul away from the cycle of physical birth and toward an eternal, intellectual life.</summary>

For this reason, regarding what you cited from the verses of **Homer** <note>original: "Homeri uerſibus"; specifically referring to the Iliad, where it is suggested that the gods' hearts are "flexible" or "pliant"</note>—namely, that the gods are **flexible**—we deem it a sacrilege to say. But certainly, everywhere not only do false things disagree with each other, but the false also disagrees with the true, so that truth can be found everywhere alongside what is false.

**Porphyry** says that even the rules of **astronomy** <note>original: "astronomiae"; in this period, astronomy (mapping the stars) and astrology (interpreting their influence) were often overlapping disciplines</note> cannot be grasped, let alone those of astrology, and that there are many disagreements within them and they are attacked by many people. 

**Iamblichus** responds: Divine prophecy can teach the nature and effect of the stars without the need for technical art. Astronomy and other arts, once given by the gods, have been confused over a long period by human opinions, and in the end, they retain only a tiny amount of divinity and truth. Yet in astronomy, there is something of the truth, however small: this is evident through the effects of the stars arising among themselves according to their measurement in the heavens, just as was predicted concerning the eclipse of the Sun and Moon and the aspects of the planets. The rules of measurements, the magnitude of distances, movements, comets, and similar things—observed for a long time among the **Chaldeans** <note>original: "Chaldaeos"; the people of Mesopotamia, famous in the ancient world for their advanced astronomical records</note> and among us—testify that the science of astronomy is true.

cannot be identified even by the judgment of astronomers and astrologers, but that the personal **daemon** <term>daemon: a guardian spirit or tutelary guide assigned to a soul at birth</term> must be sought from that source. 

**Iamblichus** says that astrologers provide rules—some providing five, others fewer, others more—for finding and distinguishing the lords of the birth charts. What then prevents the lord of the figure and the daemon from being found with difficulty through astrology, yet very easily through divine prophecy and sacrifices?

We can find our own daemon not through human arts, but through divine ones. Each person's own daemon is not distributed by some particular arrangement of the heavens or the elements, but by the entire arrangement of the world. This happens when the soul descends while the cosmos is ruling, and the cosmos accommodates a specific daemon to the soul as the executor of the life which the soul has chosen. This daemon reconciles the soul to the body, cares for the life joined to the body, directs the soul's own particular life, and constantly provides principles for our thoughts; and we perform such actions as the daemon leads us toward.

->*From where the personal daemon comes, what it does, and whether it is unique.*<-

The personal daemon <note>original: "proprius dæmon"; the unique spirit that guides an individual throughout their life</note> is not assigned from just one part of the heavens or from the elements, but rather from the whole world, from the multiform life within it, and from the multiform bodies through which the soul passes as it descends into **generation** <term>generation: the process of the soul entering the physical world and taking on a mortal body</term>. A certain lot is specifically discerned and decreed within us, distributed to our own affairs according to its own unique governance. This daemon existed in the **exemplar** <note>original: "exemplari"; the ideal or archetypal model of the individual soul in the divine mind</note> before souls slipped into generation. As soon as the soul receives a leader, the daemon himself stands by as the subsequent fulfiller of lives. As I have said, this daemon binds the soul to the body as it descends; he cares for its common 
<meta>catchword: soul</meta>

living being <note>original: "animal"; referring to the "living thing" formed by the union of soul and body</note>. He directs the soul's own life and provides the principles for whatever we reason; we perform such actions as he brings to mind, and he governs us until, purified by sacred works, we take up a god as our leader instead of the daemon. Afterward, the daemon yields to this god, either resting in his presence or contributing to the same end. 

You asked next whether several daemons are present to each person, governing different parts of the human being. We respond to this: the daemon does not merely preside over one part of us, but is present to the whole at once and leads the whole, just as he was assigned by all the orders that exist in the world. You conjectured that many daemons are present to us according to the number of our parts. Furthermore, you suggested that even within the body itself there are different daemons: one caring for health, another for beauty, and others for some other condition, with one presiding equally over these in the body. Thus, you also thought that one daemon rules the body, another the soul, and another the mind. 

However, it is better to apply such a conjecture to this very point: namely, that the body, soul, and **intellect** <note>original: "intellectus"; the highest part of the soul capable of grasping divine truths</note> are all governed by the same daemon. Do not, therefore, divide them so that there is one daemon for the body, another for the soul, and another for the intellect. For it is absurd...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that the personal daemon is a single, unified governing spirit superior to the human soul, rather than a part of the soul itself like the intellect. # IAMBLICHUS

...sends down. After, therefore, each person’s own spirit is present, it then reveals the worship appropriate to itself, and makes known its name and its own proper mode of invocation. And here is the appropriate order of **daemons** <note>original: "daimonum"; in this context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or guardian beings between gods and humans</note>. For one order is akin to those who invoke them, another proceeds from more ancient causes, and another completes a harmonious union <note>original: "conspirationem"; literally a "breathing together" or conspiracy in the sense of a unified collective</note> among themselves, contributing together toward the same end. Do not, therefore, judge divine invocations to be similar to human ones, nor compare the ineffable with things that can be spoken, nor compare those things which surpass every limit and every indeterminate mode with human commands and orders, whether these be defined or entirely undefined. For those things which are among us have nothing in common with the whole genus of higher beings, and with those who exceed us according to their entire order, and surpass our whole essence and nature. From here, indeed, the greatest errors happen to men, when out of human weakness they are accustomed to reason about the dominions of spirits, and they weigh vast, highly valued, and perfect things by small, worthless, and divided ones.

->Concerning Happiness<-

Do you perhaps suspect that some other path to happiness lies hidden besides divine worship, and you ask what that might specifically be?

<column-break/>

<page-num>369</page-num>
# ON THE MYSTERIES

But truly, if the essence and perfection of all goods are contained in the gods, and the first power and the first principle of goods are found there, then it is with good reason that we priests alone—and those who have similarly dedicated themselves to the celestial beings and have legitimately attained union with them—earnestly pursue the beginning and end of all goods. In this state, certainly, both the contemplation of truth is present, and the consummation of **intellectual science** <note>original: "intellectualis scientiae"; referring to "noetic" knowledge or the highest form of understanding that perceives divine realities directly</note>; and along with the knowledge of the gods, the turning toward ourselves and the recognition of our own self also follows. But you suspect in vain that perhaps the religious man depends upon human opinions and favors. What leisure could there be for a soul dedicated to the gods to listen to human praises?

->That Religion is True<-

But neither do you doubt correctly regarding what follows—namely, that perhaps the religious man himself is deceived, where you say the soul often fabricates great things from chance. What beginning of fabrications can there be in things that truly exist? Is it not that **imaginative power** <note>original: "potentia phantastica"; the faculty of *phantasia*, which produces mental images or "idols"</note> in us which fashions and transforms images? And when the intellectual life acts perfectly, no imagination arises; is not truth itself present with the gods according to their essence?

For such natural foretelling follows from a sharpness of the senses, or a certain sympathy <note>original: "compassionem"; the Stoic and Neoplatonic idea that all parts of the universe are physically linked and "feel" together</note>, or some other movement of natural forces. ...shivering, physicians are accustomed to foresee a fever—does such foresight seem to be particularly honorable. Therefore, only the prophecy that comes from the divine truly exhibits a divine life to us; for it possesses both foresight and divine understandings, and it makes us truly divine and brings us the legitimate good. For the most blessed intelligence of the gods is abundantly filled with all good things. 

You may perhaps suspect that divinely inspired prophets foresee what is to come, yet are not happy for that reason; for they may be able to foresee, yet not know how to make use of the things to come. But to the contrary, it must be said that every divinely inspired foreknowledge is filled with goods and goodness, and is possessed of order and decorum, and brings utility to us. For the gods, together with the foretelling, also suggest to us the faculty for avoiding and turning away from the inconveniences that naturally threaten us. ## *The Way to Happiness.*

You asked next what the way to happiness is, and in what thing happiness itself consists. Listen, then, to this. Man was once an intellect <term>Intellect: (Latin: *intellectus*) in this context, the highest part of the human spirit capable of perceiving divine truths directly</term> capable of contemplation in himself, joined to the contemplation of the gods. Then, however, he entered another soul, which was fitted or tempered around the human form. And for that reason, he is bound within the very chain of necessity and fate. Therefore, one ought to consider by what primary means he can be released from chains of this kind. There is no release except for the knowledge of the gods themselves. For the idea of happiness is to know the Good itself, exactly as it is; and the idea of evils is the forgetting of the Good and a deception regarding evil. That knowledge, indeed, proceeds together with the divine; but this forgetting and deception is inseparable from that which is fleeting <note>original: *caduco*; referring to the material world which is subject to decay and change</note>. Likewise, the former measures the essences of intelligible things <note>the eternal, unchanging realities of the divine realm</note> through the sacred ways of holiness; but the latter, falling from and being rejected by the principles, casts itself down to measure the material form. The former, again, is the recognition of its own parent; but the latter is a departure along with a forgetting of God the Fa—

<column-break/>

# DE MYSTERIIS

—ther <note>completing the word *patre* from the previous column</note>, who is super-holy and self-sufficient, remaining far removed. The former preserves true life, calling it back to the Father. The latter leads man, the ruler of his own birth <note>referring to the soul's role in governing the physical life into which it is born</note>, down even to that which never remains the same but exists in a state of perpetual flux. This, certainly, becomes the first way to happiness for you, as you possess the intellectual fullness of divine union within souls. Indeed, the sacred and deifying tradition of happiness is called the gate to God the Creator of all, or the place, or the court of the Good. It possesses power: first, indeed, the chaste and sober holiness of the soul, which is much more useful than the sober chastity of the body; then, the alignment of thought toward the participation in and vision of the Good, and simultaneously toward the expulsion of opposites. Thirdly, it offers union with the gods, the givers of all good things. After it has joined the soul—individually and specifically—first to the parts of the world and then to the divine powers diffused through the parts of the world, it then joins the soul to the whole Creator <term>Creator: (Latin: *opifex*) also known as the Demiurge, the divine craftsman of the universe</term>, and offers consensus with Him from every side, placing the soul outside of all matter, joined now only with the eternal reason of the universe. For example: in the power of the Creator himself, self-generated, self-moving, and sustaining all things...

# 174 IAMBLICHUS

...completely remaining and elevating, and intellectual, and equally adorning all things; likewise, it recalls the soul to intelligible truth <term>Intelligible truth: reality that is perceived by the mind or intellect rather than the physical senses</term>. Again, it is something that is perfect in itself and brings things to perfection, acting as an effective cause. It fits the soul together with the other powers of the creator god <note>original: *dei opificis*; a reference to the Demiurge or the divine craftsman who shapes the universe</note> step by step according to the unique property of each power. This is done so that the purified and holy soul may be perfectly strengthened in their actions, intellects, and creative faculties; and then, finally, it places the soul within the god who is the creator of all.

### *Conclusion on religion and happiness among the Egyptians.*

And here, among the Egyptians, is the goal of the religious and sacred elevation of the soul. They consider one type of Good to be divine—namely, the god who is known beforehand by the intellect—but they consider another to be human, which is the union with the Lord himself. This is exactly how the prophet Bitis explained it from the books of Hermes <term>mercurialibus: referring to the "Books of Hermes" (Hermes Trismegistus), a body of Egyptian-Greek wisdom texts</term>. Therefore, this part of the doctrine has not been overlooked by the Egyptians, as you suspect, but has been duly handed down to us as it pertains to the rites of holiness. Nor, again, do the priests consult the divine intelligence about trivial matters, but rather about those things which pertain to the purification, release, and salvation of the soul. They do not meditate on difficult things that are also useless to men; on the contrary, they study the things of the soul, which are of all 

<column-break/>

# ON THE MYSTERIES 375

things the most useful. Nor do the priests wander in error, obscured under the deceit of some seducing demon; rather, they are those who completely surpass the deceptive and demonic nature in all things and ascend to the intelligible and divine realm.

These things having been thoroughly discussed, I pray to the gods that they may grant to me and to you a true guarding and observance of these spiritual truths <note>original: *intelligentiarum*; here referring to the higher perceptions of the mind</note> which will never fail, and that they may provide the truth of eternal things throughout everlasting eternity. May they make us masters of the understanding of perfect things concerning the gods, in which the most blessed end of all good things is set before us, and which is the source of all authority and the firm foundation of mutual friendship and harmony between us.

### THE END OF IAMBLICHUS ON THE MYSTERIES.

The BEGINNING of the Platonic dialogues and the principal and firmest foundation of all philosophy, they believe, is the knowledge of our own nature: for when this is rightly known, we will be able to know more perfectly the good that is suitable for us and the evil that is at odds with us. Indeed, it is so arranged by nature that just as the essences <term>essentia: the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing</term> of things differ among themselves, so too do the specific perfections of things. Therefore, so that we may find what the perfection of our nature is and how it is obtained, we must first recognize our essence: This is indeed what is proposed in the *Alcibiades* and is the goal in all of Plato’s teaching. When we consider the essences of things, we must investigate whether the essence of a thing is among those that are indivisible, or among the kind that are divided around bodies...

For just as in Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founding philosopher of Neoplatonism; Proclus frequently cites him as an authority.</note> a "leakage" of the mind creates mere craftiness, and a fallen portion of wisdom creates sophistry <note>original: "sophistica." *A superior cause acts upon a work before and after an inferior one, and alongside it, and is more present to the work.*

Those things that are more perfect in every way, and which serve as the primary models <note>original: "exemplaris." The Platonic Ideas or Archetypes.</note>, entirely encompass the actions of their lesser images. This is so true that inferior things are never present in any situation unless the more perfect things have also, shortly before, contributed something of their own essence.

Furthermore, throughout all the orders of reality, the One itself <note>The "One" is the ultimate, indivisible source of all existence in this philosophy.</note> encompasses all other things, acting before them, after them, and together with them.

*Evil daemons also occur in sacred rites, and they deceive under the pretext of good things.*

We have found it to be true in purifications and sacred rites that lower beings everywhere put on an "image of perfection." Through this mask, they lure souls that are not yet perfected toward themselves and divert them from higher things. Just as in the contemplation of nature a "sophistical" life is an impediment—a leaning that draws the weaker soul away from the contemplation of true beings toward an imagination preoccupied with fleeting things—so too in the elevation of love, the crowd of "popular" lovers <note>Proclus distinguishes between "heavenly love" (spiritual) and "popular/vulgar love" (purely physical).</note> is an obstacle. These figures pretend to be true lovers, twisting the soul of the youth away from celestial goods and toward earthly and dark things. 

Similarly, in all the most holy purifications and sacrifices, before the **god** <term>deus: here referring to the specific higher deity being invoked in the rite</term> is actually present, the attacks of certain earthly daemons openly occur. They present strange sights that disturb those being purified and perfected, deflecting them from pure goods toward matter <note>original: "materiam." For thus the divine oracles <note>Likely a reference to the Chaldean Oracles, a text highly revered by Neoplatonists like Proclus.</note> say: *It is not beneficial for you to look upon them before you have purified and consecrated the body: since they, by soothing souls, everywhere turn them away from the sacrifices.* Therefore, just as in the sacred rites the divine first appears only when we have driven out all this demonic force that drags souls into matter: so also the divine lover, after the rejection of popular <note>original: "popularium." Referring to common or vulgar lovers motivated by physical desire rather than spiritual growth.</note> lovers, encounters the beloved. Likewise, just as a good spirit <term>daemon: In this context, a "daemon" is not an evil entity but a protective guardian spirit or a mediating power between gods and men.</term> guards each person from childhood, and examines all his actions and words, and provides for him even before his parents do, and is present after his parents as the constant governor of his whole life, and after death acts as our guide to the judges: in the same way, Socrates conducts himself toward Alcibiades. Finally, just as a good spirit is present to us while remaining mostly hidden, secretly providing for us, counseling us in silence, and ineffably correcting us: so Socrates behaves toward Alcibiades.

### *The Intellect in us always acts by illuminating, yet*
### *we do not always notice it.*

The Intellect itself indeed always acts around us, and always offers the light of understanding, even before we fall into the irrational condition. And when we live life in passions—

# THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT.

—and even when those passions are eventually calmed, we do not always notice it. It is only when we have been purged from the great tumult of generation <note>original: "generationis." The realm of physical birth and material change, often described by Platonists as a "tumult" or "storm."</note> and live tranquilly that the Intellect shines upon us; then it speaks with us, as it were, and communicates its voice to us, though it was previously present in silence.

### *On the good spirit, and on earthly and material demons.*
### *Also how each of us may be considered in two ways,*
### *namely both as soul simply, and as soul using a body.*

Socrates indeed conducts himself toward Alcibiades like a good spirit; the other lovers are like material and earthly demons, who must be driven away so that the soul may be more exposed to the good spirit. One can consider Alcibiades in two ways: both as soul simply, and as soul using a body. For these two are not the same, just as a man considered by himself is not the same as a man who is a pilot; nor is a man simply the same as a charioteer. In every way, that which is unparticipated <term>imparticipabile: A Neoplatonic technical term for a primary principle that remains pure and independent, rather than being "distributed" into the things that depend on it.</term> differs from that which is participated. And that which exists according to itself differs from that which is already reckoned together with something else. And finally, that which is set apart differs from that which is coordinated...

Since there are three substances in the intelligible and hidden gods: the first is marked by the **Good**, essentially understanding the Good itself from within, where (as the sacred oracles <note>A reference to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a text Proclus considered divinely inspired.</note> teach) there is a "paternal unity"; the second is designated by the **Wise**, where the first intelligence flourishes; the third is designated by the **Beautiful**, where the most beautiful of intelligible things exists, as the *Timaeus* says. 

Doubtless, three Unities also exist according to these intelligible causes—subsisting uniformly among the intelligibles according to their cause, but first shining forth in the ineffable order of the gods—namely: **Faith, Truth, and Love**. 

**Faith** indeed strengthens all things in the Good; **Truth** unfolds all knowledge among beings; and finally, **Love** converts all things and gathers them into the [Beautiful].

...of love resides among the gods? For this erotic affection, as **Socrates** says in the *Phaedrus*, is granted by a certain divine gift. Therefore, gods love gods: the elder indeed love the lesser through the gift of **providence**; in turn, the lesser love the greater through a certain duty of **reversion**. <term>reversion: (Latin: *conversio*) The process by which a soul or lower being "turns back" toward its divine source to find fulfillment.</term> To perfect inferior things and to provide for lower ones belongs also to souls, insofar as they are souls. Indeed, for this very reason they descend: for the sake of providing for things that are born and for the care of mortals. But to provide in such a way that the provider is neither mixed with the governed, nor affected as if enslaved, nor receives anything from that lower state—this is the unique property of the gods and good demons. Whenever this occurs in human souls, it happens through divine or demonic bounty. Priests are accustomed, in the most holy sacrifices, to lead those present into admiration and **awe** <note>original: "stuporem." In this context, it refers to a state of being "struck" by divine presence, a prerequisite for mystical union.</note>, whether through words or through things shown to the eyes. For awe is accustomed to open the soul to God. **Socrates** would never have lived a life of love so correctly, unless he had chosen it by a certain inspiration <note>original: "afflatu." Literally a "breathing upon" or divine breath.</note> of a **demon**, and held fast to that choice.

*He refutes two opinions: the first, which says there are no other*

We shall not, therefore, admit those who say that daemons are our souls which have already fulfilled this life and been translated into another. For it is not fitting to consider a daemon defined by a temporary state <note>original: "per habitudinem." This refers to a soul that might act "daemonically" but is not a daemon by its very nature.</note> as the same thing as a daemon by essence. Nor is it fitting to establish a perpetual middle order for all worldly things out of a life that changes itself in many different ways. For the demonic guardianship itself always stands in the same manner, maintaining the continuity of the universe. But the soul does not retain its order in this way, as Socrates says in the *Republic*: for at different times, it chooses different lives. Nor shall we again approve of those who think some daemons are gods—as if they were "wandering gods"—as Amelius <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> thinks. Instead, we shall follow Plato himself, who speaks of the gods as the masters of the universe, but places the flocks of daemons in subjection to the gods. And everywhere we shall approve the reasoning of Diotima, who attributes to daemons the middle order between gods and mortals.

**Since** daemons are therefore established in the middle, as we have said, the first and highest among them are the divine daemons; they frequently appear as gods because of their excellent similarity to the gods. harmonize with those that fall away? <note>original: "caducis" - referring to perishable or mortal things.</note> How can causes be joined with effects, unless bound together by such a middle ground? For nature, as this kind of medium, rules over bodily goods and provides for all natural abundances. Most of their number are occupied with matter, and they contain and weave together the powers descending from celestial matter into [earthly] matter, and they guard it continuously, preserving the variety and the "painting" <note>original: "picturam" - used here to describe the complex, colorful patterns of physical forms and appearances.</note> of forms within it.

->*The five duties of daemons: the first daemons join souls to their own gods.*<-

**Since** daemons are many and multiform, as Diotima <note>A reference to the wise woman in Plato's *Symposium* who teaches Socrates about the nature of Love and daemons.</note> says: the highest indeed join the souls proceeding from the Father to the gods who are their leaders. For every god leads first the daemons, and then the particular souls. For as Timaeus <note>A character from Plato's dialogue of the same name, discussing the creation of the universe.</note> says, the god who is the maker of these things sowed some souls into the sun, others into the moon, and others into other gods; those gods are indeed daemons <note>Proclus is explaining that even some "gods" function as daemonic intermediaries for the souls assigned to them.</note> who have been allotted souls according to their essence, and they join them to their own leaders. And yet every soul, even if it revolves around its own god, requires the benefit of such a daemon. The second daemons dispense the ascents and descents of souls, and from these, choices are made for many souls. Truly, of the most perfect souls, which [conduct] their life in generation <note>original: "generatione" - the realm of physical birth and material existence.</note> without the commerce of things that can be generated...

->A daemon is spoken of in three ways: by essence, by comparison, or by a certain disposition.<-

...according to essence <note>original: "essentiam"</note>, a daemon is not named a daemon because of a relationship to things that follow it, nor because of any similarity to something else. Instead, it has obtained this property by its very self, and is distinguished in its own existence by its own powers and by its differing modes of action. To be sure, in the *Timaeus* <note>One of Plato's most famous dialogues, dealing with the creation of the universe and the nature of the physical world.</note>, the rational soul is called an "animal daemon." However, we are investigating the daemon of the human being itself, not the daemon of the animal. We seek the one who directs the rational soul, not merely the soul's instrument. Furthermore, we seek the one who—once the animal body is finally dissolved—leads the soul to the judges, just as **Socrates** asserts in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue describing the final hours of Socrates and his arguments for the immortality of the soul.</note>. In that state, when the animal body is no longer present, the daemon leads each person to the judge. I speak of the daemon itself who had obtained custody of the person while they were living. For if the daemon has possessed the person during their life and presents them for judgment after death—namely, the human being—then it was not merely an animal that the daemon possessed. Indeed, beginning from above and commanding, the daemon governs our entire constitution.

->*Against those who say the daemon is either an acting part of the soul, or a part set over it.*<-

**BUT** neither should those be approved who, having set aside the 

<column-break/>

rational soul, say that the daemon is the very thing which acts within the soul. For example, they might say that in those living according to reason, the daemon is "Reason"; but in those living by anger, it is the "Irascible" <note>The spirited or "angry" part of the soul in Platonic psychology.</note> part; and in those living by desire, it is the "Concupiscible" <note>The part of the soul associated with physical cravings and desires.</note> part. Nor, again, should those be heard who say the daemon is that which, in our very life, presides most closely over the part that acts—such as "Reason" presiding over the angry, or the "Power of Anger" presiding over the lustful. In the first place, to say that daemons are merely parts of the human soul is the view of those who admire human life too much. Such people do not approve of **Socrates** in the *Republic*, who, after the gods and daemons, arranges the heroic and human races. Socrates even rebukes the poets for introducing heroes who are no better than humans, but are instead enslaved to similar passions. Therefore, Socrates, in rebuking such things, would be very far from the opinion that would place daemons (who are superior to heroes) among the mere parts and powers of the soul. For from these views, it would follow that things that are better by essence would be contained within to complete things that are worse. Furthermore, changes in one's way of life would lead to various changes of daemons. For a greedy man is often changed into an ambitious life. The ambitious man changes into a state living by right opinion, and this man into a state endowed with knowledge. If the daemon were just a part of the soul, the daemon...

He refutes the idea that "daemon" is just a metaphor for reason or passion, citing Socrates's hierarchical ranking of gods, daemons, heroes, and humans.</summary>

...therefore, if it were otherwise in a similar way, it would be another. For the very part acting in the soul exists as one thing at one time and another at another. If, therefore, either this acting part itself, or the part nearest to it and presiding over it, were the daemon, then surely the daemons would be changed together with the mutations of human life; and in the same life, the same soul would obtain many daemons, which can in no way happen. For the soul never changes the prefecture <note>original: "praefecturam"; referring to the office, leadership, or guardianship of the daemon.</note> of the daemon in the same course of life, but the same daemon—from birth itself <note>original: "genitura"; referring to the moment of birth or the astrological nativity.</note> until the presence of the judge of life—governs us, just as **Socrates** asserts in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue describing the immortality of the soul, where Socrates says a daemon leads the soul to judgment after death.</note>.

### The daemon is not a particular intellect, but a substance differing from the intellect, placed within the breadth of souls.

Accordingly, those who think that a particular intellect <note>In Neoplatonism, a "particular intellect" refers to an individual's highest rational faculty rather than a separate divine being.</note> is the same as the daemon allotted to us do not seem to me to rightly confuse the intellectual property with the demonic substance. For all daemons are contained within the breadth <note>original: "latitudine"; a technical term for the hierarchical range or variety of souls in the celestial order.</note> of souls and exist as posterior to the divine souls. Moreover, the intellectual order is something other than the soul, and they have not obtained the same essence, power, or action. Furthermore, souls enjoy the intellect only when

toward it they have turned, and have received light from there, and have joined their own action to it. However, they possess the prefecture of a daemon throughout their whole life and their entire way of living, and through all things which proceed either from fate or providence. For it is the daemon itself who rules our whole life, and fulfills our choices made before birth <note>original: "electiones... ante generationem factas"; a reference to the Myth of Er in Plato's Republic, where souls choose their next life before being born.</note>, as well as the gifts of fate and the rewards of the leaders and the gods. Moreover, it suggests and measures out the illuminations from providence. 

Now, in truth, we—insofar as we are certain souls—depend on the intellect alone; but insofar as we are souls using a body, we also need a daemon. For this reason, **Plato** called the intellect the "governor of the soul" in the *Phaedrus*, but called the daemon the "observer and curator of men" in various places. And yet, no one who considers rightly will find any other single providence closest to us pertaining to all our affairs, except for demonic providence and care. For the intellect is participated in by the rational soul, as we have said, but by the body not at all. Nature is participated in by the body, but by intelligence not at all. The daemon <note>A "daemon" in this Neoplatonic context is not an evil spirit, but a tutelary or guardian spirit—a divine intermediary between gods and humans.</note> truly moves all things, governs everything, and cultivates as well as arranges all our affairs: indeed, it perfects our reason, tempers our disturbances, inspires our nature, sustains the body, supplies fortuitous events, fulfills the requirements of fate, and bestows the gifts of providence. This daemon stands as the sole rector of all things within us and around us, holding the rudder of our entire life.

->*Three things concerning the daemon of Socrates: first, that it is also a god; second, that it appears through a voice; third, that it recalls but does not provoke.*<-

Regarding the daemon of **Socrates**, we must consider three things. First, that it is also called a god, as is clear both here and in the *Apology* <note>Plato’s account of the trial of Socrates.</note>. Second, that it gave a sign to **Socrates** through a voice, which appears in the *Theages* and the *Phaedrus* <note>Two other dialogues by Plato.</note>. Third, that it "recalled" **Socrates** but did not "provoke" <note>The daemon (or *daimonion*) of Socrates famously only acted as a "stop-sign," warning him against certain actions rather than commanding him to do specific things.</note> him, as the *Apology* testifies. From the beginning, for those divine souls who have chosen the intellectual life, there are divine daemons: these are supreme within the genus of daemons, but participants in the nature of the gods before all others. For just as there is something of the daemon among the gods, so too is there something of the god among the daemons. But in the former case, the substance is divine while the proportion <note>original: "proportio"; referring to the specific rank or functional relationship in the cosmic hierarchy.</note> is demonic; among these daemons, however, the property is demonic, while the proportion declares a divine essence.

### *Different daemons are ordered under different gods and hold various duties among themselves.*

What was said concerning the daemon of **Socrates**—namely, that it "recalls" but does not "provoke" <note>The daemon acted as a "stop-sign," warning him what not to do rather than commanding him what to do.</note>—is not a benefit common to all our daemons. Therefore, the character of **Socrates**, which was full of love toward men and naturally ready for good deeds, did not need dæmonic encouragement. However, the daemon would discourage him whenever he approached his work at an unsuitable time or with those who were unfit for his teaching: he was a man who needed a bridle rather than spurs. 

Furthermore, some daemons possess a power of purification and preservation from stain, while others possess a power of generation, others of perfection, and others of creation; they are divided entirely according to the properties and forces of the gods under whom they are ordered. Now indeed, according to their own substance, each protects their clients toward a

<column-break/>

blessed life. Some move us to the care of lesser things, while others draw us back from external actions. It seems, therefore, that the daemon of **Socrates** obtained a property of this kind—I mean a purifying cause and the source of an undefiled life—and was ordered under the power of **Apollo**, who presides over all purification with a uniform virtue. 

By this virtue, then, the daemon separates him from excessive commerce with the common crowd, and gathers him into the inner sanctum of the soul, toward action set apart from lesser things. Indeed, just as in the works of **Orpheus** <note>The legendary poet-prophet of the Orphic mysteries.</note>, **Apollo** presides over **Bacchus** <note>Also known as Dionysus; in Orphic myth, Apollo gathers the pieces of Bacchus after he is torn apart by the Titans.</note>, recalling him from his dispersion into the "Titanic multitude," so too does the daemon of **Socrates**, who is a follower of **Apollo**. For our intellect is the offspring of the Apollonian divinity.

the essence of the soul is not easy for everyone to grasp. Only **Timaeus** <note>The narrator of Plato’s *Timaeus*, who describes the creation of the world and the soul.</note>, therefore, declared its entire essence. For what its nature is like is entirely divine and requires a long exposition to be explained, as **Socrates** says in the *Phaedrus* <note>A Platonic dialogue where Socrates uses the myth of the winged chariot to describe the soul.</note>. 

However, it is easy to explain the powers of the divinities. For from actions—whose nearest mothers are the powers themselves—we perceive those very powers. For "Power" <note>original: "potentia"; in this philosophical context, it refers to the capacity or potential for an essence to act.</note> is the medium between action and essence, produced by essence, yet producing action. Furthermore, power itself has the greatest familiarity with daemons. For everywhere, power holds the middle position, much like a daemon: in intelligible things <note>The highest realm of pure, non-physical reality.</note>, it joins the Father and the Intellect. For power exists simultaneously with the Father, while the Intellect arises from the Father. 

In intellectual things, it joins actions with essences. For action is the offspring of power, while essence gives birth to powers from itself. Therefore, the divinities that are intermediate between us and the gods are properly designated by the name of "Power," because they possess the middle ground everywhere. For true essence and true "being" belong to the gods. But Power, duly serving the gods, has its place in daemons. Finally, action and the bringing to pass, proceeding through their power, are found outwardly in us.

->*Knowledge of future contingencies is certain and necessary among the higher beings.*<-

The divine **Iamblichus** <note>A highly influential Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who integrated theurgy and Greek philosophy.</note> and that leader of ours <note>likely referring to Syrianus, the teacher of Proclus.</note> investigate and solve the matter in this way: How is it not absurd to determine the differences between types of knowledge based on the nature of the things to be known, rather than the reverse—that is, to divide the things to be known according to the differences in the knowers? 

In this way, that which is eternal and divine by its very essence would know all things eternally and divinely; that which is human would know in a human way; that which is truly indivisible would know things indivisibly (or would anticipate those things which are divisible); that which is eternal would know even temporal things beyond time; and that which is rational would know even irrational things rationally. From these points, it is clear that gods and daemons know indefinite things definitely, and unstable things stably and firmly. 

Do we not see that many things unknown to those beings lower than us are, in the meantime, known to us? For irrational animals cannot grasp the nature of universal being, yet we are able to gather it. Why then do we wonder any further that those higher beings <note>original: "superos"; literally "those above," referring to gods and daemons.</note> firmly comprehend things which we only guess at with ambiguous and deceptive knowledge? For our weakness is not the judge of their power, just as...

...mode, nor does the irrational <note>Referring to the "irrational soul," the part of the human psyche governed by emotion and instinct rather than logic.</note> which is inferior to us possess the judgment of our reason, although the irrational—whether it is within us or outside us—may move our intellect. 

Why it might not be absurd for a conjectural foreknowledge of the future to be found in some places, while a stable, determined, and certain one is found nowhere: 

For the very nature of things cannot take its starting points from imperfect, impure things, or things mixed with their opposites. If, however, the conjecture of the future participates in ignorance and is not certain, where then is the knowledge of the future in itself? Where is that pure thing, from which that which comes after and which desires it has obtained its substance, if not among the celestial beings?

->*The celestial beings advise us well, even if they foresee that we will not obey them.*<-

Pythian Apollo <note>Apollo as the deity of the Oracle at Delphi.</note> responded to Laius <note>The father of Oedipus in Greek mythology.</note>, advising him not to beget a son; otherwise, he would be subjected to the violence of daemons <note>Here, "daemons" refers to the avenging spirits or the tragic fate that followed the house of Laius.</note>. And indeed, that famous Laius did not err <note original: "non erravit"; meaning he wasn't misled by the god</note>, but because of his own ignorance, he was encompassed by future dangers. Indeed, all the actions of upright men tend toward their 

<column-break/>

innermost parts. Therefore, if he has acted beneficently and divinely, he already possesses his goal, established in his own proper action, even if nothing external has been perfected from it. 

Similarly, daemons often act concerning us. Consequently, divine things frequently seem to meet and run before lower things, while meanwhile not departing from their own seats. But while they remain in themselves, they seem to approach because of the aptitude of the recipient. For both in the invocations of the gods and in spontaneous encounters, divinity itself seems in a way to approach us—that is to say, when we have proceeded toward it. 

It was the custom among the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, known for their strict way of life and interest in mathematics and the soul.</note> to judge those coming to them by signs established in the body, as to whether they were suited for a better life or not. For nature itself, which fashions bodies for souls, provides them with congruent instruments and indicates the images of the souls in the bodies, through which those skilled in this art <note>The "art" of physiognomy—judging character from physical appearance.</note> can also detect the character of the souls.

Similarly, if the object which is to be known by us has something of a material and unstable nature mixed within it, it undoubtedly causes our knowledge of this very thing to be indefinite and ambiguous. For knowledge of unstable things is not secure from refutation, but such things are barely comprehended through a certain assimilation <note>A Neoplatonic concept where the mind "becomes like" the object it perceives; if the object is shifting matter, the knowledge itself becomes shifting.</note>. Such also is natural virtue: because everywhere that which is imperfect, as if related to matter, is most easily changed. Self-sufficiency <note original: "sufficientia"; likely translating the Greek 'autarkeia'</note> itself first belongs to the gods. For the gods are good, and are certain super-essential goodnesses, and the fullnesses of all beings; through them, sufficiency also falls to all others: to intellects, divine souls, daemons, and ourselves. And while other things are sufficient by a certain participation, the gods are sufficiency by their very substance. Wherefore, common and unchangeable opinion defines blessedness by sufficiency. For those to whom it belongs to be well, it is also fitting to possess sufficiency.

->from the younger gods: therefore the former is more noble than the latter.<-

We say that the rational soul in us is more noble than the irrational soul, because

Truly, the nobility of human families is an image of this high birth, which nonetheless has ignobility mixed in and is changed in turn. But the stable and eternal nobility of souls is derived from the gods, around whom the Fates are said to have been of old, and from divine powers under which they were ordered. For those souls are more noble which are followers <note original: "pedissequae"; literally 'foot-followers' or attendants</note> of the more sublime gods, and dependent on greater powers, according to the distribution arranged in the universe. I assert the same also regarding cities. For from above, according to the strong, the difference descends even to the souls. And we say that some gods are indeed fiery, others ethereal, others celestial, and finally others earthly. Again, of souls, some are from the solar sphere, others the mercurial, others indeed the lunar. And such is the distribution of souls according to these places that one can truly boast of it. But nobility is not according to earthly parents and cities.

<margin>On opportunity, by which the communion of goods is everywhere perfected.</margin>
Just as the gods, applying cures for diseases—that is, for sins in the souls—and providing fruits at the right times, affect them with benefit, so also divine men seek the right opportunity <note>original: *opportunitas*, a translation of the Greek *kairos*, meaning the "opportune moment" or "divine timing."</note> for instruction. But while the gods themselves determine the measures of these opportunities by a divine and intellectual form, humans must pursue them through science. There are also those among men who hunt for these moments through demonic inspiration. For the presence and familiarity of good daemons <term>daemon: an intermediate spirit that guides humans, acting as a bridge between the divine and the earthly.</term> has a primary power within us for infallibly seizing the right opportunity everywhere, which is exactly what happened to Socrates. <column-break/>

For this reason, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed numbers and proportions governed the universe.</note> also named the primary cause itself, from which good is present to all things, as "Opportunity" itself, since it grants to all things the means to be made perfect. By some such occasion, Socrates, guided by his daemon, relied on his timing regarding Alcibiades, approaching him to say certain things just when Alcibiades was also thinking of going to him to ask for those same things. The former is the mother of the action, while the latter is the receptacle of perfection.
