...nevertheless, that which gives is perfect in itself and is moved of its own accord to bestow. Indeed, even if that power is not immediately present, the recipient is awakened toward participation through a supreme aptitude <note>original: *aptitudo*, the inherent fitness or readiness of a soul to receive divine influence</note>. For there are two types of causes: some are immobile and present to everyone everywhere, while others are mobile, being present at certain times to perfect things and at other times remaining distant. Certainly, the intelligible things <note>the higher, non-physical realities or Forms</note> are present everywhere in the same way, always bestowing their gifts upon all in the same manner. Sensible things <note>physical objects perceived by the senses</note>, however, can be present to those participating in them or absent by turns, just as the Sun is now present, filling everything with light, and then departs. Since these things are so, I say that when an aptitude for one of the immobile causes exists in the one about to participate, then that cause is simultaneously present, and the work of the efficient cause is fulfilled. In such cases, only the unfitness of the subjects usually prevents the gifts, since those things which are to deliver them always do so, and are always everywhere the same. ->*Those things you saw more attentively in your homeland, you follow their images here before all others.*<-

Our souls wander here among the images of those things which they saw in the homeland <note>The "homeland" refers to the intelligible or heavenly realm where the soul exists before incarnation</note>, and they are more deeply affected by those images whose patterns <note>original: *exemplaria*, referring to the Platonic Archetypes or Forms</note> they had contemplated more attentively there. For some souls are suited to certain spectacles, and thus some dwell upon certain images rather than others: for they love the likenesses of those things they inspected there. Indeed, whichever souls were followers of great Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> and circled along with him—he who holds the rank of leader among the twelve princes of the universe—these souls, having proceeded even to this place, certainly seek after a commanding <note>original: *imperiosam*, a life of power or leadership</note> style of life according to the appearance of their god. However, they are ignorant of what is truly imperial: they pursue a merely apparent sovereignty among images. Hence Socrates says in the Re-

<meta>catchword: public</meta>

***

<page-num>423</page-num>

public that souls recently departed from the heavens chiefly choose commanding lives. Plato places the most excellent life in the contemplative, the second in the ambitious <note>original: *ambitiosam*, the life seeking honor and spirited action</note>, and the third in the voluptuous or greedy. Souls coming from heaven and being most rightly educated choose the contemplative life. Those also coming from heaven but being educated poorly choose the ambitious life; the rest, coming from the earth, choose the remaining lives.

->*It is a natural sentiment in all people that the gods know the secrets of souls.*<-

All men naturally speak to the gods through their innermost thoughts, passions, and appetites, being persuaded—evidently through immutable preconceptions—that divinity itself knows all things, even the hidden movements <note>original: *momenta*, the "turning points" or impulses of the mind</note> of souls. Certainly every union and community formed by reason requires the presence of a god. For what else both unites the many and gathers together those things that have been separated, if not divinity?

### *God by His providence confirms our free choice.*

The Gods set forth lives for souls, and for those very souls, after they have made their choice, the Gods determine certain lots that suit the chosen life. In this way, the freedom of choice <note>original: *libertas arbitrij*, referring to the human capacity to choose a path of life</note> is contained within the midst of providence; it is moved and determined from that source, and it turns within that middle ground. These matters are clearly described in the *Republic* <note>Referring to Book X of Plato’s Republic and the Myth of Er</note>, where the prophet sets forth lives for the souls, receiving the lots from the knees of Lachesis <note>Lachesis is one of the three Fates (Moirai); she represents the "allotter" who determines the length of life</note>, and crying out among the souls, "O ephemeral souls," <note>original: *O animę diurnæ*, literally "souls of a day"</note> and so forth. Indeed, the presentation of lives is made by Lachesis through the intermediary of the prophet. However, the choice concerning the lives proposed there belongs to the souls themselves. Now truly, the prophet there, anticipating all the choices of the souls within himself, only then casts the lots. Certainly, the matter itself which seems unstable and indefinite is always pre-apprehended in the higher and more perfect realms according to a single limit, both stably and in an orderly fashion.

### *Three opinions of Plato.*

From Plato’s words we gather three things here. First, that to be in a state of evil is to be judged altogether worse than not being at all. Second, that the separation of the soul from the body frees us from the evils that dwell in this perishable region, and from the hin-

<meta>catchword: ab impe-</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>425</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON</header>

-drances which here impede the attainment of a fitting end <note>original: *conuenientis finis*, the "appropriate goal" or "purpose" of a human life</note>. Third, that the very desires of souls have the greatest power over the forms of life, and that we are not such that we are shaped and moved by external things alone. For we bring forth choices from within ourselves, through which we live our lives.

### *Higher beings hold a certain judgment over things that are uncertain.*

You will receive from this an admirable opinion, namely: that those things which are more excellent <note>The "superior" or divine beings</note> uniformly anticipate inferior things everywhere; but truly, inferior things are never equal to the power of the superior. Likewise, the cognitions of superior beings firmly comprehend within themselves the actions of inferior ones. However, the cognitions of inferior beings can never comprehend the entire action of the superior. That which is superior receives nothing from the inferior into itself; just as the heavens do not receive any suffering or influence <note>original: *passionem*, in the sense of being "acted upon" by something lower</note> from the changes of the things below. Nor does the immovable cause introduce anything worldly <note>original: *mūdanum*, related to the physical world or *cosmos*</note> into itself from the motion of worldly things; nor do eternal things at all admit into themselves anything from things acting in time. Finally, this which is necessary, while it knows all things, [remains stable] even in the knowing of that which is contingent <note>The text says "undergoes change" (*mutationem sustinet*), but Proclus’s argument elsewhere suggests the divine knows the changing in an unchanging way; here he may be describing the paradox of how the necessary interacts with the accidental</note>.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the nature of the soul and its relation to divine reality. ->*A twofold argumentation through negation and affirmation: the former resolves, the latter composes, and both agree with the very nature of the soul.*<-

If Alcibiades is unable to assign a time in which he thought he did not know those things about which he now deliberates, certainly he neither knew them at some time, nor ever learned them from teachers. <note>Proclus is referencing Plato's dialogue *Alcibiades I*, where Socrates demonstrates that Alcibiades cannot define justice because he cannot point to a time when he actually learned it.</note> But if he neither sought nor received them from others, surely he neither learned nor discovered them. If he neither learned nor discovered them, deservedly he does not know them. If he does not know them, he is not a good judge in those matters where he cannot assign a time when he thought himself not to know. You see indeed how, if a dispute is conducted in this way, we proceed now by composition and then by resolution. We speak through affirmation by composition <note>original: *compositione*, often meaning "synthesis" or building up a complex idea from simple ones</note>, and through negation by resolution <note>original: *resolutione*, meaning "analysis" or breaking a complex idea down to its first principles</note>. This composition and resolution, of course, entirely suits the nature of the soul, which indeed falls from perfections to lower things through the composition of reasons <term>rationum: here referring to the *logoi*, or the rational principles that structure the soul</term> and the addition of certain foreign garments <note>A common Neoplatonic metaphor for the layers of materiality or "vehicles" the soul accumulates as it descends into the physical world</note>, until it is enclosed in this thick and solid bond <note>The physical body, often described in this tradition as a "prison" or "tomb" for the soul</note>. Conversely, however, it rises back to the heights through resolution and the expulsion of those things which disagree with its very nature, until, emerging naked—as the sacred utterances <note>Likely referring to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a primary source of spiritual wisdom for Neoplatonists</note> hand down—

<meta>catchword: forms</meta>

---

it is joined with forms <note>original: *speciebus*, referring to the Platonic Ideas or purely intellectual archetypes</note> entirely separated from matter. For this reason, argumentation proceeding through affirmatives descends from perfections to more imperfect things. But that proceeding through negatives, conversely, [ascends].

->*The Good itself, although it alone transcends intellectual essence, nevertheless stretches itself down to the lowest things.*<-

The Good itself, as if consisting in itself above intellectual nature—if it is right to say so—descends even to the last things, illuminating all and preserving them, adorning them, and meanwhile turning them back to itself. First, indeed, it is present to those things that truly exist <note>The eternal, unchanging realm of the Forms</note>; second, to divine souls; third, to the spirits <note>original: *numinibus*, referring to daemons or guardian deities who bridge the gap between gods and men</note> presiding over the human race; fourth, to our souls; and thereafter to animals and plants, and to all bodies; finally to formless matter itself, the lowest dregs of things. Truly the Good itself, secretly and ineffably before every order, offers its own gift to all; but these things participate in it everywhere, in one way and another, each according to its own order. And so far as each thing is naturally fit, it brings back good from that source. These indeed...

->*Mercury is the author of discovery and instruction for us.*<-

Mercury, as the messenger of Jove <note>The Roman name for Zeus; in Neoplatonism, Jove represents the Divine Intellect or Demiurge</note>, explains the paternal will to souls, and thus exhibits instruction to us; and again, as he is the author of inquiry, he provides discovery <term>inventio: the act of "finding" or uncovering knowledge already latent within the soul</term> to his followers. Now indeed, when instruction <term>disciplina: learning or knowledge received from an external source</term> comes from the higher powers into souls, it is more excellent than discovery; but when it comes from equals, such as from men rousing the cognitive power within us, it is inferior to discovery. Discovery, therefore, is the middle path, suited to the nature of the soul which is moved by itself. For through discovery, that very power living and operating by itself within us is most clearly declared. Instruction, however, relates to both sides: according to the better side, it fills the soul from its superior causes; but according to the lesser side, it rouses the vital power within us from those things which are outside us, by a certain condition of being moved from elsewhere. Moreover, that a certain knowledge of things is born in us even from the higher powers, the gods themselves often enough declare by their manifest presence and expositions, showing to souls the order of the universe, and running before them as if...

...guides on the very journey toward the divine, and hanging torches, as if they were lamps, to signal the path.

->*Because of the notions of things innate within us, we think we know everything.*<-

Our souls are weighed down by a twofold ignorance: thinking indeed that they know many things because of the notions of things ingrained in them from the beginning, but being ignorant because of forgetfulness. He, therefore, who is weighed down by this twofold ignorance, seeks nothing further, just as the wise man himself does not seek. And in this very respect, he is in some way similar to the wise man, just as matter is similar to God through a certain "dissimilar similarity," as someone rightly teaches. <note>This "dissimilar similarity" is a famous Neoplatonic paradox: God is "nothing" because He is above all being; matter is "nothing" because it is below all being.</note> For just as matter is formless, so is God; and both are utterly infinite and unknown. Although all these things apply to God according to the better sense <note>as the source of all</note>, they belong to matter according to the worse sense <note>as the absence of all</note>.

->*The soul through acquired knowledge becomes like the mind; through twofold ignorance, it becomes like matter.*<-

The soul, through knowledge itself, turns out to be like the intellect, grasping the knowable through its very action, just as the intellect grasps the intelligible. But through twofold ignorance, it becomes like matter. For just as matter seems to have all things, while it possesses nothing in

<column-break/>

<page-num>431</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT.</header>

reality; so too, the soul struggling with twofold ignorance seems to itself to have what it does not have. Accordingly, there is a twofold knowledge of souls. One is indeed indistinct, through a simple and naked understanding; the other, however, is articulated, possessing certain knowledge, and free from ambiguity. For we seem, as he <note>Proclus is likely referring to Plato's *Meno*</note> says, to know all things as if through a dream, and to be ignorant of the same things while awake—inasmuch as we possess the reasons <note>original: *rationes*, the inner rational principles that mirror the divine Forms</note> through our essence, and breathe out, as it were, the knowledge of them from here, but we do not sufficiently possess them according to action and production. Therefore, time does not precede the notion of the forms <note>original: *specierum*, referring to the Platonic Forms or Ideas</note> that is innate and constant within us through our essence; for we have had this from eternity. But time does precede the knowledge brought about through the production and distinction of these reasons. And so we are able to assign a time when we first received this knowledge. For I know what a circle itself is, having learned it at this time; or what the form of justice is at another; and similarly concerning other things, of which we also possess knowledge according to action. And so, regarding the thing itself, or the thing of which we remind ourselves, we do not sufficiently recall the time. But for the recollection <note>original: *reminiscentiæ*, the Platonic concept of *anamnesis* where learning is actually remembering eternal truths</note> itself, there is certainly some determined time.

<summary>Proclus explains the "twofold ignorance" of the soul, which feels it knows the truth through innate ideas but has forgotten how to articulate them. He compares the soul's state of potentiality to matter and its state of active knowledge to the divine Intellect.</summary>
<keywords>innate ideas, twofold ignorance, matter vs God, Platonic Forms, anamnesis, recollection, essence vs action, intellect</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the text from page 431, finishing the discussion on how the soul mimics the intellect or matter, and transitions into a description of the "Seven Ages of Man" as they relate to the planets. The catchword "compe" from the previous page's end completes the word "competentem" (fitting) on page 433.</meta>

<page-num>432</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON</header>

<margin>Seven ages of man, corresponding to the seven planets.</margin>
The order of our ages follows the order of the universe. The **first age** follows the power of the **Moon**; for in that time, we live according to our nutritive and vegetative faculties <note>the basic biological functions of growth and feeding</note>. The **second age** follows **Mercury**, when we apply ourselves to the study of letters, the music of the lyre, wrestling, and similar games. The **third age** follows **Venus**, when the body matures for reproduction and we are immediately spurred toward procreation. The **fourth age** follows the **Sun**, for then vigor reigns, the perfection of age hastens on, and we reach our middle years. The **fifth age** follows **Mars**, in which we strive for power and victories. The **sixth age** follows **Jupiter**, which desires prudence and a life of active civic service. The **seventh age** follows **Saturn**, in which it is natural to cease from procreation, to separate oneself from bodily concerns, and to transfer oneself to another, incorporeal life. 

Higher forms of knowledge always embrace the knowledge of lower things in a singular and more excellent way. For whatever the **senses** recognize in a material condition, the **imagination** perceives in a more immaterial way. Whatever **opinion** considers without knowing the reason, **science** comprehends through the cause. And so, in succession, more excellent things always contain within themselves, through their eminence, the entire absolute knowledge that is fitting to lower things.

<column-break/>

<page-num>433</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT.</header>
Therefore, nothing concerning us is hidden from the <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "daemonem"; a guiding spirit or personal divinity assigned to an individual</note> who is set over us: not the movements of the soul, nor our natural power, nor any change of fortune. Instead, he alone looks upon and governs all things. In this universe, all the ends of everything arranged within it lead toward the very end of the world itself. For as the world was meant to be perfect—just as <term>Timaeus</term> <note>a character in Plato’s dialogues who describes the creation of the universe</note> says—all animals, both divine and mortal, were brought into being. Similarly, in a well-ordered city, the goals of all individual parts serve the goal of civic expertise. Likewise, just as each thing involved in the process of "becoming" has its being according to a single specific form, and is therefore not infinite; yet the "intelligible" itself <note>the realm of pure thought and forms</note> is all things, since it contains the causes of all sensible things. Thus, any private craftsman is largely ignorant, being skilled in only one thing. But the civic leader is absolutely prudent, for he knows both his own goal and the goals of others, and directs all other arts toward the single life of the city.

...are participants. After these things, the life of humans, when rightly ordered, looks up to the harmony of morals and the elegance of actions derived from that source. The gift of those same higher beings also descends even to the brute animals and the plants. For these, too, are by nature participants in harmony. For the higher beings, through a worldly harmonic principle, contain and perfect all things, and they adapt them to each other and to the world.

Indeed, they join the body to the **intellect** through the mediation of the **soul**, according to a harmonic principle. They join the cycle of generation to the constant cycle of **identity** <note>original: "identitatis"; the Platonic concept of Sameness or the unchanging divine realm</note> through the medium of the cycle assigned to **alterity** <note>original: "alteritati"; the Platonic concept of Difference or the changing material realm</note>, if I may put it that way. Finally, they join the **earth** to **fire** through intermediary bonds.

Furthermore, they cultivate every soul with harmonic principles, and they couple every body everywhere with similar measures, and they perform every movement everywhere with musical measures. Therefore, the musical habit in us is indeed a gift of the **Muses**, although it is the final image of them. For the artistic and contemplative habits in us have presiding gods as their guides and derive their origin from them.

### *He who is ignorant of the final cause, is ignorant of every cause.*

Ignorance of the **final cause** <term>Final cause<gloss>The ultimate purpose or "end goal" for which something exists</gloss></term> regarding any matter whatever, ensures that the other causes 
<meta>catchword: pertaining</meta>

<page-num>435</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT.</header>

pertaining to it are likewise ignored: because the **end** <note>the goal or "telos"</note> is the first, chief, and most powerful of causes. For it is for the sake of this end that **efficient causes** <note>the agents that bring something into being</note> act, and for this that things being made are completed. For this reason, in the *Timaeus* <note>a dialogue by Plato concerning the creation of the world</note>, such a cause is considered by the wise to be the best to hold onto.

In the *Sophist*, Plato teaches that the depravity of the soul is twofold: one indeed is **ignorance** occurring in the rational part, but the other is the **discord** of the irrational part toward the rational. Such discord is the **disease** of the soul, while ignorance is its **deformity**. For since the reason holds the order of "form" within the soul as a whole, the depravity of reason is deservedly the soul's ugliness, just as the virtue of reason is the soul's beauty.

Indeed, ignorance arises because of the dominance of the **irrational power**, while knowledge arises because of the command of the **rational power**. However, the deformity of the soul happens when reason is overcome; specifically, when it produces its own actions as discordant, incongruous, ineffective, and unsuited to the end goal. In cultivating the soul, it is necessary to move the soul toward the contemplation of things once the impediments have been removed. For the knowledge of truth is innate within us; however, we are prevented from noticing it because of the passions arising from our earthly birth.

->*The end of war is justice; the end of peace is friendship, which is more desirable than justice.*<-

Indeed, the end of war is justice. But the end of peace is a certain other more excellent good, namely friendship and union. For the end of all virtue is—as the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who emphasized mathematical harmony and communal living</note> hand down and **Aristotle** confirms—that once all have been made friends, we no longer require justice; specifically, when "mine and not mine" <note>original: "meum & non meũ"; referring to the concept of private property or individual ego</note> have been abolished. Yet, even if all were just, humans would still require friendship to bring them together. 

That injustice is the beginning of wars is declared by war itself, which material forms wage among themselves. For heat fights against cold, not when they are separated in space, but when one strives to occupy the place of the other. Since it lacks its own place, it rightly resists the one coming from the outside and attempting to drive it from its seat. Therefore, the rational principles <term>Rational principles<gloss>Translated from "rationes insitæ"; these are the internal blueprints or laws of nature that govern how things grow and interact</gloss></term> inherent in nature run together without discord. For each [con]...

---

<page-num>437</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT.</header>
<sig>Dd</sig>

...sists in itself. But material forms, since they cannot remain apart from matter, rightly struggle among themselves over a shared lodging; for matter cannot receive both contrary forms into itself without confusion.

->*How the soul is variously clothed in its descent, and is purified again, and returns in its turn.*<-

The descent of the soul into the body has indeed separated it from divine souls, from which it was filled with intelligence, power, and purity. It has, however, joined the soul to generation and nature, and to material things, by which it has been imbued with forgetfulness, error, and ignorance. For as the soul descends, multiform types of life and various "garments" <term>Garments<gloss>In Neoplatonic thought, these are the 'layers' or lower faculties the soul acquires as it moves from the divine realm into the physical world</gloss></term> from the world are attached to it, pulling it into a decaying composition and standing in the way of the contemplation of separate <note>meaning: divine things that exist apart from matter</note> things. 

Therefore, the soul must be led from here toward that ever-watchful and upright nature. It must cut away the secondary and tertiary powers that arose during its descent—just as the sea-god **Glaucus** <note>A mythological fisherman who became a sea-god; Plato used him as an image of the soul, obscured by the "weeds and shells" of worldly existence</note> is covered in seaweed, rocks, and shells. It must restrain the impulses that carry it outward. It must remember again the separate things and the divine essence from which its descent began, and toward which it is proper for all life to strive.

->*The soul is self-moving by its own nature, while the body is moved from without;*<-
->*but because of their mutual intercourse, each*<-
->*takes on the condition of the other.*<-

**The soul** by its essence is <term>self-moving<gloss>Translated from "mobilis ex se ipsa"; in Platonic thought, this is the defining quality of a soul—it is the source of its own motion and life, unlike a rock or a tool which must be moved by something else.</gloss></term>, yet when joined to a body it somehow becomes "moved from without" as well. For just as the soul, by its very presence, gives the body a final trace of self-movement, so the soul itself, due to its physical companionship, has taken on the mark of a dependent condition, being moved by external forces. Therefore, by its self-moving power, the soul is fertile and inclined toward discovery; it gives birth to reasons and sciences. But because of its condition of being moved from without, it frequently requires being stirred or awakened by others. Indeed, more perfect souls are readier to make discoveries, while less perfect souls require more external assistance. For the former are more truly self-moving and participate less in a lower nature, while the latter move themselves less, suffering a stronger physical influence. Nevertheless, these lower souls also, when they make progress—namely by rising up from the body and gathering themselves together out of <insert>the influence of</insert> matter—suddenly become more fertile in discovery regarding those subjects where they were previously sterile and uncertain due to the clumsy sluggishness of a life contingent upon

<column-break/>

<page-num>439</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON</header>
<sig>Dd 2</sig>

matter, and the filthy numbness contracted from the process of <term>generation<gloss>Translated from "generatio"; this refers to the process of being born into a physical, changing body, which was often viewed by Neoplatonists as a "forgetting" or a numbing of the soul's true nature.</gloss></term>. We, therefore, maintaining a <note>original: "mediocritatem"; referring to the philosophical "middle way" or moderate path between two extremes.</note> moderate path, assign the causes of the rational nature and its condition as they pertain chiefly to its habits of imperfection and perfection; and we judge such paths to lead toward their perfections. However, those who assign reasons for these things without maintaining this moderation—either rising too high toward the divine or sinking too low toward the base—wander far from the truth of the soul. For we do not approve of those who teach that the soul, having fallen into a "moist" body <note>A reference to the ancient theory that the soul is "dampened" or weighed down by the physical humors of the body upon birth.</note> and being hindered by that obstacle, is mindless at the start, and that as the moisture gradually evaporates due to innate heat and becomes more tempered, the soul's power of wisdom grows strong. For this mode of perfection must be judged physical and material; it assumes that the soul's perfection arises from the balanced mixing of the body's elements. On the contrary, the soul possesses its own substance before the elements and before all generation; it is a certain kind of life that is mixed neither with the body nor with nature. Nor, on the other hand, do we admit those who think the soul is a certain part of the divine essence, and that this part is exactly like the whole and always perfect.

<summary>Proclus argues that the soul is naturally self-moving but becomes sluggish when joined to a body. He rejects the materialist view that intelligence is merely a byproduct of body chemistry, as well as the radical view that the human soul remains perfectly divine even while on earth.</summary>

I believe this position requires some explanation. For time is twofold: one kind is born together with natural life and the corporeal movement of the universe <note>This refers to "physical time"—the measurement of motion in the material world.</note>; the other, however, proceeds through an incorporeal life. For before knowledge that is not yet fully realized, there is no time; but before knowledge perfected in action, time existed.

->*The many steps through which we ascend from the multitude to the One through contemplation*<-

Plato and Pythagoras command us to flee from the "multitude" <note>The "multitude" refers to the chaotic variety of the material world and the many distractions of the mind.</note>, so that we may attain the simplest truth. We must flee the multitude of the "external people"—those crowds who distract and deceive us in many ways. Even more so, we must flee the multitude of the "interior people," for these distract and deceive us much more. First, therefore, flee the varied multitude of the <term>passions<gloss>The "affectuum"—the emotional disturbances and desires that cloud judgment.</gloss></term>; second, the multitude of the senses; third, the multitude of the imaginations; fourth, the multitude of the opinions depending upon them. For every multitude I have mentioned is so diverse within itself that some parts are contrary to others in every respect. For this reason, it is better to betake oneself to the <term>sciences<gloss>The "scientias"—here meaning the higher branches of knowledge like mathematics and philosophy, which deal with unchanging truths.</gloss></term>, in which the multitude no longer contains any contrariety. For even if passions are contrary to passions, senses to senses, and imaginations to imaginations...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's exploration of how the soul moves from a state of fragmented, external knowledge toward its internal, divine core. It transitions from the idea of innate knowledge mentioned on the previous page to the hierarchical stages of the soul's ascent: from discursive science to intuitive intellect, and finally to the "One."</meta>

<page-num>444</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON</header>
<meta>catchword: teeth</meta>

Opinions may conflict with other opinions, yet no true science is ever found to be contrary to another science. <note>Proclus distinguishes between "opinion" (subjective and often conflicting) and "science" or "knowledge" (*scientia*), which represents a higher, unified grasp of truth.</note> Therefore, in this multitude of propositions and notions, let us gather them into a single whole, and let us also connect the number of sciences with a certain single bond. For so far are they from being contrary to one another, that even one notion serves another; all lower sciences minister to the superior one and have their beginnings from them. It is necessary here, moreover, to proceed from the many sciences that presuppose one <note>This "one" science is Dialectic, which in the Platonic tradition is the master science of first principles.</note> to that very one itself, which presupposes nothing further, and to duly refer all things to this primary science. 

But after the study of science and its pursuits, it is now beneficial to set aside compositions, divisions, and the many-formed paths of discourse, and from there to ascend to the life of the intellect—to its simple intuitions and perceptions. For science is not the highest peak of our cognitions; rather, above it is the Intellect. <note>In Neoplatonism, "Science" involves step-by-step reasoning (*discourse*), while "Intellect" is a flash of total, immediate understanding.</note> I speak here not only of the Intellect as it is separated from the soul, but also of that very illumination infused into the soul from above, regarding which Aristotle says: "It is the Intellect by which we recognize the limits." <note>original: "Intellectum esse, quo terminos cognoscimus"; a reference to Aristotle's *Posterior Analytics*, where he argues that we grasp first principles (limits) not by logic, but by a direct intellectual intuition.</note> And Timaeus says that this very thing never occurs in any other place except in the soul. Toward this Intellect, therefore, as we as-

<column-break/>

<page-num>445</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.</header>
<sig>Dd 5</sig>

cend, let us contemplate the intelligible essence together with it—specifically through individual and simple perceptions, observing the undivided and simple kinds of being. 

But indeed, after the venerable Intellect, it is finally permitted to awaken the very highest existence of the soul (if I may call it so), through which we are "one," and under which our internal multitude is unified. For just as through our intellect we touch the divine intellect, so also it is possible to reach the "first One"—from whom union resides in all things—by means of our own "one." This is, as it were, the "flower of our essence," <note>original: "essentię nostrę florem"; this refers to the *anthos tes ousias*, a famous Neoplatonic concept of a hidden, divine spark at the soul's center that is even deeper than the intellect.</note> through which we are most closely joined to the divine. For everywhere, "like" can be grasped by "like": things that can be known are grasped by science; things that can be understood are grasped by the intellect; and the most unified measures of being are grasped by the unity of the soul. 

Now, this unity, and the action performed through it, is the summit of our actions. Through this, we are made divine—namely, when fleeing from all multitude, we take refuge in our own unity, and we become "one," acting in a unified way. Thus far, we have advised that multitude must be fled, proceeding in order through the grades of knowledge. Next, we shall proceed similarly through the grades of the things to be known, to prove the same point...

<page-num>446</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS. ON</header>

Let us depart. Flee all sensible things <note>Sensible things (*sensibilia*) are objects perceived by the five senses, which Neoplatonists considered less "real" than mental concepts.</note>, for they are crowded together and divisible, and entirely subject to change; therefore, they cannot be grasped by pure knowledge. From these things, therefore, transfer yourself to incorporeal essence. For every sensible thing has an adventitious <note>original: "aduentitiam" — meaning external or added from the outside, rather than inherent.</note> unity, and is by its very nature dispersed and full of infinity. For this reason, its "good" is also divisible and external, both distant and departing from itself, and residing in a seat that is not its own.

But when you have truly ascended there and have been placed among the incorporeal, you will behold that psychic <note>original: "animalem" — in this philosophical context, it refers to the realm of the Soul (*anima*), not "animals" in the modern sense.</note> order which is above bodies. It is moved by its own power, acting through itself, and possessing its own substance in and from itself. Yet, it is still multiplied, and it anticipates within itself a certain appearance of essence that is to be divided among physical bodies. There, surely, you will see many conditions of reasons, various proportions, and many bonds. Likewise, you will see certain wholes, and parts, and psychic circles, and a multiform variety of powers.

Furthermore, you will see the perfection of souls, which is not eternal, nor consisting as a whole all at once, but is unrolled in time and turning within its own discourses <note>The soul’s knowledge is "discursive," meaning it moves step-by-step through an argument, unlike the Intellect which sees everything at once.</note>. For such is the nature of the soul. But after the multitude belonging to souls, bring yourself to the intellect, and the intellectual

<meta>Catchword: intellectual</meta>

---

<page-num>447</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.</header>

kingdoms, so that you may possess the unity of things. There indeed, be a contemplator of that nature. Behold a nature remaining in eternity, a vigorous life, and a wakeful intelligence, which lacks nothing of life and which does not require the cycles of time for its perfection. 

When you have inspected these things, and seen by how great a distance they are better than souls, seek next whether there is any "multitude" there; and since the intellect is one, ask whether it is also universal. Likewise, since it is uniform, ask if it is additionally multiform. You will find indeed that it is so. When, therefore, you have perceived the intellectual multitude there—although it is thoroughly indivisible and united—lead yourself across again to another principle. Consider the super-intellectual essences, their unities, and finally the Unity that is absolute and set apart from all things. 

Having traveled thus far, you will have left behind all multitude and reached the very source of the Good itself. Since it is clear through these steps that the perfection of the soul is attained by this specific act—that we flee all multitude, whether external, internal, or even that of the universe itself—we can also conclude from here that our souls do not merely gather their knowledge from sensible things,

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s Neoplatonic argument that true knowledge is found by looking inward toward the soul’s essence rather than outward toward the fragmented, changing material world.</meta>

<page-num>448</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON</header>

nor should one seek to find the "whole" and the "one" from particular and divided things, but rather to bring forth knowledge <note>original: "disciplinam" — referring here to systematic learning or the soul’s inherent wisdom.</note> from the innermost depths, and to correct that which is imperfect in apparent things. For it is not fitting to believe that those things which truly *are not* <note>In Platonic thought, material things "are not" truly real because they are constantly changing, unlike eternal truths.</note> are the primary causes of the knowledge existing within the soul. Nor can those things which differ among themselves, and which require the soul’s own reasons and arguments—being themselves ambiguous—precede a science that remains entirely the same. Nor indeed can those things which are variously changed generate reasons that consist in unity; nor can indeterminate things be the causes of a determined intelligence.

Therefore, it is not fitting to receive the truth of eternal things from the many, nor the judgment and discernment of universals from sensible things <note>Sensible things (*sensibilia*) are objects perceived by the five senses.</note>, nor the judgment and opinion of good things from things lacking reason. Instead, it is necessary for the soul, entering into itself, to investigate there the true good and the true reasons of all things. For the essence of the soul itself is full of these, but they lie hidden due to the **oblivion of birth** <note>original: "obliuione geneſica" — the Neoplatonic idea that the soul forgets its divine origins and inherent knowledge when it is "born" into a physical body.</note>. Thus the soul seeks the truth while looking at external things, even though it possesses that truth within its own essence; and it explores the "good" outside, having deserted itself. From this point, therefore, everyone ought to begin the knowledge of themselves. For if we [turn toward] the multitude of men...

<page-num>449</page-num>

...if we distract our gaze into the multitude of men, we will never discern their one form <note>original: "speciem" — in the sense of the Platonic Idea or the "universal" human nature.</note>, obscured as it is by the multitude, division, and discord, and by the multiple changes of those who participate in that form. But if we turn our sharp gaze into ourselves, here surely we shall behold both one reason and one nature of men, removed from all disturbance. 

Rightly, therefore, does **Socrates** separate the soul from the sight of the multitude in order to learn what a human being truly is, and he refutes the opinions that act as impediments to this contemplation. For the multitude is a hindrance to us in the conversion of the soul toward itself and toward the knowledge of the one form. For here, variety overshadows the one, "otherness" obscures identity, and dissimilarity clouds similarity. For around matter, the forms are confused, and better things are mixed with the worse.

# PROCLUS ON THE SOUL AND THE DEMON.

...to be multiplied. Nevertheless, we admit that the vast majority of men are ignorant and wicked, while those of the opposite sort are very few indeed. For it is not natural for souls to lead a life alongside bodies and to dwell within the realm of **generation** <note>original: "generatione" — in Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the material world of birth, change, and decay, as opposed to the eternal realm of Being.</note>; on the contrary, a separate, immaterial, and incorporeal life is much more suited to souls. Therefore, when they dwell in the realm of generation, they are like people living in a pestilential region. But when they live outside generation, as **Plato** says, they are like those who dwell in the meadows <note>A reference to the "Meadow of Judgment" or the "Plain of Truth" mentioned in Plato's *Phaedrus* and the Myth of Er.</note>. Just as one should not wonder that among those living in diseased places, the vast majority are sickly and only a very few maintain their natural health; so also you should not wonder that many souls placed in the realm of generation are subject to passions and are wicked. On the contrary, it would be astounding if souls involved in such bodies, bound by these knots, and surrounded by such great change, were ever found to be sober, pure, and undisturbed. Is it not astounding that a soul lives immaterially among material things, and preserves itself untainted somewhere among perishable things? And that, having drunk from such cups, it is not lulled to sleep by these **drugs**? <note>original: "pharmacies" — here meaning potions or enchantments that cloud the mind.</note>

<column-break/>

For in truth, oblivion, error, and ignorance are like a drugged drink, turning souls away toward the **place of dissimilarity** <note>original: "locum dissimilitudinis" — a famous Platonic concept describing the state of the soul when it is far from the divine Likeness and lost in the chaos of the material world.</note>. Why then do you wonder that many are like wolves in their manner of life, many like pigs, and most are surrounded by some other species of brute? For this earthly place is the lodging of **Circe** herself <note>In the Odyssey, the sorceress Circe turned men into beasts; Proclus uses this as an allegory for how worldly desires strip away human reason.</note>, and many souls, because of immoderate desire, have been baited by her poisonous cups. Rather, wonder at this: if any among mortals are ever found who have not been charmed by such potions, nor even ensnared; if any, relying on the gift of **Mercury** <note>The god Mercury (Hermes) gave Odysseus the herb "moly" to resist Circe's magic. Here, it represents the gift of Reason or Philosophy.</note>, devote themselves to reason and knowledge. For just as you should not wonder if you look upon tormented souls in **Tartarus** <note>The deepest abyss of the underworld.</note>—for that is the place for such things—so also you should not wonder if many souls living in the realm of generation are disturbed, ignorant, and mad; for the realm of generation requires such souls. Just as in heaven all are good, and in Tartarus all are wicked, so in the realm of generation, many are depraved, while fewer are upright. For the realm of generation does not incline toward the better and more divine of the extremes, but toward the worse.

# PROCLUS ON

<page-num>452</page-num>

->*The wicked man agrees neither with others, nor with himself.*<-

The wicked man cannot agree with himself. For it is necessary, both because of his rational nature, to see the truth in some way, and because of his disturbed **imagination** <note>original: "imaginationem perturbatam" — in Neoplatonism, the faculty that processes sensory images; when clouded by passions, it leads to delusion.</note>, to be largely ignorant and at odds with himself. This is revealed by repentance, which arrives once the disturbances of the mind have subsided. Therefore, the intemperate man, because of an intellect kindred to divinity, sometimes thinks and speaks of divine things; but because of his lust and disturbed imagination, he departs far from divine **temperance**. And since he is always at war with himself, it is no wonder that he cannot agree with others.

->*Whoever knows something, agrees entirely regarding it.*<-

It is necessary for those who know something to be in concord about it. The first cause of this concord is the determinate nature of things themselves; the second is that the faculties of judgment for knowledge are the same in everyone; the third is that in **first principles** <note>original: "primis principijs" — the fundamental, self-evident truths from which all other knowledge is derived.</note>, the intellect is united to itself. Therefore, whatever is capable of understanding is also a participant in unity. Knowledge is a kind of illumination depending on the intellect; concord, however, is an illumination resulting from

<column-break/>

# THE SOUL AND THE DEMON.

<page-num>453</page-num>

resulting from unity; for it is the union of differing things. It is necessary, therefore, for those who share in the same knowledge to agree with one another.

->*Each of us is a soul, and it possesses within itself all divine and natural forms.*<-

Plato’s entire purpose in this book is to recall us to the knowledge of ourselves, and to demonstrate that our **essence** <note>original: "essentiam" — the fundamental nature or "what-ness" of the soul.</note> consists in **forms** and **principles** <note>original: "speciebus rationibusque" — the eternal blueprints (Species/Forms) and the rational structures (Rationes) of reality.</note>, and that the soul produces all sciences from itself, and recognizes within itself all divine and natural forms. A perfect knowledge of ourselves would be to distinguish our powers from our essence, and our actions from our powers. However, we obtain a more common knowledge of ourselves by knowing our powers from our actions, and our essence from our powers. These three indeed flow together in the soul. For its essence is in act, and its action exists essentially. This action becomes intellectual according to the act, and the act becomes kindred to the essence, according to its own perfection.

->*The soul leads itself by free motion, provides good to itself, purifies itself, and educates itself, even when it seems to be educated from elsewhere.*<-

Animals, indeed, being captured by reason, are driven...

...are governed by external forces and cared for from elsewhere, namely under that condition by which the mover itself moves them; they are, of course, deprived of that faculty by which a thing is able to lead and preserve itself. But the **rational soul** <note>original: "Rationalis autem anima"</note>, because of its property of being self-moving and self-operating, is able by its own nature to act upon itself, to move itself, and to provide the good for itself. Now, indeed, our purification does not happen to us from external things, but takes its origin from the innermost parts of the soul. For every evil happens from external things and is foreign to the soul, but good comes from the depths within. For the soul is naturally **good-formed** <note>original: "boniformis" — a Neoplatonic term suggesting the soul's natural alignment with "The Good" or the divine source.</note>; and the more perfect it is, the more it claims for itself a life that is self-moving, whereas it becomes moved by other things only because of its commerce and involvement with the body. 

For this reason, whatever it receives from external things remains placed outside itself, like sensory objects and things perceived through the **imagination** <note>original: "imaginatiõe" — the faculty that translates sensory data into mental images.</note>. Only those things are truly in the soul which are made by the soul within itself and are produced by it. Therefore, the soul is purified by itself, since reason, beginning from itself, ends in itself. By this reasoning, we rightly understand what Socrates says—specifically during a debate—that the one who "speaks" is properly the one who responds. For if this person is refuted, and being refuted is thus purified,

<column-break/>

# THE SOUL AND THE DEMON.

<page-num>455</page-num>

certainly while he is being purified, he purifies himself and frees himself from ignorance, applying the refutation to himself; this is indeed consistent with the nature of the self-moving soul. This saying certainly confirms that **learning is recollection** <note>original: "disciplinas esse reminiscentias" — referring to the Platonic doctrine of Anamnesis, where learning is actually the soul remembering truths it knew before birth.</note>. For the fact that those who respond say everything from within themselves is the greatest sign of recollection; namely, that souls bring forth reasons and discourses from themselves and need only someone to awaken them. 

The soul is not like **blank tablets** <note>original: "tabellas uacuas" — a reference to the "tabula rasa" or clean slate; Proclus argues against the idea that the mind starts empty.</note> without letters, which receive their shapes from the outside. For they are always inscribed, and the writer himself is within. Yet not everyone can read what is inscribed, or even know that things are written there; for due to a "beneficent" **oblivion** <note>original: "obliuionem" — likely referring to Lethe, the river of forgetfulness, which Proclus ironically calls beneficent perhaps because it allows for the process of earthly trial and discovery.</note>, their eye is surrounded by filth, and because of this very forgetfulness, they fall into the passions. The only task, therefore, is to take away the obstruction that has been placed there. Knowledge injected from the outside is not necessary; for souls have within themselves the **gates of truth** <note>original: "ianuas ueritatis"</note>, though they are closed off by earthly and material forms. If, therefore, someone demonstrates things most diligently, the souls—prompted from elsewhere but bringing forth learned responses from within themselves—declare by this very act that the Platonic saying is true: that the soul knows all things, and needs only someone to [awaken them].

# PROCLUS ON

<page-num>460</page-num>

...powers, when they bestow themselves, they diminish. However, Knowledge <note>original: "Scientia"</note>, remaining one and the same, undiminished and self-sufficient, offers itself equally to one and to many. And the soul, therefore, is similarly present to the whole body and all its members, although different members participate in it in different ways.

->*Someone can be prophetic without knowledge; but a prophet knows certainly what he pronounces.*<-

Where Plato says, "you are a diviner" <note>original: "vaticinator" — one who predicts the future through ritual or instinct</note>, he signifies that the person presages what he predicts through opinion, not through knowledge. For diviners are not endowed with knowledge, but are carried along by opinion. But those who are not only diviners but also true prophets <note>original: "vates" — an inspired seer</note> already possess knowledge, and they hold a knowledge superior to the human kind. He also suggests that the impulses and movements of more noble souls are in some way stirred by higher beings <note>original: "superis" — the celestial gods or higher spiritual entities</note>, because they act even beyond opinion, and often even if they work without formal knowledge.

->*The Good, the beautiful, the just, that which is intelligible beyond the intellect, the intellectual, essence, life, and intellect.*<-

Among the principles of things, the **Good** itself stands above **beauty**, and beauty stands above **justice**. For the Good exists above the intelligible realm <note>The 'intelligible' refers to things that can only be understood by the mind, rather than the senses.</note>, situated in an inaccessible place. Beauty

beauty, however, remains hidden indeed among the first intelligibles, but appears more explicitly at the very end of that order. Finally, justice remains united in the first order of intellectual beings, but consequently shines forth at the conclusion of the intellectual procession of the gods. Again, the Good itself reigns among the gods, beauty among the minds, and justice reigns among souls: for which reason, that which is just is indeed beautiful, yet not everything beautiful is also just, but the cause of beautiful things itself precedes justice. Likewise, every beautiful thing is good, but the fountain of all good things precedes every beautiful thing. 

Again, the just is indeed good, joined to the Good through the mediation of beauty: but the Good is higher than both. Thus you will find this to be true even when considering the extremes of things. For the material cause <note>The basic 'stuff' of the physical world.</note>, although it is some kind of good, is nevertheless shameful and deformed. It participates in the One, yet it is devoid of form <note>original: "speciei" — referring to the Platonic 'Idea' or 'Form' that gives shape to matter.</note>. That which is sensible <note>Meaning things perceived by the senses.</note> possesses traces of beauty, but none of justice. Hence in the *Phaedrus*, Socrates says that among fleeting images there is no splendor of justice or temperance; but beauty alone has this privilege, so that it might appear most clearly everywhere.

...and would be most desirable. Where, therefore, there is justice, there also is beauty; where beauty exists, there also is the good—whether you wish to look at the first principles themselves or at the reflections of those principles stretched out to the furthest extremes. Indeed, all things participate in the **Good** itself, for it is the principle of all things. But only those things that possess some form <note>original: "speciem" — in Platonic philosophy, this refers to the 'Form' or 'Idea' that gives a thing its specific nature</note> participate in the **Beautiful**. Finally, souls alone participate in **Justice**. Now, in the center of all things—which is the nature of the soul—all these are interconnected: the good, the just, and the beautiful. The soul's "good" is also its beauty and its justice; likewise, its justice is simultaneously beauty and good. Similarly, the beautiful is both good and just. This statement is true not only for this specific trinity but for many other things as well. Just as among the first principles, **Being** <note>original: "ens"</note> precedes **Life**, and Life precedes **Intellect** <note>original: "mentem"</note>; and similarly in their effects, where not everything that possesses being also possesses life, nor is every living thing immediately endowed with intellect; but in turn, all things that possess intelligence also live and exist, just as all living things exist by the very fact of their living. While such a distinction exists in the furthest reaches of reality through this kind of trinity, these elements flow together in the soul, where being, life, and intellect all exist. Indeed, its life and intellect are

<column-break/>

<page-num>463</page-num>

<header>THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.</header>

also its essence; and similarly, its intellect and essence are its life. For there is one simplicity in the soul, one single substance <note>original: "substantia"</note>. Neither its being, nor its living, nor its understanding is something added from the outside <note>original: "aduentitiū" — something external or incidental rather than innate to the soul's nature</note>; rather, its intellect is essential and living, its life is intellectual through its very essence, and finally, its essence is both intellectual and living. Therefore, all things are everywhere, and from all things comes a single unity in a similar fashion; its "good" prevails through beauty and justice, its "beautiful" is both good and just, and again its "just" is filled with the good and the beautiful. The subject is certainly one, but the rational definitions <note>original: "rationes" — the logical principles or descriptions used to distinguish concepts</note> are diverse. Here, we do not consider these three to be identical in their definitions, nor do we think they are different in their underlying subject; rather, we preserve their differing definitions while maintaining their single subject. For this reason, these qualities always coincide through the actions of the soul. Just as the definitions of the virtues are different, yet one person possesses them all—nor can it happen that you participate in justice while lacking temperance, or that you have these two while lacking the others—so too is this trinity connected to itself. Every good thing is simultaneously a participant in the beautiful and the just, and the same applies to the rest. Therefore

# PROCLUS ON THE SOUL

<page-num>464</page-num>

<header>464 PROCLUS ON THE SOUL</header>

Socrates linked the just and the good through beauty. For beauty is their fitting middle ground and bond. Timaeus <note>A reference to the character in Plato's *Timaeus*</note>, however, says that the most beautiful knot is that which makes both itself and the things it binds together into a single unity as much as possible. Remember, indeed, that only evil is contrary to the good itself, while the good is contrary to nothing; from this it appears that through harmony, things are mutually good. To evil, however, both evil and good are equally opposed.

### *He proves that every just thing is, by its very nature, both beautiful and good.*

We shall confirm that everything just is beautiful through the following reasons. Since the soul is a certain multiplicity, and within it there is a first part, a middle part, and a last part <note>These correspond to the Platonic divisions of the soul: Reason (first), Spirit (middle), and Appetite (last)</note>, tell me: when do we say justice is created within it? Is it when the middle or the last part attempts to dominate those above them, or rather when the first commands the middle, and the middle commands the last? But if it were the case that the worse prevail over the better, those higher parts would no longer be "worse" by nature; for that which is fit to be titled "better" is more honorable by its very nature. If, therefore, it is impossible for the same thing to be naturally better and worse at the same time, it is necessary for justice

<meta>catchword: then</meta>

---

<page-num>465</page-num>

<header>THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON. 465</header>

then to be found in the soul when that which is best within it holds command over the whole of life. The middle part, being subject to the better, prevails over the last. For then each part of the soul has what is appropriate to it: the first ruling, the second supporting <note>original: "stipans" — attending to or escorting</note>, and finally the last serving the better. Thus, the "just" itself is by nature a distributor of what is fitting for each part of the soul; it is the cause of each part preserving its own duty and of its proper dignity being assigned, and is thus the preservation of the whole order. Now, an order and moderation of this kind, being fitting to nature, is naturally beautiful. Therefore, justice is the cause of beauty, and is itself beautiful.

There are, however, two types of justice: one found in contracts, which preserves **arithmetic equality** <term>arithmetica æqualitas: a simple one-to-one balance where everyone receives the same amount regardless of status</term>; the other is concerned with distribution, consisting of **geometric equality** <term>geometrica æqualitate: a proportional balance where rewards are given based on merit or worth</term>. Thus, it preserves arithmetic equality so that we do not defraud a partner in contracts by receiving more than we ourselves gave. Then indeed, in the other form, it distributes unequal things to unequal people, preserving a geometric proportion according to the dignity of each, so that just as the persons differ from one another, so also the things distributed to the persons differ. And so every justice

...justice, as we have said, is equal, and every equal thing is beautiful, for the unequal is disordered and ugly; therefore, every just thing is beautiful. Furthermore, beauty exists in bodies when form overcomes matter. For matter itself is formless and ugly; and when form is overcome by matter, then the form is filled with a certain lack of form and ugliness, and it turns out to be something formless, having been made similar to the underlying nature <note>original: "subiectæ naturæ"—referring to prime matter which lacks any inherent qualities</note>. If, therefore, that which is intellectual within our soul plays the role of form, while the irrational part plays the role of matter—for intellect and reason are counted in the order of the "Limit" <note>The Pythagorean/Platonic concept of *Peras*, or the principle of order and boundary</note>, while the irrational is placed in the genus of the "Unlimited" <note>The principle of *Apeiron*, or chaotic potentiality</note>: for by nature it is indeterminate and lacks measure—it is necessary for beauty to shine forth in the soul as well when reason truly reigns. Those modes of life that lack reason are thus subjected to reason. But justice itself gives the command to reason and assigns servitude to the irrational part. For it attributes to each what is fitting to it: to the ruling part, it designates leadership; to the inferior part, it designates obedience. Since in the craftsmanship of the world, the irrational is subject to us, and the irrational is subjected to the reason inherent in us, 

<meta>catchword: as its vehicle</meta>

as its vehicle <note>original: "uehiculum"—referring to the *ochema*, the "astral body" or subtle vehicle the soul inhabits to interact with the material world</note>. Likewise, the just is something perfect and defined, while the unjust is judged to be imperfect and indefinite; and it wanders into the infinite, never halting its step, overstepping the boundary of justice. Therefore, justice itself imposes measure and limit wherever it is present, and thus makes all things perfect. Since it is such, it deservedly makes the soul beautiful. For beauty naturally follows that which is perfect and measured, just as ugliness accompanies the unmeasured and indeterminate. Therefore, the just is beautiful by nature. Finally, the Craftsman of the world <note>The Demiurge, or divine creator in Platonic thought</note> adorned this whole universe through justice. ...lovable by its own nature, since even the lowest form of beauty, bearing the image of divine beauty, is lovable and moves souls toward it at first sight. This is confirmed in the *Phaedrus* <note>Plato’s dialogue exploring love, beauty, and the immortality of the soul</note>. For in truth, **the beautiful** <note>original: "καλὸν" (*kalon*)</note> is so named either from the word **to call** <note>original: "καλεῖν" (*kalein*)</note>, because it summons souls toward itself, or from the word **to charm** <note>original: "κηλεῖν" (*kelein*)</note>, because it delights those who look upon it; certainly, it is lovable according to its nature. Therefore, love is said to lead the lover toward the beautiful. Whatever is lovable is also desirable; for love is a certain robust and vehement desire for something. And whatever loves, desires something that it also lacks. Moreover, every desirable thing is also a good, whether it be a true good or an appearing one. For many things that are not good appear to us as things to be sought, because they present themselves to those who desire them as if they were good. Now, it was demonstrated by Socrates in the *Meno* <note>The Latin text reads "Memnone," a common early modern variant for the dialogue *Meno*</note> that it is clearly impossible for those who know the nature of evil to desire it. In every term, this must be applied: namely, whether it is

appearing, or truly so. For if it is beautiful and appearing, it is surely both lovable and desirable, and a good that is a companion to such beauty. But if it is beautiful by nature, it is also lovable, and likewise a good. Yet what could be the object of desire? Could it be evil? But it is impossible, once its nature is known, for it to be sought by anyone. For all things desire the good, but no desire is directed toward evil. Nor is desire directed toward anything that is neither good nor evil. For what is of that sort is done for the sake of another, and no end <term>end: *finis*, the ultimate purpose or goal of an action</term> exists; every object of desire, however, is an end. And if any of those things that are evil is desired, it is longed for as a good because it appears to be good. And if something not beautiful is loved, it is loved as beautiful because it appears to be so. If, therefore, everything beautiful is lovable, and everything lovable is desirable, and everything desirable is good: consequently, everything beautiful is good. And vice versa, every good is desirable, and the desirable is lovable, since to love is to desire vehemently. Hence, in the *Symposium*, Socrates says that the good is lovable just as the beautiful is. If, I say, every good is desirable, and the desirable in turn is lovable, and the lovable is beautiful: it follows that the good is also...

...all becomes beautiful. Let no one now object to us that the Good itself is superior to Beauty, nor that there is a dual nature to that which is called "lovable." For we are not presently disputing the first principles of things <note>The "First Principles" usually refer to the Neoplatonic "One" or the "Good" which sits at the very top of reality</note>, but rather those beautiful and good things that exist within us. 

Therefore, that which is good in us is simultaneously desirable and to be loved. We acquire and possess it through love—and by love I mean an earnest and inclined pursuit. If anyone reflects upon themselves, they will clearly perceive that this kind of internal good brings us more piercing loves than the beauty manifest to the senses. Thus, what is good is also beautiful. 

This is why Diotima <note>The wise woman of Mantinea in Plato's *Symposium* who taught Socrates the "Ladder of Love"</note> instructs lovers that after encountering beauty in the senses, they should transfer themselves to the beauty inherent in actions, duties, and sciences, and there vigorously exercise the "eye of the soul" <note>The *oculus animae*, a common Neoplatonic metaphor for the intellect's ability to "see" spiritual truths</note>. Next, they should proceed toward the intellect, where the primary and divine beauty reigns, so that the truly beautiful itself may flourish in the soul's power within us. For what in us is more beautiful than virtue and knowledge? What, on the other hand, is uglier than vice and ignorance?

## ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

->*Man is a soul using the body as an instrument. Therefore, the evils of the body do not belong to the soul or to the man, just as the defects of tools do not belong to the craftsman or his art.*<-

Many mistakenly believe that wounds and death are evils. For which of these is truly an evil to us? Certainly, such a thing does not pass into the soul, which is who we truly are. The passions <note>Here used in the classical sense of *passio*, meaning "things acted upon it" or "suffered by it"</note> of the instruments do not change the virtues of those who use them. For instance, a carpenter does not lose the art of cutting if his saw <note>original: "seca"</note> happens to be blunt; nor, if our happiness consisted in the craft of carpentry, would we consider the carpenter unhappy simply because he lacked a saw. 

Now, just as the soul has an instrument <note>the body</note>, so too the body has certain instruments through which it moves external things. A defect in these does not harm the healthy state of the body; likewise, the passions of the body do not pass into the soul. Therefore, even if death is an evil for the body, it is not an evil for the soul. If, then, the beauty of an action is in the soul, while an evil meanwhile occurs in something else, it has not yet been shown that the same thing is at once beautiful and evil. One may also distinguish by dialectical reasoning that one thing is something according to itself...

<summary>Proclus argues that the soul's ascent to divine beauty begins with sensory beauty but must move toward the beauty of virtue and intellect. He concludes that because the body is merely an instrument of the soul, physical "evils" like death or injury cannot diminish the soul's inherent virtue or happiness.</summary>

# PROCLUS ON
<page-num>472</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON</header>

...but the other is so by accident <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accidental" property is one that isn't essential to the thing itself. For example, a brave act is "beautiful" by its nature, but "unfortunate" only by the accident of the hero dying.</note>. For a brave action is beautiful in itself; yet it is bad, if it ever be called bad, only by accident: because it just so happens that the one acting bravely dies. Even if you wish to claim that death is among the number of evils, the brave duty is not bad according to its own nature of being brave. Therefore, that which is beautiful is also "bad" only in an accidental sense, while being brave is its true nature. That act is therefore beautiful, while the other aspect <note>referring to the death or loss</note> is the evil. It has been shown that a thing is never bad for the same reason that it is beautiful, but only by accident, on account of death.

Accordingly, he who separates the **Good** from the **Beautiful** ignores the very essence of man; he places one in one category and the other in another. He places the **Good** in the body, and the **Beautiful** in the actions of the soul. But in truth, man himself is the mind <note>original: *animus*</note>; he is an essence segregated from the body. Whatever is in the mind is both beautiful and good, even if some inconvenience to the body follows from it. For the body is not a part of the man, but his instrument. Indeed, an evil affecting the instrument does not belong to the user of that instrument.

### How these two differ: namely, "according to itself" and "as itself."

Phrases of this kind—namely, *according to itself* <note>original: *secundum seipsum*</note> and *as itself* <note>original: *qua ipsum*</note>—are distinguished even in the works of Aristotle. For that which belongs to something "according to itself" might not belong to it "primarily." 

<column-break/>

<page-num>473</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.</header>

But that which belongs to a thing "as itself," besides belonging to it "according to itself," also belongs to it primarily and is perfectly equal to it. 

If, therefore, the **Beautiful** is the cause of the soul's proportion <note>original: *commensuratio*; the harmonious balance of the soul's parts</note>, and for this reason is called beautiful—and if it ensures that the better part of the soul rules over the worse, and if it perfects us and purges the soul's deformity—then by this very reason, it is also the **Good**. It is not good by accident, but by the very reason that it is beautiful. For if it is proportioned insofar as it is beautiful, and it is good insofar as it is proportioned (for the **Good** is indeed a measure), then it certainly exists as the good insofar as it is beautiful.

Similarly, that which is **Ugly** <note>original: *turpe*; can also mean shameful or base</note> is evil insofar as it is ugly. For insofar as it is ugly, it is formless, undetermined, and disorganized; and by this very reason, it is evil. Therefore, insofar as it is ugly, it is certainly evil. 

Thus, the same thing is always both beautiful and good, and conversely, the same thing is equally ugly and evil. Keep this rule in mind, which Aristotle also used in his *Posterior Analytics*: if any two things are convertible <note>meaning they are interchangeable or logically equivalent</note>, then their opposites are also convertible. If, therefore, the **Beautiful** and the **Good** are convertible with each other, then their opposites—namely **Evil** and **Ugliness**—are likewise convertible with each other.

## SACRIFICE AND MAGIC.
### TRANSLATED BY MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'Q' containing a woodcut illustration of a figure, possibly a philosopher or scholar, seated in a study with books.</image-desc>
Just as lovers proceed by reason from the beauty that appears to the senses toward divine beauty little by little; so also the ancient priests, when they considered in natural things a certain kinship and sympathy <note>original: *compassionem*; in this context, it refers to a "shared resonance" or "feeling together" between objects, not modern pity.</note> of some things for others, and of manifest things to hidden powers, and found all things in all things, they established their sacred science. For they recognized the highest things in the lowest, and the lowest in the highest: in heaven, there are indeed earthly things according to their cause and in a celestial manner; on earth there are heavenly things, but in an earthly manner. For from where else do we think those plants move, which they name <term>heliotropes</term> <note>literally "sun-turners"</note>, that is, followers of the sun, toward the movement of the sun? Or the <term>selenotropes</term> <note>literally "moon-turners"</note>, that is, followers of the moon, which turn toward the moon? For indeed, all things pray and sing hymns to the leaders of their own order. But some do so in an intellectual way, others in a rational way, others in a natural way, and others in a sensory way. Therefore, the sun-follower, in whatever way

it can, moves toward the sun; and if someone were able to hear the pulsing made by it in the circling air, he would certainly perceive that through such a sound it makes a certain song composed for its king, in whatever way a plant is able. Because of this, one may look upon the sun and the moon on the earth, but according to an earthly quality. In heaven, however, one may see all the plants, and stones, and animals according to a celestial nature, possessing intellectual life. When the ancients contemplated these things, they applied certain earthly things to certain celestial ones, from which they drew down divine virtues into a lower place, on account of a certain likeness. For indeed, likeness itself is a sufficient cause for binding individual things to one another. For if someone heats hemp <note>original: *canabim*</note> or papyrus, and then brings it near a lamp, even if he does not touch it, he will see the hemp suddenly ignited, although it has not touched the fire; and he will see the ignition descend from above to the lower parts. What indeed shall I say of the **Lotus**? The lotus folds its leaves into itself before the rising of the sun; but when the sun rises, it unfolds them little by little. It seems to honor the sun by this dilation and contraction of its leaves no less than humans do with the gestures of their cheeks and the movement of their lips. Not only in plants, which have a trace of life, but even in stones one may behold an imitation and a certain participation in the higher lights: just as the **sunstone** <note>original: *helitis*</note> imitates the solar rays with its golden rays; while the stone called the **eye of heaven**, or the **eye of the sun**, has a shape similar to the pupil of an eye, and a ray flashes out from the middle of the pupil.
